content:
After 12+ years in sales, here are the 8 questions CFOs ask before every software purchase. (ngl they're brutal. but if you help your champ master them....whoa nellie)

And they def need the help... 99.999% of champions I've ever worked with eventually hit a moment of panic:
"What do I say when Finance starts asking the hard questions?"

👉 Most CFOs won't tell you what they're really thinking. They just kill your deal silently.

But I've spent 9 years watching Enterprise deals die in Finance. And I've learned what CFOs actually need to hear.

Here are the 8 questions every CFO is asking behind closed doors, courtesy of the "Only CFOs" newsletter, as highlighted by Nate Nasralla :

1. Why do we need [X product] now? We were fine before. 
2. What bucket does this fall into, and can you quantify it?
-----Improves efficiencies
-----Increases revenue
-----Mission critical (e.g. cybersecurity)
-----"Candy": nice-to-have tool that doesn't really fit into the above groups 
3. Is the spend in the budget? If not, how will you make up the difference? 
4. How does this tool tie into our company objectives for this year? 
5. What tools do we already have that do something similar? And if similar tools exist, why can't we use those? 
6. Implementation: What are the people / time requirements? 
7. Support costs: Will we need to upgrade soon to enterprise /other tier? 
8. Pricing:
-----If usage-based pricing: I want a detailed analysis on how pricing works and modeling for what our planned usage will look like.
-----If seat-based pricing: I don't want to buy a bunch of extra seats for planned growth. That got a lot of people in trouble when headcount growth halted and layoffs happened.

The deal-killers? Numbers 1, 3, and 5.

At Salesforce, I watched 6-7 figure deals die instantly when the champion couldn't answer those 3 questions clearly.

Which of these questions makes your Champions the most nervous?

content:
Every buyer is sitting in our meeting with 1 quiet question running in the background. And the answer almost always comes down to 1 of 6 emotional drivers.

Because the question is not "what's in it for the company." It's "What's in it for ME."

Here are the 6 emotional drivers (h/t to Geoffrey James for these):

Altruism - if I do this, I help my team.
Greed - if I move now, I get rewarded.
Fear - if I don't act, my career is at risk.
Envy - if I stall, my competitor wins.
Pride - if I do this, I look like a visionary.
Shame - if I don't, I look like I missed it.

Here's what that looks like IRL.

I had a champion at Tableau named Rick. He kept telling me the hours his team was working weren't sustainable.

I almost treated it as a throwaway comment. It wasn't. That was Altruism.

Rick wanted to be the person who protected his people.

So I stopped leading with platform features and started showing exactly how we'd cut his team's workload in half.

The deal didn't just close. It doubled in size during negotiations. (which is not the way it normally goes....)

Our job isn't to guess which emotion is driving the buyer. It's to listen for it.

The words are usually already there.

This is 1 of 3 lessons on why buyers actually move (and why "logical" deals stall). I broke all 3 down in a new video, including how to pair these emotions with the way each person makes decisions.

Full breakdown here: https://linktw.in/KpOtGU

Which of these 6 have you surprised you the most that they moved a deal?

A lot of your buyers overbought software in 2020 and got burned. Now you're the one paying for it.

In 12 years of selling, I've never seen it this hard to build pipeline.

What's stacked against us right now: 

-> Budgets are tight, so everyone wants a consolidation play 
-> They all want AI, but nobody wants to be the one who bought the wrong thing 
-> The SDR role that used to feed us is shrinking, so more of the number lands on the AE

Translation: build more pipeline, in the hardest market of your career, with fewer prospects willing to even pick up.

And here's the cruel part.

The tools that are supposed to help us build pipeline are quietly eating the hours we'd use to build it.

Every seller I coach has at least 27 tabs open. Some have 50+. CRM, data tool, LinkedIn, a spreadsheet, three Slack threads, the deck, and two they forgot were open.

Every time we switch tabs to research or build a list, our attention resets. That tax is brutal for enterprise reps, because enterprise deals get won in the deep work: the account plan, the champion strategy, the exec narrative. None of that happens in the 90 seconds between tab 14 and tab 15.

So here's the shift I'm watching the sharpest reps make.

They stop tab-hopping to do research. They ask their AI assistant, connected straight to their data, to pull it: 

-> Stay in one window 
-> Ask in plain English: "find CFOs at companies that fit my ICP and are showing intent" 
-> Get the list back already enriched, with titles, direct dials, and company info. No exporting, no copy-paste. 
-> Spend the time you just saved on the part only a human can do

When your manager says "we need more pipeline," the fix shouldn’t be "work more hours."

It's "stop burning us out on grunt work a machine can do in seconds." 😇

Fewer tabs = More selling.

content:
After 12+ years in sales, I've got good news for anyone who gets "Happy Ears" a lot. 
 
(btw, I spent the early years of my sales career battling that same thing) 
 
Luckily, a mentor shared their secret with me. 
 
 
Maybe you can use it to pressure test your Q2/Q3 deals....Here it is: 
 
3 Questions + 1 Rule for all Opportunities 
 
 
The Three Questions 
--> Why Anything 
--> Why Now 
--> Why Us 
 
 
The One Rule 
--> NONE of the answers can mention any of your product's features as the reason 
 
You can ONLY mention a product feature IF you know the outcome it creates or prevents. 
 
 
 *********** 
For a past deal this sounded like: 
 
--> WHY ANYTHING: Pipeline creation is strategic initiative #1 for Exec Buyer (RVP Sales) in 2026. They have an aggressive goal: 17% YoY increase 
 
--> WHY NOW: Can be implemented in under 60 days (feature), which means there's still time to impact Q3 pipe, and even Q3 revenue (impact). 
 
--> WHY US: RVP knows that her biggest competitor started with us last year & they are losing more deals than ever to this competitor. And the RVP's team has seen only 6% increase in ARR and 9% renewal churn. This is the data she's presenting to CFO as proof that 1) the strategy works & 2) there's a high risk of doing nothing. 

*********** 
 
 
If we can't answer the 3 Why's - with metrics 
 
We need to quickly dive deeper with Discovery - or move on 
 
If we show our pipeline some tough love now, we can prevent a lot of pain from Happy Ears in the future.

content:
I got ghosted a lot after Pricing meetings as a new AE. I made 3 big mistakes. Here's how I fixed them - 
 
 
Where I effed up (accidentally):
 
---> Going in blind 
---> Doing all the numbers myself 
---> Yes means nothing without HOW 
 
 
How I fixed it: 
 
---> Going in blind 
 
Presenting pricing to an Executive Sponsor without a Champion looking over the deck first was my 1st problem. 
 
I was going in blind at a crucial point in the deal. (Which also put my Champion at risk.) 
 
I learned to set up a pre-meeting with my Champion. 
 
This sounds like --> 
"Aaron, I'm working on the proposal for Angie. I want to make you look good. And make the best use of Angie's time. Can I send you what I've done so far, and put 15 minutes on your calendar Thursday morning at 9am for us to look at it together?" 
 
 
TL:DR --> No presentation without collaboration 
 
 
 
---> Doing all the numbers myself 
 
Every software company in the world has some sort of ROI tool. 
 
It was easy to plug all the numbers in myself. 
 
Don't repeat my mistake. 
 
 
Our champion - and ideally others from the buying committee- should collaborate on the business case. 
 
If you don’t get their input, they won't believe the numbers. 
 
Buyers need to know where the numbers came from anyway. They're the ones who have to defend them. 
 
And that will happen at an internal meeting you won't be invited to. 
 
 
Asking for an ROI session sounds like --> 
“We have a couple of internal resources to help you put together the business case. Most folks find them helpful because they don’t have to start from scratch. The first pass at this should take 15-20 minutes. How is 9 AM on Thursday?” 
 
 
TL:DR --> No calculation without collaboration 
 
 
 
---> Yes means nothing without HOW 
 
This stunningly-obvious-in-retrospect mantra is from Chris Voss, and fixed my longest running mistake. 
 
What often gets us ghosted after a pricing meeting is telling them how much it will cost in terms of dollars, but giving them no idea how much it will cost in terms of time. 
 
 
Every pricing meeting should include an overview of implementation. 
 
One slide for a small - midsize deal. 
 
For enterprise, the pricing meeting should include folks from implementation and CS. 
 
 
Up to this point, the buying committee has likely only seen people from sales. 
 
Helping Buyers put names and faces with those who will implement & support them is a way to lower risk. 
 
 
The sale may be 'the end' for the rep, but it's just the beginning for the customer. 
 
Clients need to feel secure about what happens in the next chapter of this adventure. 
 
Or they won't go. 
 
 
TL:DR --> No price presentation without implementation 
 
 
Hopefully this saves someone from making my same mistakes. 
 
What did I miss? Let's help some people close their Q2 deals!

content:
A seller I coach booked a meeting with an executive without sending a single follow-up. No "great connecting, let's find time." No chasing. 

The difference was a point of view.

For six months she's been building a real opinion on her industry. Not a pitch. Not talking points. An actual stance on where the space is heading and what the smart players should do about it.

So when she lands in front of executives, she's not angling for a reason to reach out later. She just shows up like a peer who sees their world clearly.

One of them booked time on the spot at a conference. She moved a relationship with a chief R&D officer forward in a LinkedIn DM. (Her note is below.)

Executives don't book meetings because we asked nicely. They book because we said something worth their time.

A point of view is the thing that gets the meeting.

If you want to start building yours:
   - Pick one shift happening in your buyers' world based on the conversations you've had so far this year. Then use your customer success stories (either from deals you've won, or from anecdotes from your team, or the testimonials on your website) to create a real-life POV on how you help. 
   - Pressure-test that POV with your leadership. Once you validate it, practice saying it out loud until you can do it without notes. And until you can write it in less than two sentences in an email. 
   - Then when you speak to your customers or send them a message, lead with the POV, not the product. The product is just how you back it up.

What's one opinion about your buyers' industry you'd be willing to defend in a room full of executives? 

And if you don't have one, now is the best time to start. You would be shocked (SHOCKED!) at how few sellers do this... and therefore how easy it is to differentiate yourself by putting in a little work. 😇

This is the thing we don’t talk about enough with top performers. We're not worried about missing quota. We're worried we're one-hit wonders. That we got lucky. That we can't repeat it in the next role, or even the next quarter:

"I've been in the top three every year, but I've never been number one."

A client said this to me last week, so I asked her what she thought was holding her back.

She said, "I don't have a system. So I feel like everything has to be customized. And it takes SO much time that it limits how many deals I can work."

And here's why the "one hit wonder" fear makes sense: there's this belief that every deal is a special snowflake. That what worked last time won't work this time. That we just have to figure it out fresh every single time.

The problem is we were never taught otherwise.

Companies teach us how to adhere to their selling process. They teach us nothing about aligning with a buying process. What we put in Salesforce is essentially so our leaders can forecast deals. It does not help us progress them.

So we hit quota, but we have no repeatable process. We close the big one, but we're not confident we could do it again. We look successful on the outside, while quietly terrified on the inside. (I've BEEN this person.)

This is the unlock: Having a repeatable system. Not a CRM stage. Not a forecast category. A framework we can follow no matter what deal we're in. A scaffolding.

Because the difference between top 3 and number 1 is knowing exactly what we did that worked, so we can do it again on purpose.

content:
⛔️Warning: Don't accept a position with a company “going upmarket” without asking these 5 questions. 
 
When I made the move, I didn’t know about these land mines... 
 
The company I joined was hugely successful. I thought going upmarket would be smooth. 
 
I was wrong. 
 
 
Here are 5️⃣ issues I wish I’d asked about: 
 
 
🎥 GOT ENTERPRISE STORIES? 
Most true ENT companies couldn’t care less about success in SMB/ Mid Market. United Airlines will not be impressed with our product's success in a company with 150 employees. 
 
--> Key qq: "What are the best stories about how ENT accounts have created success with this product?" 
 
 
🐏 HOW DO BATTERING RAMS GET PAID? 
Sellers in companies "going upmarket" spend 2-3 years educating the Enterprise about the product's existence. 
 
Since you’ll essentially be a battering ram trying to crack enterprise accounts, how will you get paid? 50/50 split? If so, don't count on making anything more than your base for 2-3 years. 
 
--> Key qq: "Show me the comp plan" 
 
 
📅 DO THE TIMELINES MATCH? 
I had a deal with a 19k person financial services org that took over 24 mos to close. 
 
That wasn't unusual in ENT. Most of the team didn't make quota for 2-3 years. 
 
--> Key qq: "Since you are going upmarket & it takes time to educate the Enterprise market, how will quotas be structured?" 
 
 
🧙🏻‍♂️ WHO ARE THE GURUS? 
Who are their advisors & sales leaders? I wrongly assumed our company was being advised by folks who had experience going upmarket. (ie qualified to give us directions because they had made the journey before.) 
 
Same with Enterprise leaders. Best if they *have made the upmarket journey before*. NOT just leaders who've always been with enterprise orgs. 
 
--> Key qq: "Can you walk me through who our top advisors are? Hiring philosophy for the ENT sales leaders?" 
 
 
👮🏼‍♀️ HOW GOOD ARE WE AT THE BIG 3? 
Security, Reporting & Governance - ENT handles these much differently than SMB. 
 
These 3 issues were why big deals took so long to close-if they closed at all. 
 
I and several of my peers lost 7 figure deals - even though there was pain, motivated Exec buyers & good multi-threading. The deals died because we didn't have one of the Big 3 that ENT orgs required. 
 
--> Key qq: "Can you walk me through how the product meets the Security, Reporting & Governance of ENT orgs? 
 
 
Real talk: Founders get overly confident when there's lots of traction in SMB & MM. 
 
They're convinced that the ENT will “fall in line “. Just deals with extra 0’s. 
 
⚠️NOT true 
 
 
Take it from someone who's been there & got the hoodie. 
 
Asking these questions can save a lot of❤️‍🩹 
 
What did I forget?

content:
In May 2021, I was so depressed I had trouble getting out of bed. For the 5th week in a row. 
 
Just moving enough to push the covers back, sit up & walk to the kitchen....it was almost too much effort. 
 

Once I was up, all I wanted to do was sit and stare at the wall. 
 
Not an exaggeration. I literally just wanted to sit and stare. 
 

To say this was "not like me" is an understatement. 
 
I've been a driven Type A since birth...."She's got a motor" is how one colleague described my work ethic. 
 
So, even though my brain felt foggy and slow, I realized this was deeply abnormal. 
 

Luckily I reached out to my doctor and started medication for depression the same week. 
 
I was amazed at how much better I felt in the next few weeks, even though it took several months to get the dosage exactly right. 
 

Depression and anxiety run in my family, but I had always been able to manage with coping skills. Journaling, yoga, exercise, etc. 
 
But after a huge loss in our family in 2021, coping skills weren't enough anymore. 

Looking back, I should have started medication months before I did. 
 

That's 1 of the BIGGEST things depression does - clouds your judgment. Including judgment about your own mental health. 
 
HINT: If you are wondering "am I depressed?", you probably are. Worth getting a professional opinion. ASAP. 
 
  
What I'm glad I did: 
--> therapy 
--> medication 
--> talking with friends & family (should have done this sooner)
 
 
What I wish I'd done: 
 --> seen a doctor faster
 --> used FMLA to rest & recover, instead of "pushing through"

What you can do:
—> take that one next step you’ve been thinking about
If you've been thinking about getting help, please don't wait. 

_______________________________
 
***ALSO...Sadly there is still a stigma within some families, cultures and religions around mental health. 

When I was growing up, many of my family members didn’t really believe that mental health was “a thing.” 

I was also raised in a fundamentalist Religious denomination where you were just supposed to pray about things. Without taking any other steps. That kind of thinking kept me trapped - for years.

_______________________________

It's been a long journey for me. Hopefully this helps some others get started on their own path.

repost.content:
DISCLAIMER: I run a tech company. So take this with the grain of salt if you want :)

But recent posts here reminded me, as someone who sees the "bills" every month, that many builders underestimate the cost by 5x-10x.

Not the build cost. 
The own-it-for-a-while cost. 
Building is 10%. Running and supporting is the unglamorous 90%. 

So here's a real-world checklist.
Every unchecked box is a cost, whether you build OR buy. This isn't a case for buying. It's a case for planning for the work.

PRODUCTION
[] Who's on-call at 3am?
[] What's our uptime SLA, and who signs it?
[] How do we catch bugs before users do?

SECURITY & COMPLIANCE
[] Who runs security forever, not just at launch?
[] SOC2, GDPR, HIPAA. Who owns each, and the audits?
[] Pen tests, vulnerability scans & patching, key rotation. On whose calendar?

THE STACK TAX
[] Every integration we build is one we maintain when the API breaks. Who's on it?
[] How do we evolve the data model without breaking customers?
[] Backward compatibility: today's feature is a future contract. Who holds that line?
[] Deploys, rollbacks, feature flags. Is our release pipeline managed?

PERFORMANCE & COST
[] Fast at 1K rows. Still fast at 1M?
[] Who watches the infra/token $$?
[] Who optimizes compute and storage every month/quarter?

DOCS & SUPPORT
[] User docs and internal docs. Who owns them in year 3?
[] When tickets come in, who answers?
[] Is helpdesk a side hustle or a real function?

PEOPLE
[] Can we hire and retain engineers as good as a vendor whose only job is this?
[] If developers leave, who takes over?
[] Is the knowledge written down, or in someone's head?

Sometimes building is right. When it's your edge, build it and own every box on this list with pride. When it's not, buy it.

Feel free to modify this checklist. It's yours 😎

content:
I walked away from the biggest deal of my career. Here's why that made me more money. And the 3 questions I learned to use.

First, the deal:  $13.7M. Would've blown my quota out of the water.

And the CEO had everything on paper:
→ A problem we could solve
→ He agreed the problem existed
→ Budget approved
→ Desperate to fix it

So we met.

And then we met again.

And again.

Five in-person meetings.

And every single one drifted the same direction.
He wanted to know how we built the product.
He asked about customization.
He floated "partnering" to develop features.
He asked about source code access.
Five meetings. Same questions. Every time.
Meeting five is when I finally let myself say what I'd been avoiding:
This isn't a buyer. This is a builder trapped in a buyer's process.
His energy peaked when we talked about his team's capabilities — not ours.
His questions were about architecture, not outcomes.
He didn't want to buy the solution.
He wanted to own it.
So I made the call that physically hurt.
I pulled it from my pipeline.

My manager: "Are you sure?"
My commission math: "But - "
My ego: "You're just giving up."

Here's what happened with the 30+ hours I got back that month:
→ Focused on a $1.8M deal that actually wanted to buy
→ Closed 3 others while he was still "evaluating"
→ Finished my best year ever

That CEO?
18 months later - was still building.
Still solving the same problem.

The time we spend convincing builders is time we could spend closing buyers.
And we can usually tell the difference early, if we're willing to look.

Three questions I ask now before any deal stays on my board:
1./ Do they ask about outcomes or architecture?
2./ Do they light up more about building or buying? 
3./ Is their real goal solving the problem — or owning the solution?

If the answers point to "builder," I'm out.
Doesn't matter what the number says.

The best deals aren't always the biggest ones.
They're the ones that actually close.

What's the largest deal you've walked away from - and what did it cost you to stay too long before you pulled the trigger?

content:
She'd been working a $300K deal at a healthcare system for months. And she was stuck. Here's why:

Strong champion on the technical side.

C-level decision maker who was interested, but still needed to say yes.

The problem?

Her technical champion couldn't explain the need (to non-technical leadership) in a way that landed.

So in our coaching call, we talked about the power of analogies.

The analogy she built?

A jar of marbles.

Green marbles = every new platform, service, or integration they'd added over the last 5 years.

Red marbles = every potential outage or patient-impacting experience that came with it.

Five years ago, the jar was small. Mostly green.

Today?

The jar is massive.

The red marbles have multiplied.

And every time they add a new service, they're reaching into that jar - and the odds of pulling a red marble go up.

She drew it in Paint.

Not Canva. Not a polished slide. Paint.

And I loved it.

Because it looked real.

Not a vendor deck.

A sketch that said: I thought about your world before this meeting.

She sent it with one page. What 9they'd need to measure success. Where they were vs. where they wanted to be.

And the technical champion went from struggling to explain the project... to confidently presenting it upward.

Your champion is not a salesperson.

They don't know how to take something complex and make it obvious to people who don't live in the details.

That's your job.

Give them the words.

Give them the analogy.

Give them the sketch - even if it's drawn in Paint.


When was the last time you built something specifically to help a champion sell internally?

content:
The hardest part of a discovery call isn't asking the right questions. It's not having to ask so many. 
Here's what I mean.

When a buyer walks into a call, they're already tired.

Tired of explaining who they are.

Tired of educating sellers on their world.

Tired of answering the same 10 questions from every AE they've met.

The reps who stand out show up with a point of view first.

Not "tell me about your biggest challenges."

More like:

"In this role, I talk to [persona] all day. And the biggest heartburn I hear about is usually A, B, or C.

What did I miss?"

(Not "did I miss anything." WHAT did I miss. Small difference. Signals a lot.)

Two things happen when you open this way:

--> They feel understood before you've asked a single question.

--> They correct you. And that correction is where the real discovery starts.

We don't need a 10-question interrogation.

We need them to feel like we get their world — so they'll let us into the real one.

content:
Here's how you can multi-thread without "going around" your Champion
(because ~67% of sellers avoid it ...they're afraid of stepping on their Champion's toes).

Here's the truth: Your Champion actually needs you to multi-thread.

And I learned exactly how to do it without going around them - straight from a VP of Sales who closed $47M in ARR last year.


Here are his 3 insights (and how to use them):

⭕ It's risky to be the champion for a big purchase
Your Champion put their neck on the line to get you in the door. They're using their social capital with every email they send about your solution.
The LAST thing they want? To look like they didn't do their homework.


⭕ 3 Power Levels of personas need to be in an evaluation to de-risk it
Champions are experts at how to do their jobs - not how to buy our thing. They appreciate it when we guide them.

Try this: "Typically when folks evaluate XYZ, leaders from Legal Operations, Finance, and HR all get involved. Would it make sense to include Shonda, your VP of HR, and Christina, your VP of Finance in our next conversation?"

You're not going around them. You're protecting them.


⭕ We should communicate differently to each of the 3 levels Power Levels 
 Each persona cares about different things:

✅ Executives: Does this help us reach goals and/or lower our risk?
✅ Managers: Does this help my team with a metric that matters?
✅ End users: Does this help me do my job easier/faster/better?

EXAMPLE: Here's what a meeting recap email sounds like for a CFO or VP of Finance:

"Anna, I met with your Legal Ops team today about hard savings from workflow automation.

- They quantified $3.6MM in savings / year
 - And they identified these savings will be immediate, as IT involvement isn't needed

You should have the invite for our next meeting on the 28th. Will send you the readout afterward.
Cheers"

Notice what's missing? Any mention of product features. Or even our product's name.

Just quantified impact, timeline, and specific ROI. In a format they can read on their phone without scrolling.

_________________

The bottom line:

When we know how to help our Champions navigate the buying process, everyone wins... literally.

As always - it's about them, not about us/our stuff.

_________________

What's something that seems counterintuitive that you've found works for multi-threading?

content:
Cost of inaction got a rep to President's Club. But if we'd used it 2 months earlier, it would have killed the deal. Cost of inaction only works after 3 things are true:

1. They've agreed they have a problem worth solving.

If we quantify the cost of inaction before they've bought into the problem, we look irrelevant. They're not ready to hear it.

2. We have a real champion, not just a coach.

A champion has influence, has something to gain personally or professionally, and wants us to win. Not just "someone who takes our calls."

Champions tell us which metrics actually move the needle internally.

3. We've validated pricing with that champion first.

To quantify the cost of doing nothing, we have to know the cost of doing something. If pricing hasn't been discussed, the comparison falls flat.

One more thing:

Never surprise leadership with COI before your champion sees it.

An old boss told me: Kindergartners like surprises. Executives do not.

Build it with your champion. Let them shape it. Then they become the one presenting your math internally, not you.

Cost of inaction is powerful. But timing is everything.

Here are 10 ways to talk about procurement without losing momentum.

1.)  “What do you need from me to make Procurement boring?”

5.) “When this goes to Procurement, what’s their default move?”

6.) “If deals get stuck in Legal, where do they usually get stuck?”

7.) “Who has authority to approve exceptions?”

8.) “If this needs to be live by [date], what’s the latest we can sign and still hit that?”

9.) “What’s the vendor setup step that slows things down for you? (W-9, insurance, security questionnaire, vendor portal, etc.)”

10.) “Can we do a quick 15-minute ‘path to paper’ call and map the exact steps + owners?”

Most enterprise deals don’t push, slip or die because the buyer doesn’t want it.

They go sideways because the process shows up late and eats the calendar.

We've all had this happen. Slammed in Q1. Pipeline looking strong. Then Q2 hits and it's... quiet.

Not because we didn't work hard.

Not because we weren't talented.

Because Q1 success is great at hiding a rhythm problem.

Here's what I mean.


When we're busy closing, prospecting feels optional.

When we're on a roll, it's easy to coast.

When the pipeline is full, it's hard to imagine it won't always be.

And then it isn't.


We call this a pipeline problem.

But the pipeline is almost never the actual problem.

The problem is that prospecting only happened when there was room for it.
That's surge selling.

And surge selling gives us the same result every single time — regardless of talent:
Great quarter.
Quiet quarter.
Panic quarter.


The fix isn't more activity.

It's building a rhythm that runs whether we're slammed or not.

The sellers I know who avoid this cycle don't prospect more than everyone else.

They just never stop.

I used to think I was working my deals every week. Then I paid attention to what I was actually doing. Most of it looked like this:

→ Updated close dates

→ Logged call notes

→ Moved a stage

→ Sent a meeting recap

→ Chased the calendar invite

All of it took time.

None of it moved a deal forward.

Because there's a difference between admin work and actual deal progression.

And most of us are doing one and calling it the other.

Admin work keeps your CRM clean and your manager off your back.

Deal progression answers the questions your buyer is asking between your meetings - the ones they'll never say out loud.

Admin looks like:

→ Logging a note

→ Updating a stage

→ Scheduling the next call

Progression looks like:

→ Figuring out what the economic buyer needs to know before they can say yes

→ Sending the thing that removes a concern before they have to voice it

→ Building the 1-pager your champion can actually use internally

Admin requires a screen and a login.

Progression requires thinking.

And thinking requires protected time - which most of us don't have because we've scheduled ourselves into back-to-back calls until 5pm.

By the time we sit down to "work on deals," we have nothing left.

So we update stages instead.

And wonder why the pipeline isn't moving.

What would change about your pipeline if you blocked 3 hours a week specifically to think about what each deal needs before it needs you?

content:
The hardest part of the 1st year in an ENT role isn't the learning curve. It's the "Valley of Despair." 

I went through it at Salesforce, Outreach and Tableau.

And I've seen it in almost every AE I've coached in their first 6 months in a new enterprise seat.

It's doing all the right things and having nothing to show for it yet.

You're building the pipeline.

You're multi-threading.

You're running discovery the right way.

You're sending the follow-ups, making the asks, doing the research.

But every QBR, you have to sell the story of what's coming instead of pointing to what's closed.

And when someone asks how it's going, you say: "Great - lots in the works."

Because it's true.

But on the board, we're still sitting at $0.

So we plunge into the "Valley of Despair".

Because you've made the investment, you're doing the work, and the results just haven't caught up to the effort yet.

It happens in a new role.

It happens the first year of a new territory.

And it happens outside of sales - like at the gym.

The folks who get through it hold 2 things at the same time:

→ Trust that the right actions compound - even when you can't see it yet.

→ Honest clarity on whether those actions are actually right - or if something needs to adjust.

Both of which are bolstered by regularly checking in with other top performers, mentors, coaches, and sales leaders.

Just like a trainer at the gym, they can validate the approach, talk about others who've been there before, and encourage us not to give up. 

Because the worst thing to do in the Valley is hustle harder on the wrong things.

The second worst thing is give up on the right things because the results haven't arrived on your timeline.

I know this because I've been in the Valley myself.

And because I've watched reps come out the other side of it - usually faster than they expected - once they stopped letting the scoreboard tell them whether to believe what they were doing.

If you've been here before... what was the one thing you held on to that let you  trust the process long enough to see it work?

Here's what most sales training gets wrong:

We hand people call scripts and demo decks and talk tracks. We say "use these exact words." In some orgs, you have to "certify" on the decks.

And then sellers get on a call and it sounds like they're reading from a teleprompter. The buyer can feel it. And the seller can feel that the buyer can feel it.

So they stop using it. And now the training was a waste.

My approach is different. I don't care if you use my exact words. I care about the principle underneath them.

So in coaching, we start with principles.

This is what we're trying to accomplish.

Now - how would YOU say it so it sounds normal coming out of your mouth?

Because a discovery framework that sounds robotic will not get used. A multi-threading approach that feels forced will get abandoned after two calls. A closing technique that doesn't match your personality will make you sound like every other seller your buyer talked to this week.

The best sellers I've worked with don't sound like their coach. (Or anyone else.) They sound like themselves - with better structure underneath.

It's like music. I work with a platform that sells to big acts - Tim McGraw-level artists. And their sales team had to learn the same principles every seller learns. But they had to say it in a way that felt natural to musicians and managers.

Same principles. Completely different language.

That's the work. Not memorizing what to say. Figuring out how to say it so it's yours.

When was the last time you abandoned a sales technique because it didn't feel like you? (For instance, the photo is how I respond when told to use a boring "About Us" slide.  Ummm no.)

"What if I step on my champion's toes by going around them?" I hear this constantly. EVERY rep worries about this. And ... my first question back is always: are we sure this person is a champion - or are they a contact?

Taking a demo with you does not make someone a champion.

Neither does:

--> Being nice on every call

--> Saying "this looks really interesting"

--> Introducing you to one other person

--> Telling you they're excited about it

A champion does things that cost them something.

They advocate for you when you're not in the room.

They surface the real decision process.

They bring you into meetings you didn't have access to.

They mobilize people - not just support you.

The difference matters enormously.

Because if we're treating a contact like a champion:

--> We protect a relationship that isn't doing any real work.

--> We don't multi-thread because we think we don't need to.

--> We rely on one person who can't actually get us to yes.

And we feel the difference in Q3, when the deal that "looked great" in Q1 is still in stage 3.

Single-threaded deals don't stall because of bad luck.

They stall because we confused being liked with being championed.

content:
A mentor told me something years ago that I still use almost every week. "Real deals aren't fragile." She said it when I was scared to make a move. Here's what happened.

I had a late-stage deal going nowhere.

My contact was engaged. Progress felt real. But nobody at power had been involved.

So I drafted an email and asked my boss to send it directly to their CEO.

He did.

Two hours later, my contact emailed me.

Upset.

"Someone from your company reached out to our CEO. He wasn't expecting that."

I panicked for about 10 seconds.

Then I said:

"That sounds like it came as a surprise. I get it. And... I don't always have full control over what my boss does, just like you probably don't always control what yours does either."  (smiling, light tone = crucial on this one)

He was still ruffled.

And yet...three weeks later, I was on-site.

Three months later, we closed.

Because the deal was real.

It could handle a bump.

I think about this every time a rep tells me they're afraid to multi-thread, or to push for an executive intro, or to do something that might "rock the boat."

Real deals don't fall apart over one email.

Shaky ones do.

And honestly?

Better to find out now.

content:
Ever walk into a conference and immediately regret every life choice that led you there? Here are 6 things that helped me.

Confession: As an introvert, I used to DREAD conferences. Standing alone, clutching lukewarm coffee, desperately hoping the earth would swallow me whole.

After ~2 years, I realized I was just doing it wrong.


Recently coached a seller heading to her first treasury conference and dreading it. 

Here's the exact 6 things I told her (that transformed how I approach conferences):


1/ Figure out WHO will actually be there
Most conference websites are marketing fluff. Dig deeper:
→ Check speaker titles (reveals attendee seniority)
→ Look for "free tickets to treasury managers" (tells you the audience)
→ Notice if sessions are Strategies vs. How-To's (execs attend the former)

We discovered speakers included retired CFOs and VPs of Treasury. Real decision-makers, not just end users.


2/ Create your "value-first" conversation toolkit
Nothing kills networking faster than forced small talk. Come armed with value:
→ 2 podcast recommendations per persona
→ Names of a few thought leaders + recent news
→ Customer success stories for common challenges

Now instead of awkward silence, she can say: "Just discovered this Treasury podcast by Eleanor Hill on AI implementation. Have you checked it out?"


3/ Stack rank your target accounts
You can't remember 100 accounts while speed-networking. Create a mobile list of:
→ Top 20 "dream" accounts likely to attend
→ Specific folks you want to meet

When you see name badges, you can quickly check priority level.


4/ Focus on executive-level sessions
Skip the technical "how-to" sessions. You're not there to learn the job - you're there to understand the people who do it.

Must-attend sessions:
→ Anything with "CFO" or "VP Treasury" speakers
→ Business problems your software solves
→ AI and future of treasury discussions

These teach you their vocabulary, priorities, and fears.


5/ Master the art of non-salesy follow-up
Instead of collecting LI profiles for follow-up, create reasons for valuable 2nd conversations:

"Based on your challenges, I'd love to introduce you to [customer exec] who recently solved something similar. What's the best way to connect you two?"

They give contact info because they WANT you to follow up.


6/ Set a clear success metric
My client's goal: 10 quality conversations. Not leads. Not demos. Just 10 genuine exchanges where she learned something valuable or provided value.

This removes the desperate "I need to sell something" energy that repels prospects.


Bottom line: Conferences are about showing up with purpose and a plan.

When you know exactly who to meet, what value to provide, and how to follow up meaningfully... suddenly conferences transform from anxiety-inducing nightmares into pipeline accelerators.

Challenger says 97% of their clients ask for extra help with this skill. More than any other they teach. And it's the least talked about.

What is it? 

"Constructive Tension"

And it boosts win rates by 28%.


Candidly, it's effing hard to do. Because we have to: 

 --> challenge the Buyer's thinking, ie highlight a misunderstood problem, probe an underappreciated pain point or question their process
 --> explore assumptions and dig for answers... empathetically
 --> steer the conversation without being aggressive


Typically, we think of this as asking hard/uncomfy questions in Discovery.

But it's also super effective in qualifying mid-late stage deals.


Here's what that sounds like IRL:

 --> "Can you walk me through each step of how this project could get a June signature, so we can start set up & training in July?"

 --> "Typically we see customers getting a purchase done fastest when the IT teams meet about integrations at the same InfoSec does security reviews. Any reason this wouldn't work for your teams?"

 --> "Could we schedule a call between our Legal departments instead of waiting for the 2nd set of redlines?"


When we do this *empathetically* - in the spirit of teaching Champions how to buy - this can be one of the biggest value adds.

It helps champions move faster and waste less time. Because Champions are experts in how to do their jobs, not how to buy our stuff.

content:
There are 3 things I did differently to get hired by 3 multi-billion dollar tech companies. 3 specific things to stand out in the 1st interview. And the last one is the most important. 
 
 
--> I came with a Point of View 
Based on things like the specifics of the job description, their headcount growth on LinkedIn, their reps' quota attainment & company news. 
 
This sounds like: 
 
"Taylor, I'm excited to be talking with you about this opening today. It looks like your org announced earlier this year they're focused on moving upmarket & just launched an enterprise-level product. 
 
I think that probably means you're looking for AEs with prior Enterprise experience. And who are used to hunting/prospecting for new logos. 
 
That's what many companies in your position seem to be prioritizing, but what did I miss that you're focused on?" 
 
 
--> I researched 1 specific on the recruiter 
I always wrote down the first & last name of who was doing the phone screen. And did both LinkedIn & Google searches on them. 
 
I looked for 1 thing we had in common - college major, past company, volunteer interests 
 
Or 1 interesting fact - unique career path, unusual skill, or non-traditional background. 
 
People LOVE to talk about themselves. (Everyone's favorite subject.) 
 
When we kick off the interview with a question that shows we did deep research, it shows we're prepared AND we make them feel good. Win/win. 
 
"Taylor, I was doing my homework on LinkedIn and saw you majored in music. (I may have even watched a couple of YouTube videos to see your guitar solos.) 
 
There has to be a good story on how you went from music to recruiting? [Let them tell the story.] 
 
I'm so encouraged that XYZ company seems to be looking for the right people - rather than just checking boxes." 
 
 
--> I asked the same 3 questions at the end of the call. 
 
Almost every recruiter ends the phone screen interviews by asking "What questions do you have for me?" 
 
This is not the time to go deep. They've only scheduled this for 15-30 min, and it will irritate them if you make them late. (Plus the hiring manager will have specifics anyway.) 
 
I asked these every time: 
 
 -->"Taylor, I'm intrigued by what caught your attention about this company. What made you want to work here?" Gets them talking about their favorite subject again. 
 
 --> "Sounds like a great place to be! And also, no place is perfect. If you could wave a magic wand & fix 1 thing about this place, curious what it would be?" This is where you start to ID red flags. 
 
 --> "One last thing: what's the best thing about working here?" Ends the call on a positive & back on their fav subject. 
 
 
 
Forbes says 98% of people fail the interview. 😱 
 
But a little prep can put us in that other 2%.

"If we don't find him a foster by 5pm, the shelter is out of time."
That's how Chico ended up at our house.

He came home so skinny you could count every rib. Flinched if anyone moved in his peripheral vision. Wouldn't take food from my hand for the first two days.

That was 12 weeks ago. Swipe to see him now.  

Here's the full story: Adobe Acrobat reached out as part of their Small Business Month initiative. They're giving Acrobat licenses, mentorship sessions, and hands-on tools to small businesses and non-profits.

They  asked me to choose one that matters to me and spotlight them. For me, picking Forget Me Not Rescue in Dallas, the one that saved Chico, was a no-brainer.

Thanks to Adobe, Forget Me Not is getting a free 12-month Adobe Acrobat license, a one-on-one session with me, and access to a live Adobe Acrobat tips session hosted by their product Evangelist. Real tools, not just a shoutout.

While we've been getting Chico healthy, I've been getting a crash course in how rescues actually run.

Rescues operate like underfunded startups. Volunteers stretched thin - most doing this on top of full-time jobs. Donations earmarked for vet bills, not software. Every minute spent on paperwork is a minute not spent finding a dog a home.


Here are 3 things I’m encouraging, Forget Me Not (and all small operations to do with Adobe Acrobat):

1/ Build the form once. Make it look like you have a whole design team. Acrobat comes with Adobe Express built in - professionally designed templates for flyers, social posts, infographics, intake forms, whatever you need. Pick a template, swap in your colors and logo, done. No design experience needed, no hiring a freelancer. For a rescue that needs adoption event flyers, surrender packets, and social posts on a shoestring budget, that's a game changer.

2/ Skip the printer. Acrobat's e-signatures work on a phone at an adoption event. No "I'll bring it back next weekend." Signed. Done. Moving on.

3/ Tell AI Assistant what you need. "Convert this to a Word doc." "Delete page 2." "Redact the address on page 3." Acrobat's AI Assistant handles it in one step - no menu-hunting, no learning curve. For a rescue handling sensitive surrender forms, vet records, and payment info, that's not a nice-to-have.


Small operations can't out-staff bigger ones. But they can out-system them.
And honestly?

I can't think of a better use of technology than giving the people doing this work - on nights and weekends, out of their own pockets, with no one watching - a few hours back to spend on what actually matters.
More dogs like Chico, finding homes.

Grateful to Adobe for celebrating Small Business Month all of May by putting real tools in the hands of small businesses and nonprofits across the country. Glad to be part of it.

content:
Can we please talk about the politics around pipeline? 🤫 And if you think there are no politics here ...oh honey... bless your heart

Nobody tells you this when you start, btw.

Your manager won't pull you aside on day one & explain the unwritten rules around pipeline management.

But here's the thing: how you handle pipeline affects your relationship with your manager AND their boss.

Think of pipeline like navigating through unfamiliar territory. There are roads that are safe, and routes that will get you pulled over. But nobody gave you the map.

So let me draw you one. Including both the Philosophy & Politics of each.


There are 3 main areas where your manager is measured on pipeline:

1) Creating Pipeline
-->Philosophy: When does an opportunity actually count?
Different orgs have wildly different views.
At Salesforce, we had Stage 0 deals - "Aspirational pipe." Meaning they had a problem we could solve & we were actively working it.

For ENT reps, this approach makes sense. Helps execs align resources early.

Other teams? "Qualified deals only." Meaning real interest after a demo.

-->Politics: AE-created pipe & CYA
a) AE vs SDR created opps - In some orgs, there's massive pressure to show AE-sourced pipeline. This affects your relationship with the SDR team AND how your manager looks to leadership.

b) CYA piping - Some managers will ask you to add questionable deals just to show coverage. "Put it in so we look good."

2) Moving Deals Through
-->Philosophy: Deal velocity

-->Politics: Also deal velocity (but with more scrutiny)
Your manager is measured on how many deals sit in each stage & how long they stay there.

The bigger the deal, the more eyes on it.

3) Taking Deals Out of Pipeline
-->Philosophy: Forecasting accuracy

-->Politics: CYA (again)
Some managers aren't going to like this one, but I wish someone explained it to me years ago.

With forecasting, sometimes you have to weigh YOUR internal standing against your manager's.

In healthy relationships, you collaborate on this. But sometimes you'll get pressure to leave a dead deal in your pipe because your manager needs the coverage.

**Real talk: Proceed with caution. Understand how much relational capital you have vs your manager vs their boss. And how forecasting accuracy will affect each of you.

______________

How to navigate this:

Ask your manager early: "Different leaders view pipeline differently. I want to make our team look good and make sure we're aligned. How are you thinking about when Opps should be entered? Moved to next stage? Taken out of pipe?"
______________

Important callout ➡️ You may not agree with the politics. I've fundamentally disagreed with the approach at several places I've worked.
But it's still critical to understand how pipeline works at your org.

Would love to hear from sales leaders: What else should reps understand about pipeline politics?

📸: Zora... who has no time for politics

In 2023, I sat in a New York conference room and heard an AE say he never shares what's working with his team.

I thought I misheard him.


Then he doubled down: "Why would I share my secrets?"

I asked if they had open territories. Nope. All named accounts.

(Meaning his success literally can't take anything away from other AEs' success.)

I wouldn't be where I am without sellers who believed the exact opposite.

Scarcity mindset sellers protect their "secrets" and plateau at 100%.

Abundance mindset sellers share everything and blow past 150%.

- Clarify your own thinking

content:
It's still pretty easy to hurt my feelings.

We have this idea in sales that resilience means things bounce off you. That you get a "no" and you just shrug. That rejection is just part of the game and the best sellers don't feel it.

That's not how it works.

The best sellers I know - the ones who've been at the top for years - they all feel it. Every lost deal. Every ghosted follow-up. Every "we decided to go another direction."

It stings. Every time.

The difference isn't that it doesn't hurt. The difference is what we do next.

It's kind of like being an athlete. Your ankle hurts today. Okay. Yeah, it hurts. And we keep moving forward.

It's not a personality trait. It's a decision. A daily one.

So if we're going to be honest about what sales actually is - it's a profession where we put half our paycheck on the line based on our performance. No one in accounting does that. No one in marketing does that. No one in product does that.

And then we wonder why sellers struggle with confidence.

Maybe we should stop pretending it's easy and start being honest about the fact that it's hard - and we choose to do it anyway.


PS - If you've seen my newsletter, you know my signoff is “You can’t hurt my feelings, I’m in sales, babe, LOL”...that's the resolve talking. The daily decision.  It really should be "You can actually hurt my feelings. But I'm in sales so Imma keep going anyway"... but let's be honest, that's too long and just not as catchy  ;)

content:
Here are 10 ways to ask about budget without making it weird. ("Asking a hard thing in a soft way": budget edition.)

1.) “Before we go too far… is there a number already attached to this initiative?” (Simple. Neutral. No pressure.)

2.) “When you say ‘approved’… approved for what range?” (Forces clarity without sounding like you’re pushing.)

3.) “Do you have budget set aside, or do we need to build a business case to unlock it?” (This respects reality. And it tells you what motion you’re in.)

4.) “What have you typically invested in solving problems like this?” (Asks for precedent, not their wallet.)

5.) “If we land on the right solution, is budget the constraint… or is it prioritization?” (This is the nicest way to ask: do you want it?)

6.) “What would make this an ‘easy yes’ financially… and what would make it a ‘hard no’?” (Gives you boundaries fast.)

7.) “Would it be fair to bracket this?” Then give 2 ranges: “Are we talking closer to $25–50k… or $150–300k?” (They can correct you without feeling pinned.)

8.) “Who else has to sign off on spend like this?” (Not budget, but it’s budget. And it surfaces procurement early.)

9.) “What’s competing for the same dollars right now?” (Shows you’re thinking like them, not like a seller.)

10.) “If we solve this, where does the money come from?” Budget bucket, headcount, tool consolidation, churn reduction… you learn what they believe.

If you want the even softer opener, steal this line:

“Ok if I ask an uncomfortable question so we don’t waste each other’s time…”

What’s your go-to way to ask budget without spooking the room?

content:
Every seller I know either wants to get into a big company or get out of one.

When they ask me for my advice on which path to take, I say:

"What's your tolerance, and which tradeoffs can you actually live with?

Big companies give us process, structure, a recognizable name, and genuinely good benefits.

But they also give us deal desk queues that take a week to quote a $700K deal. Approval chains that go 3 levels deep before we can do anything creative. And the feeling of being employee number 86,941.

Startups give us autonomy, variety, and the chance to actually shape something. We wear a lot of hats. We move fast.

But we also absorb a high level of chaos. In the super early stage companies we get no inbound. No brand recognition. No one warming our prospects up before we get on the call.

Neither is easier. Neither is better.

I figured out big companies weren't for me when I realized I'd rather deal with moderate chaos than with the bureaucracy of a company that size. That's not a knock on big companies. It's just self-knowledge.

The sellers who struggle most are the ones who took the job because of the logo without asking what they were actually signing up for.

content:
Every deal I've ever lost in enterprise had the same thing in common.

It didn't die at the end. It died in the middle - during the part where most of us go quiet.

We have a great first call. Discovery goes well. The champion is excited. And then we hear "we'll follow up next week" three times in a row and wonder why the deal stalled.

Here's how I think about keeping momentum through the messy middle:

1. Every call ends with a joint action plan.

Not "I'll follow up next week." That's not a plan.

A real next step looks like: here's what I'm doing, here's what the Champion is doing, and here's when we reconnect. Both sides have things to do.

If only we have action items, we're the only ones invested.

2. Send something useful between meetings that they didn't ask for.

A buying guide with evaluation questions. A framework for how to pitch this internally. Prep for what their CFO will ask.

We're not just staying top of mind - we're making our champion's job easier.

That's the difference between following up and actually enabling them to sell for us when we're not in the room.

3. Create micro-deadlines that serve their timeline, not ours.

"If we can get the security review kicked off by Thursday, we stay on track for you to implement in March and see impact by May. Before your next board meeting."

Not "we need this by Friday to hit our number." They don't care about our number. They care about their timeline.

So we tie every deadline to what matters to them.

4. Multi-thread before we need to.

The worst time to meet the economic buyer is when the deal is on the line. The best time is when everything is going well and the introduction feels natural.

If we wait until we need executive support to ask for it, we've already lost leverage. We should be building those relationships when there's zero pressure.

And the last one is the most important...

5. Ask the uncomfy question early.

"What would cause this to stall or die?"

If we ask this in meeting two, we have time to solve it. If we ask it in meeting eight, we're doing triage.

Most of us avoid this question because we don't want to plant doubt. But the doubt is already there. We're just choosing not to surface it.

Momentum isn't something that happens to us. It's something we build - deliberately - call by call, action by action.

Our Friday meeting question last week: "What's a moment in your life that shaped how you work today?" I was not prepared for those answers.

I have 3 women on my team. From Syria, the Philippines, and the US.

3 countries. 3 completely different life experiences. A few months of working together.

And somehow it already feels like something I didn't expect to build this fast.


Every week, Rue - our marketing coordinator - opens our Friday meeting with a connection question. Not "what's on your plate." Something real.

"What's something you're proud of that most people don't know about you?"

"What's giving you energy right now — and what do you need more of?"

The answers stop me every single time.


These women are proud. Not in a loud way. In a quiet, earned way.

Proud to be doing meaningful work. Proud to be providing for their families.

Proud of where they came from and what they've built.


I would never have known any of that if we'd stuck to status updates.

But we are MORE than our jobs. MORE than our number.


It's easy to lose sight of that when the calendar fills up and the to-do list never ends.

But when you build connection intentionally into your culture, 1 + 1 + 1 stops equaling 3.

It starts equaling 10.


To Rue and Joy - thank you for showing up as your full selves. It makes me want to do the same.

content:
3 hidden risks to our deals: focusing too much on execs, missing the real decision-makers & making it hard/complicated to buy. Here are 3 things to focus on instead-

 - Reduce complexity to speed up deals
 - Identify the Mobilizers who drive change
 - Work with all 3 power levels to lower buyer risk

Easy enough to say WHAT to do.

I found out HOW to do these the hard way. Here's what I learned - maybe it will save you some time...

---> Reducing complexity to speed up deals

Time kills deals. And complexity makes everything take longer.

Top 2 ways I've seen reps make things easer:

1/ "Making sense" selling - Coming with POVs & value adds to help Buyers make good decisions 

2/ Teaching Buyers How to Buy - ending every call with "Typically what comes next is..." to prescribe next steps.
 

---> Working with all 3 power levels to lower buyer risk

Executives are important to a deal, but they won't make decisions in a vacuum. So if you ONLY focus on execs, your deal is at risk....

Because it is RISKY to be a buyer. If their name is attached to a huge purchase that fails, their job is on the line.

So execs lean on Managers, technical experts/IT and end users in evaluations.

THIS is why multi-threaded deals have a 5X win rate (!!!)

The top reps I've talked with know they have to work at all 3 power levels - and communicate WIIFM to each - 

1/ Executive
2/ Managers
3/ End Users

---> Identifying the (often hidden) Mobilizers who drive change

Sellers who target "Mobilizers" are 31% more likely to be high performers.
(Challenger data)

Top-performers spend their time focused on the 3 who are the best at building consensus & creating change (the Mobilizers): ​
​The Go-Getter
The Skeptic*
The Teacher ​

​*The Skeptic pushes back on the idea because they’re exploring it thoughtfully. 

IMPACT of these 3 Actions (Challenger data):
---> Closed 26% more deals
---> Brought in 27% more revenue
---> Shortened sales cycles by ~1 mo

I don't know about you, but I will do just about anything that brings me more deals + more revenue + shorter cycles.
(gotta be legal and ethical of course. sad to have to have the disclaimer but we've all seen things...)

content:
Here's the story of how I spent $14.88 to get a $702k deal unstuck.

After 9 months of working closely with my Champion, she said she was ready to sign. But then she went dark. 

What I didn't understand yet: She wasn't ghosting me. She was paralyzed by risk.

I tried calling & emailing with reminders of
--> The problems she was solving for
--> How our solution 'ticked all the boxes'
--> The ROI and business case we collaborated on

Nothing.

In desperation, I went for a walk and put myself in her shoes. What would I be worried about in her position?

I realized we'd done a lot of work around how our solution could solve many of her problems.

We'd done a lot LESS talking about how to ensure her org would adopt our solution.

So here's what I did:

I bought the book "Switch: How to Change When Change is Hard" for $14.88 on Amazon.

Before sending it, I highlighted specific sections about leading organizational change and reducing resistance.

I included a note: "Thought this might help as you roll this out. The highlighted parts reminded me of our conversations."

Two days after it was delivered, she called. Her team formed a "book club" to apply the lessons book inside their whole department.

Two months later, the deal closed.

Why did this work?

The authors of "The Challenger Sale" explain: The status quo isn't considered one person's fault. But if somebody says, "Hey, we should do this enterprise-wide thing..." now the solution is attached to their name.

It's a lot of risk for our Champions.

Buyers are experts in how to do their jobs. They are NOT experts in:
--> How to buy our stuff
--> Change management
--> Driving organizational adoption

My $14.88 investment showed I understood her real fear: What happens AFTER the purchase.

Now when deals stall near the finish line, I ask myself: Is it about price/features? 

Or is my champion feeling that weight of risk?

What's your best move to help champions with the fear of "What Happens After We Sign"?

content:
"Sales Reps, don't introduce your Sales Engineer as your "technical expert." 
 
It's not good for you, them, or the prospect." 
 
oof... guilty as charged. When I saw this post by Rew Dickinson , I wished I could re-do all those intros I did in demos. :( 
 
He's got a better way... here's the full post. (And sellers, give him a follow!) 
 
--- 
 
This is how I see AEs introduce SEs most often: 
 
AE: "This is Rew, my Solutions Engineer. He can answer all of your technical questions and show you how the software works." 
 
This may be true, but it's not the best intro. It's not the Sales Reps' fault either. SEs should tell their Sales Reps how they would like to be introduced. 
 
--- 
 
Here's a better option: 
 
AE: "For this meeting, I was able to get one of our Solutions Engineers, Rew, to join us. He has a great deal of expertise working with our clients and is basically here to offer free advisory and solutions expertise as you are going through this decision-making process. I've given Rew some of the background on your business already, and he may jump in with some more questions to better understand your needs." 
 
--- 
 
Notice the difference?? 
 
The first introduction paints the SE almost like a human instruction manual on all of the software's features/technicalities. It puts the SE in a position where they have to wait until the prospect has a question before speaking. Then, they become reactive, which is exactly what you don't want them to be. 
 
The second introduction, however, paints the SE as a guide that the client can trust and puts the SE in the position of being a client leader. Which is exactly where you want them to be. 
 
--- 
 
Now it's your turn. 
 
How do you introduce your SE? Drop your scripts below.

content:
Some sales leaders don't want me to tell you this. But after 15 years in sales and coaching 300+ AEs, I'm going to say it anyway:

Sometimes the territory is the problem. Not your effort.

And I say that as someone who's turned around dead territories and made them profitable. 

AND also as someone finished quarters at 30% despite being the #1 rep for activity. (I was selling high-tech solutions to pool contractors and steel manufacturers. Not kidding. But that's a whole different post.)

The "More Activity" Myth
When leadership says "just make more calls," they're avoiding the real conversation.

I was leading the team in emails, calls, and activities in ** both ** situations. The math didn't work because the fundamentals were broken.

There are 3 ingredients to sales success:
1. Timing - market conditions, target companies need what you're selling
2. Talent - your skills and experience
3. Territory - PMF, viable prospects, realistic quotas

Sellers control exactly **one** of these.

Here's what to do if you suspect you have a sh*t territory:

1.) Run the Numbers First
--> Analyze territory potential vs. quota
--> Document deal sizes, win rates, sales cycle length

2.) Present Data, Not Emotions
--> "Based on historical data, sellers in this territory needs X opportunities to hit Y quota"
--> "Current pipeline math requires Z% win rate, which is 3x industry average"
--> "Here's what success would require..."

3.) Make a Plan If leadership won't address the fundamentals. A plan to either:
--> Stay and survive - if you believe they'll fix it
--> Find a better fit - if you think they can't (or won't)

—

Life's too short to fight unwinnable battles.
Sales is hard enough when everything's aligned.
Don't let anyone convince you that effort (or activity) alone fixes broken fundamentals.


PS- if you're a seller who's been in this situation, would love to hear what you did. If you're able to share, I guarantee it will be a big encouragement to your peers. You will probably never know how much it means to them.🤗

content:
The sellers with the worst imposter syndrome are almost never the ones you'd expect.

It's not the new reps. It's not the people struggling to make quota.

It's the top performers.

I've been in sales for 13 years. I've coached hundreds of enterprise AEs.  Here's the pattern I see over and over-

1. We hit a big goal.
2. We immediately set a bigger one.
3. We haven't achieved the new goal yet - so we feel like we're behind.
4. We look around and assume that everyone else has everything figured out.
5. We avoid the thing that scares us most - executive conversations, on-site meetings, asking for the close.

Not because we can't do it. Because we're terrified of being "found out."

I had a rep last week who made $270K in a down year. (Income. Not revenue.) She told me she avoids going on site to meet executives because - and I quote - "I don't feel like I belong in that room."

That is the hidden tax of being a high performer in sales. We're so used to achieving that when something feels hard, we assume the problem is us.

It's not.

The confidence gap isn't a skill gap. It's an evidence gap.

We forget what we've already done because we're so focused on what we haven't done yet.

The sellers who are able to work through imposter syndrome are the ones who remember to "feel the feelings" AND consider the evidence.

content:
I walked away from the biggest deal of my career. $13.7M. Would've blown my quota out of the water.

But here's what that "loss" taught me...

The CEO had everything: 
✓ A problem we could solve 
✓ Agreement he HAD the problem
✓ Desperate need to fix it 
✓ Budget approved

But one thing kept nagging at me.

Every meeting, he'd ask about customization. 
About "partnering" to build features.
About source code access. 

Classic Build vs. Buy syndrome.

After our 5th in-person meeting (yes, FIVE), I finally saw it clearly.

This wasn't a buyer. This was a builder trapped in a buyer's process.

His personality screamed "I'll do it myself." 
His energy peaked when discussing his team's capabilities.
His questions focused on HOW we built it, not WHAT it could do. 

So I made the call that physically hurt:

I removed it from my pipeline.

My manager: "Are you SURE?" 
My financial plan: "But the commission..." 
My ego: "You're giving up."

Here's what happened next:

→ Freed up 30+ hours that month 
→ Focused on a $1.8M deal that actually wanted to buy 
→ Closed 3 other deals while he was still "evaluating" 
→ Finished with my best year ever

And that CEO? 
18 months later, still building. 
Still solving the same problem.

The real lesson?

Not every deal is YOUR deal.

Some buyers aren't buyers—they're builders in disguise. And the time you waste convincing them is time you could spend closing real deals.

Three questions I now ask myself:

1./ Are they asking about outcomes or architecture?
2./ Do they light up more about building or buying?
3./ Is their real goal independence or results?

If the answers point to "building," I'm out. No matter the size.

Because the best deals aren't always the biggest ones. 
They're the ones that actually close.

What deal have you walked away from that taught you the most?

content:
Here's how to stop overthinking Enterprise deals:  stop wasting time on what Buyers personally care about.

I mean, who has time to dig into their individual career goals, their political standing with the exec team, or the market pressures in their industry?

Instead, just focus on the business case alone. Show them the 938% ROI your internal data predicts. Who can argue with that? 

Got a 47-slide deck that breaks down the numbers six different ways? Send it after every call.
Sure, some deals will push. But that's just because some buyers are too dumb to really get how amazing our product is.

Working with a VP who keeps saying things like "I just started in this role" and "I need to build credibility with the C-suite first"?

What he REALLY needs to understand is our 3-year TCO analysis. So just send that. Twice if he doesn't respond the first time.

Got a CTO telling you she's nervous about implementation timelines because her team is already underwater?

I mean we could explore that. Ask what "underwater" means for her specifically. What it would mean for her if things went smoothly versus if they didn't. But that feels too personal.

Instead, show her your implementation roadmap and assure her it will only take 90 days.

Look, buyers are professionals. They don't need us to understand their personal stakes.
They just need us to show them the numbers and get out of the way.
If they can't see the clear business value, that's on them.

______________________________________

Obviously, I'm kidding.
Buuuuuuutttt I spent my first 9 months in enterprise sales doing stuff like that.

Hiding behind business cases because asking about someone's personal stakes felt too... salesy? Intrusive?

I didn't realize I was making buyers do all the work of connecting the dots between "this will save the company money" and "this will make me look good to my boss."

In my latest YouTube video, I walk through the exact questions I ask to uncover a buyer's personal stakes - the ones that actually move deals forward instead of letting them die in "we'll circle back" limbo. You can check it out here: https://bit.ly/3M1ZD9g

Because the truth is: when we understand what the buyer personally wins, selling takes a lot less effort.

content:
"How do I get him to sign without being annoying?"

The contract was out. The pilot proved value. The Champion was bought in. Pricing was agreed on. But the buyer just wasn't signing.

Walking through this with a seller I coach. I asked her one question: Does the Champion know what happens after he signs?

Silence.

Here's what I've learned the hard way. When a contract is sitting unsigned with no objections left, it's almost never about the product. It's about risk.

They're worried about implementation going sideways. 
Onboarding being a mess. 
Adopting something new and it not working. 

And we don't realize this is what's happening because we're thinking, "They already said yes. What's the holdup?"

The holdup is they said yes to solving the problem. 

They haven't said yes to the process of getting there. 

Because we haven't shown it to them.


So here's exactly what we worked on:

We built a simple onboarding timeline.
A one-pager. Five or six milestones. Specific dates. 
Starting with contract execution and ending with a success review meeting.


The key details that matter:

-The first milestone is NOT "contract signed." It's the outcome they want to achieve. That has to be front and center.

-Every milestone gets a real calendar date. Not "Day 1, Day 14." Actual dates. They'll respond to actual dates. "Oh, Alex is on leave until the 22nd, so that needs to shift." Now they're planning their own onboarding. That's buying behavior.

-Embed the timeline image directly in the email body. Don't attach a PDF. Don't send a link. A link is homework. They should be able to see the whole plan without clicking anything.

-If you can, introduce whoever will onboard them. With a photo. Something human. A real person with a name and a face reduces risk in a way that no case study can.


She sent that email a few hours after our call. The buyer opened it immediately. 
Called her five minutes later. Signed.
$140K total contract value.


None of that happened because of one "magic" tactic. 

It happened because she stopped hoping buyers would figure out the path forward and started showing them.

Most of the time, the deal isn't stuck. The buyer just can't see what comes next.


This is just one of the concepts we cover in my group coaching program.

This is the story of a CXO who saved my deal, but never replied to my email.
Here's what happened... 
 
I inherited a deal in my 1st year at UserGems. It was multithreaded (kinda) when I got it. 
 
There were 5 people involved from the Buyer side. That was the good news. 
 
Bad news - all 5 people worked in the same department.

He never attended a meeting. 

Never responded to the "keeping you in the loop" emails I sent.

When the buying group threatened to walk away from the deal unless we slashed our pricing by over 60% (because they didn't understand our differentiators)....
 
We used the thread with our VP of marketing to send the business case to the Executive Buyer. 
 
He understood the value, and ultimately rescued the deal. 
 
 
We don't have to go it alone when we're multi-threading. 
 
Aligning executives can be a powerful way to engage with CXOs and VPs.

content:
I once lost a $340K deal because I didn't know what I didn't know. My VP sat in on the final presentation. Afterward, she pulled me aside and said: "You almost missed 3 opportunities to address their unspoken concerns about implementation risk. That's why I interrupted you towards the end."

I had no idea what she was talking about.

Turns out, she had a whole mental playbook for navigating those exact concerns. Specific phrases that work. Stories that land.

But none of that was written down anywhere. And she'd never thought to share it with the team. 

She was busy and didn’t have the time to impart all of the knowledge living rent-free in her head.

This is the part that kills me:

Sales leaders have playbooks in their heads that could easily 2x their team's performance.
→ They know which questions expose budget vs. bandwidth vs. priority issues
→ They've seen every objection pattern and know what actually works
→ They can read buying signals you didn't even know existed

But the playbooks are invisible to the people who need them most. And if that knowledge stays locked in their heads (or only comes out during deal reviews when it's too late), reps are flying blind.

Coaching isn’t just about feedback; it’s about transferring how leaders think. Science backs this up: the most effective coaching activates the same decision-making patterns top performers use in real time.

So what can you as a seller do about it?

Make it stupidly easy for your VP to share their playbook.

Try asking your leaders:
→ "When I'm in negotiations, what are the 3-5 'give/gets' you've seen work best? I want to document this for the team."
→ "You've closed deals at the executive level. What evidence do they typically need to build the internal business case? I'd love to capture this."
→ "What are the top objection-handling ideas in your head that you wish every rep knew?"

Ask these in a 1:1. Record the 15-min conversation. Socialize it with the team. Send it to Enablement.

Make the invisible -> visible.

Your sales leaders' wisdom shouldn't be a secret.

content:
It's 2019. I'm in Tableau's Austin office, trying to stave off a panic attack.

My next meeting was with a CFO. And I knew I had nothing compelling to share with him. Don't misunderstand .... I had the meeting all planned out. Solid deck. Clear agenda. Good discovery notes.

But I knew IN MY GUTS that this CFO was probably going to tune out.

Because the features that got the accounting staff and IT analysts excited? The CFO would never use them.

We talk about features.
We walk through demos.

But executives don't care about HOW our solution works. They care about what changes if they buy it.

They're asking themselves:
→ Does this solve a problem that's costing me money or opportunity?
→ Is the risk of doing nothing higher than the risk of doing this?
→ Can I explain this to my board in 30 seconds?

If we can't answer those questions clearly and fast, we're noise.

And here's the really uncomfy truth: We get one shot. Maybe two.

After that, we're the seller who "doesn't get it." And we won't get another meeting.
