content:
After 13 years in sales and coaching hundreds of enterprise AEs, I've learned there are only 3 things that determine whether investing in yourself actually pays off.

If even one of these 3 is missing, it won't work.

1. We have to be in a situation where we can win.

Coaching doesn't fix product-market fit. It doesn't fix bad territories. It doesn't fix a company that's imploding.

I always ask: how many people on your team are hitting quota? If nobody is, the underlying problem isn't your skills. And I don't want people to throw money at developing skills when the real issue is the environment.

2. We have to have invested in ourselves before.

Time, money, or both. If someone has never spent a dime or an hour on self-development, jumping into coaching isn't the right first step.

The people who get the best results already have a foundation. They've listened to podcasts. They've read books. They've asked for feedback. They have the muscle of learning already built.

3. We have to have a very personal "why."

Not "I want to hit quota." Everyone wants to hit quota.

I mean the real thing. The thing that's your driving force. That you've promised yourself you'll do.

For me, when I got into tech sales, I had 3 little kids. And the life we had, I was like, this is not what I want. I wanted to take them on vacations I didn't get to go on. If they needed to go to private school, I wanted to have that option.

That was my why. It wasn't a number. It was a picture of what life could look like.

The sellers who get the best results from any development investment are the ones where the personal stakes are real. Not theoretical. Not aspirational. Real.

Before you invest in anything this year - coaching, courses, certifications - run it through these three questions:

-> Can I win where I am?

-> Have I invested before?

-> Do I know exactly why this matters to me?

If the answer to all three is yes, invest aggressively. If any of them is no, fix that first. Aggressively.

What's your personal "why" this year? Not the number - the real thing behind it.



📸 2 of the kiddos on our first beach trip.

PS-  team leaders - the "personal why" question is a great team builder. Bonus points if you have them do slides with images & everyone presents in a team meeting. One of the best exercises I've seen. s/o to Liz Strauss Clyman for that one.

content:
One of my mentors told me something that completely changed how I think about burnout in sales. He said,

"Rest is not the same as restoration."

And I was like, "wait, what?"

"You can take time off. You can stop working. But if your internal bucket is empty, the rest doesn't do anything except slow you down."

That hit me. Because I had been doing exactly that.

Taking a weekend off. Maybe a vacation. Coming back and feeling just as drained as before. And wondering why.

Because sales takes and takes and takes. We put half our paycheck on the line based on our performance. We get rejected daily. We carry the stress of a pipeline that could collapse at any point.

And then we take a day off and expect that to fix it.

It doesn't.

Rest stops the bleeding. Restoration fills the tank back up.

Rest is the absence of work. Restoration is the presence of something that gives us energy.

For some it's a sport. For some it's jigsaw puzzles or hiking or music or yoga or learning about wine.

The point is it's not just "not working." It's actively doing something that pours back into us.

I started asking myself: "does this restore me, or does it just give me a break?"


PS- being outside definitely restores me. I am also trying to learn to crochet - "if you work with your mind, relax with your hands" and all that - but so far, it has just frustrated me. 

What's the thing that actually restores you - not just rests you?

content:
In 2022, I went into H2 extremely short on pipeline. Like my pipeline was so small that when I started thinking about it, I got overwhelmed & became paralyzed with fear. Cue spiral into full panic attack mode.

One Saturday morning, I sat down at the computer (after a week of trying to convince myself to prospect, but instead just wasted time worrying).

Told myself I would not get up from the computer until I had a solid plan for creating opps that could close quickly.

These are the 3 things I came up with. They're the same 3 things I coach AEs on today.

-> Previous Exposure
-> New Strategy
-> Industry Shift

After analyzing 100s of closed-won deals, these 3 compelling events show up again and again:

1) PREVIOUS EXPOSURE:
My old boss used to say: "They have to tell us no a couple times before they tell us yes."
→ Pull CRM report of accounts with previous opps 
 → Upload to Sales Nav as an Account List
 → Check if contacts from past opps changed jobs in the last year
 → Find NEW contacts at accounts who previously worked at your current customers

2) NEW STRATEGY:
Look for:
 → New leadership (especially VP/CXO level)
 → Reorganizations
 → New initiatives
Set up Google Alerts for target accounts with terms like "appoints new," "reorganization," "strategic initiative"

3) MASSIVE INDUSTRY SHIFT (external pressure forcing change)
→ Read industry publications for the 2-3 massive shifts in sectors you sell to
 → Look at your Closed-Won deals - what common pressures were those industries facing?
 → Prioritize accounts in those industries that ALSO have previous exposure or new leadership

Reality Check: These won't ALL turn into pipeline. But they have the HIGHEST PROBABILITY.

*Previous Exposure = less education needed, shorter sales cycle
*New Strategy = budget allocated, urgency built in
*Industry Shift = problem is undeniable 

When you focus on accounts with these commonalities, you're fishing where the fish are actually biting.

The AEs I coach who do this consistently see 2-3x more meetings booked and 41-57% shorter sales cycles.

If you want help implementing this in your territory (including access to the Point of View tool I use & templates for each type of outreach), DM me about 1:1 or group coaching.

content:
Here are the 8 questions CFOs ask before every software purchase. (And they're brutal.)

Every champion I've ever worked with eventually hits a moment of panic:
"What do I say when Finance starts asking the hard questions?"

👉 Most CFOs won't tell you what they're really thinking. They just kill your deal silently.

But I've spent 13 years watching Enterprise deals die in Finance. And I've learned what CFOs actually need to hear.

Here are the 8 questions every CFO is asking behind closed doors, courtesy of the "Only CFOs" newsletter, as highlighted by  Nate Nasralla :

1. Why do we need [X product] now? We were fine before. 
2. What bucket does this fall into, and can you quantify it?
-----Improves efficiencies
-----Increases revenue
-----Mission critical (e.g. cybersecurity)
-----"Candy": nice-to-have tool that doesn't really fit into the above groups 
3. Is the spend in the budget? If not, how will you make up the difference? 
4. How does this tool tie into our company objectives for this year? 
5. What tools do we already have that do something similar? And if similar tools exist, why can't we use those? 
6. Implementation: What are the people / time requirements? 
7. Support costs: Will we need to upgrade soon to enterprise /other tier? 
8. Pricing:
-----If usage-based pricing: I want a detailed analysis on how pricing works and modeling for what our planned usage will look like.
-----If seat-based pricing: I don't want to buy a bunch of extra seats for planned growth. That got a lot of people in trouble when headcount growth halted and layoffs happened.

The deal-killers? Numbers 1, 3, and 5.

At Salesforce, I watched 6-7 figure deals die instantly when the champion couldn't answer those 3 questions clearly.

content:
I struggled with the leap from Mid-Market to Enterprise sales. 

Like one day being a top college athlete, and the next,

getting my a$$ handed to me at the pro level.

I had NO idea how different Enterprise would be. 

Luckily, I had great mentors gave me 3 key pieces of advice:

---> Build an Internal Network
---> Planning Will Save You
---> Stay in Sync


---> Build an Internal Network
Find out who you'll work with in Legal, Finance, and Deal Desk.

Put a short intro call on their calendar. Find out their story.

Their likes and dislikes. Ask how best to work with them.

Then mark your calendar to reach out to them every few weeks - and ask for nothing.

Establishing relationships before you need something from these teams can be crucial later. (And just a good decent thing to do.)


---> Planning Will Save You

Start creating account plans for your top high-value accounts.

Both to show high-level strategy and drive accountability around execution.

You will use them with all your co-selling teammates, including executive alignment with internal leadership. These shared documents are invaluable.



---> Stay in Sync

Have regular sync/prep meetings on the calendar with your teammates in Pre-sales, Support, and Customer success.

And do not cancel or schedule over these calls. They are sacred.

Regular time together cuts down on miscommunication, saves 100s of Slack messages, and creates alignment.

You'll have fewer fire drills re: deal strategy, saving a renewal, etc.

content:
It was one of the lowest points in my career. But it should have been one of the highlights.

Instead, my anxiety exploded to a new high and my mind was constantly racing.

I was coming off 2 years where I averaged 127% attainment.

I had just been hired by a billion dollar, public tech company.

And after the first few weeks in that role, I went from feeling "on top of the world" to "completely out of my league."

You know that saying "If you're the smartest person in the room, you're in the wrong room"? Mission accomplished. 😨

EVERYONE on my new team was accomplished and ambitious and whip-smart.

And knew wayyy more than me about all the tech.
If you could see my Google history from that time 🙈
I was looking up everything: Data warehouse, data lake, IoT… wtf?

And it wasn't just technical knowledge.
These sellers had skills that were next level. 
They were doing things I'd never done. Account Planning, User Roundtables, creating Centers of Excellence in accounts.

Any previous confidence evaporated and I was completely overwhelmed.

I was afraid I'd fail - and fail big. 
That I'd inevitably be "found out" and fired.

In desperation, I reached out to a mentor. She was Director of Sales at another public tech company, and she said the most surprising thing I could have imagined.

"I know exactly how you feel."

She went on. "Every time I've started a new role or a new company, my initial thought has been 'I can't hold court with these people.' "

As soon as she said that, I took the first deep breath I'd taken in weeks.

And then she sent me a video. It's Atlassian CEO's TED talk on Imposter Syndrome.

Hearing CEO Mike Cannon-Brookes talk about all the times he's felt like he doesn't know what he's doing and doesn't deserve to be there - and how he copes with it - forever changed my mindset.

Somehow, it's even better when you know that his company is worth $54B, and his personal net worth is over $13B.

Once I knew other people - LOTS of people! Successful people! - felt this way, it freed up my mind to take the next right steps.

I blocked time each week to read up on the technical stuff I didn't know.
And I set up weekly sessions with a sales coach.

That last one? Game changer.
Not because I learned some magical new tactic.

But because I finally had structure. Accountability. And a system for turning what I was learning into what I was actually doing in my deals.

I stopped consuming random content and hoping something would stick.

The chaos in my head finally quieted down.

Nine years later, I still remember how desperate I felt during those first few weeks. Drowning in content. Paralyzed by imposter syndrome. Not knowing where to start.

That's exactly why I built my group coaching program.
It's what I wish existed back then.

If you're feeling overwhelmed, scattered, not sure how to execute what you're learning - you're not alone.

And you don't have to figure it out by yourself.

content:
$600K deal. $4 million problem.

Here's how one of my clients closed a stalled deal and made President's Club.

A casino opening a new location needed 2,000 hires before opening day. 

Her product: on-site drug testing that gets results immediately instead of waiting weeks on labs.

It was June. Her leadership wanted it closed by July. But the casino wasn't opening until April. So..... 9 months away.

The buyers believed they had no reason to move fast.

So we calculated what waiting would actually cost them.

Industry benchmark: $4,000 cost per hire. If they wait until 3 months before opening and 1,000 candidates fail drug tests, they're scrambling to hire 3,000 people instead of 2,000.

That delta? $4 million.

Her solution was $600K.

She stopped selling a drug testing product. She started solving a $4 million problem.

Deal closed in September. President's Club.

Here's the lesson:

Unless we contrast deals with the cost of doing nothing, all the buyer has is an anchor around "this is what it costs."

No context. No urgency. No reason to move now.

Cost of inaction makes the invisible -> visible.

What's the "cost of waiting" in your deals right now? Does your buyer know?

PS - when you create a visual for Cost of Inaction, it hits different. This is the graph we used for the casino deal. Took AI about 2 min to create it.

content:
IRL scenario from last year: $1.2M deal. Stuck in procurement for 2 weeks.
The seller's doing everything right - sending polite follow-ups to "Brandon" in procurement every few days.

But nothing's moving.

Sound familiar?

Here's the thing most sellers miss: Brandon doesn't care about your timeline.

Brandon gets paid whether your deal closes this quarter or next year.

So we flipped the script....


In my coaching session with this seller, I asked one simple question:

"Who has the most to GAIN if this deal gets signed?"

Not Brandon. Never Brandon.

Here's who actually cared:

-> Sarah (Account Manager): She owns the [big box store] relationship. CEO expects her to grow it from $20M to $50M. Without better data? She's toast.

-> Mike (VP of Sales): Reports directly to the CEO. Already promised the board they'd hit that $50M [big box store] goal.

-> The CEO: He's been on 3 podcasts talking about their 2.5x growth plan at [big box store]. His reputation is on the line.

These people? They have EVERYTHING to gain.

Brandon? He just wants clean paperwork.


Instead of email #47 to procurement, here's what we did:

Email 1 → Sarah: "Quick update: Contract's with Brandon for final review. When's your next [big box store] meeting? Want to make sure you have competitive insights ready."

Email 2 → Mike: "FYI - procurement has the contract. Given your [big box store] strategy session next month, we'll have insights ready within 4 weeks of signature."

Email 3 → CEO: Subject: "Closer to $50M at [big box store]" "Exciting news - Brandon has the contract for final review. Based on Sarah's July 25th meeting, we can deliver competitive insights by July 23rd if we stay on track."

Here's What Happened Next

CEO forwards the email to Brandon: "Where are we with this? Need it prioritized."

Deal signed in 48 hours.

The Lesson?

We gotta stop following up with people who don't care about our timeline.

And start updating the people who have everything to gain.

Procurement moves when business pressure is applied. 

Not when sellers send reminder emails.


Think about your stuck deals right now.

Who has the most to gain if it closes?

That's who you should be talking to.

What's your approach when deals get stuck in procurement?

Also Sales Leaders: “Our team really prioritizes work / life balance. We know you have a life outside of work.”

Ummmm these 2 things can’t both be true.

Because here’s what “balance” actually requires:

Not more pep talks.

Not another “time management” training.

Not a new spreadsheet template.

It requires leaders to put their money where their mouth is and give reps the infrastructure to execute.

Right now, most sellers are trying to do enterprise selling with:

   - Deal data in the CRM
   - Calls in Gong
   - Content in Seismic
   - Signals scattered across 6 tabs
   - “Next steps” living in someone’s memory (or a notes app)

So reps do what humans always do when systems don’t connect:

They create a duct-tape system.

Usually… a spreadsheet.

And the data backs it up:

85% of enterprise reps manage their book in spreadsheets.
10% use inbox.
5% use CRM.

That’s not a “rep problem.”

That’s an execution problem.

And it’s getting worse because buyers now show up ~80% through the sales cycle. By the time a rep gets pulled into the deal, the buyer has opinions, constraints, and a short list. Preparation can’t be a 12-tab scavenger hunt anymore.

That’s why I’m paying attention to ZoomInfo  GTM Workspace. (Check it out here: https://lnkd.in/gi3NhgJq ) 
Not because sellers need “more data.”
Because sellers need one workspace where execution happens, with complete context, so strategy can actually turn into action (and action into pipeline).

If you’re a sales leader who genuinely cares about work / life balance, here’s the standard:
   - Stop expecting Olympic-level output with hobby-level tools.
   - Invest in systems that reduce tab-hopping, manual research, and copy-paste admin.
   - Give reps tech that helps them execute across 50+ accounts without burning out. (What a concept.)

Strategy alone doesn’t win deals. Execution wins deals.

This is the thing we don’t talk about enough with top performers. We're not worried about missing quota. We're worried we're one-hit wonders. That we got lucky. That we can't repeat it in the next role, or even the next quarter:

"I've been in the top three every year, but I've never been number one."

A client said this to me last week, so I asked her what she thought was holding her back.

She said, "I don't have a system. So I feel like everything has to be customized. And it takes SO much time that it limits how many deals I can work."

And here's why the "one hit wonder" fear makes sense: there's this belief that every deal is a special snowflake. That what worked last time won't work this time. That we just have to figure it out fresh every single time.

The problem is we were never taught otherwise.

Companies teach us how to adhere to their selling process. They teach us nothing about aligning with a buying process. What we put in Salesforce is essentially so our leaders can forecast deals. It does not help us progress them.

So we hit quota, but we have no repeatable process. We close the big one, but we're not confident we could do it again. We look successful on the outside, while quietly terrified on the inside. (I've BEEN this person.)

This is the unlock: Having a repeatable system. Not a CRM stage. Not a forecast category. A framework we can follow no matter what deal we're in. A scaffolding.

Because the difference between top 3 and number 1 is knowing exactly what we did that worked, so we can do it again on purpose.

3/Helping Reps come with a Point of View: Industry trends, Persona insights, an AI story. Not just asking customers what they want - sharing ways sellers can guide Buyers to sidestep blind spots & see value.


And that was just the content side. Adobe’s great culture was also on full display. 3 other things I loved:

1/ Spotlight on tributes: Sellers and sales leaders created videos celebrating SC’s, CSM’s, Deal desk, and team members. It can be easy to forget to say thank you. Instead, they’re intentional about it.

2/ Shout outs: Sales leaders like Samantha King and Abby Dulany getting specific about what they saw their teams doing well & getting those sellers visibility on a larger stage.

3/ Silliness: Adobe’s team takes sales seriously. But it’s clear they don’t take themselves TOO seriously. Those pirate selfies (and videos) were epic.


Sessions like that don’t just happen. Kristine Karaman Maddy Moss Robyn Eames, Valerie Thompson and Matt Crosby put in so much work - and it shows! Appreciate you having me.

content:
2 of the 3 tech unicorns I've worked at train their AEs on 2 core concepts that salespeople don't typically learn: 
 
 
--> Towards v. Away language 
--> Above the Line (ATL) v. Below the Line (BTL) 
 
 
1) Towards v. Away language 
 
-> 80% of people are motivated by moving Away from Pain (more people would run from a German Shepherd than towards a Gold medal*) 
 
-> But sales reps talk about Gain, aka moving Towards: "time back in your day", efficiency & ROI 
 
 
Here's how it sounds IRL: 
 
-> Towards sounds like, "Because my product automatically detects buying signals like hiring, promotions, and champion job changes...your sales reps will save 29% of their time and you'll see a 18x ROI." 
 
-> Away sounds like, "What goes away [by using my product] is sales rep's spending hours on manual research, low morale from not seeing results, and the frustration of your team missing their number." 
 
 
->>>TL;DR = talk about what problems go away 
 
 
 
 
2) Above the Line (ATL) v. Below the Line (BTL) 
 
-> "The Line" is the 'power line', so Directors, VPs, CXOs = Above the Line 
 
-> BTL thinks about their team v. ATL thinks about market share & risk 
 
 
IRL example: 
 
-> ATL value prop sounds like, "With [my product] you reduce 3 risks: Your top competitor doesn't get in the door first, you don't lose more market share, and you don't have to explain your inaction to investors." 

-> BTL value prop sounds like, "What goes away [with my product] is worrying about too little pipeline, missing quota & losing your job." 
 
 
 
->>> TL;DR = choose the right language for your audience 
 
 
 
It takes time and effort to wrap our heads around these. 
 
But there's a reason the unicorns teach them. They win deals. 
 
Wanna try your hand at it? Write your value prop in "Away" language in the comments. (I double 🐶 dare you. It's harder than it sounds.)
 
 
 

 
*ATL/BTL concepts from Skip Miller’s book Proactive Selling. Credit for "German Shepherds v. Gold Medals" comes from the book Secrets of Question-Based Selling by Thomas Freese

content:
After 12+ years in sales, I've got good news for anyone who gets "Happy Ears" a lot. 
 
(btw, I spent the early years of my sales career battling that same thing) 
 
Luckily, a mentor shared their secret with me. 
 
 
Here it is: 
 
3 Questions + 1 Rule for all Opportunities 
 
 
The Three Questions 
--> Why Anything 
--> Why Now 
--> Why Us 
 
 
The One Rule 
--> NONE of the answers can mention any of your product's features as the reason 
 
You can ONLY mention a product feature IF you know the outcome it creates or prevents. 
 
 
 *********** 
For a past deal this sounded like: 
 
--> WHY ANYTHING: Pipeline creation is strategic initiative #1 for Exec Buyer (RVP Sales) in 2026. They have an aggressive goal: 17% YoY increase 
 
--> WHY NOW: Can be implemented in under 60 days (feature), which means there's still time to impact Q1 pipe, and even Q1 revenue (impact). 
 
--> WHY US: RVP knows that her biggest competitor started with us last year & they are losing more deals than ever to this competitor. And the RVP's team has seen only 6% increase in ARR and 19% renewal churn. This is the data she's presenting to CFO as proof that 1) the strategy works & 2) there's a high risk of doing nothing. 

*********** 
 
 
If we can't answer the 3 Why's - with metrics 
 
We need to quickly dive deeper with Discovery - or move on 
 
If we show our pipeline some tough love now, we can prevent a lot of pain from Happy Ears in the future.

How do you think about testing the deals in your pipe?

content:
After 7+ years in ENT Sales, I've learned a non-icky way to drive urgency. 

Make the urgency Buyer Centric. 

Easier said than done. So...


Let's take Q4 as an example. Here are 7 things weighing on executives in December:

1/ Reporting Financial Performance

2/ Next Year's Priorities & Strategies

3/ Innovation and Market Differentiation

4/ Metrics They're Measured/Bonused On

5/ Risks: Gaps, Competitors, Market conditions 

6/ Headcount: How to attract, retain, and develop top talent

7/ Personal life: Balancing End of Year with holiday events & travel 


Here are 11 ideas to tie our solutions to these 7 priorities, to keep Execs engaged in our Q4 and Q1 deals: 

1/ Reporting Financial Performance - 
Are they excited to announce their results or dreading it? How will you help them repeat good results or improve on bad outcomes?

2/ Next Year's Priorities & Strategies - 
What have you heard from your Champion about these? What success stories will you tell about how others achieved those same things, so Buyers are excited to move forward?

3/ Innovation and Market Differentiation -
How does your solution help them stand out? Can they get 1st movers advantage & grab market share? Does it help them provide a better customer experience?

4/ Metrics They're Measured/Bonused On - If they're a public company, check out their Schedule 14A (annual proxy statement) on their investor relations page. How will you help your Champion make money?

5/ Risks: Gaps, Competitors, Market conditions - 
Are all their competitors working with you? Can you help them do more with less? Do you help them thrive, even in tough times? (Key is business impact, not features)

6/ Headcount: How to attract, retain, and develop top talent -
Will you help them give employees reasons to come & stay - something the org only gets by being your customer?

7/ Personal life: Balancing End of Year with holiday events & travel -
Can you help them see around corners re: possible roadblocks to your deal because of Security, Legal or Procurement? Can you use a Visual Timeline or MAP to show them exactly how the deal gets done before they go on holiday vacay?

This is what creates real urgency. Not just "everyone gets a discount."

I was surprised when a CMO recently told me that he'd never been asked this question on a Discovery call. But he definitely wanted to answer it (!!)
 
Here it is: 
 
"How can I best match your urgency?" 
 
 
Here's how the full version sounds at the end of a Discovery call: 
 
 
"Mary, it was great to talk with you today. 
 
Would it be ok to ask 1 more question? 
 
There are typically 3 reasons folks join these first calls. 
 
--> Sometimes people join these calls because they are in education mode and just want to understand new tools. 
 
--> Sometimes people join these calls because they have a big problem they needed to solve 6 months ago. 
 
--> And, sometimes people join these calls because they probably need to do something about this problem in the next 12 months, but it's not urgent. 
 
 
 Curious where would you put yourself on that scale? Asking because I never want to chase anyone. 
 
If today was purely education, that's ok." 
 
 
 
Asking about urgency at the end of the call helps us know what Next Steps to suggest. 
 
It's a win/win question, as it helps us align with executive priorities and makes our Buyers feel heard. 
 

Curious what others are doing...What do you think works the best to close out your Discovery / first calls?

content:
If I was starting a new sales role today, here are the 5 things I’d do in the first 5 days- 
 
 
1/ Find the accounts in my territory that are most likely to buy (aka the most like past buyers). 
 
I'd do this by creating a CRM report of Closed Won deals for the Past 2 years, with these details: 
 
 
- industry 
- location 
- age of company 
- $ ARR amount 
- # of employees 
- names/personas involved in the purchase 
 
THEN I'd create a report of Prospects with similarities in my territory/account list. 
 
^^This is the low hanging fruit. 
 
 
 
2/ I'd find 3-5 consistent top performers and ask them 3 simple questions: 
 
—-> Who are the best personas for us? 
--> Which are their 2-3 top business problems we solve (+vocabulary they use)? 
--> What's the # 1 thing to do/not do when just starting in this role? 
 
^^This is a shortcut for how to start off with a Bang...without trying to reinvent the wheel. 
 
 
 
3/ I'd set up intro calls with internal folks like Finance/Deal desk, Legal, Product, Support, Solution Consulting, Channel partners, Systems Integrators, etc... anyone who I'll regularly interact with on deals. 
 
Start figuring out the best "Gives" for each person - do they like Starbucks, Slack shout outs, special beverages for EOQ/EOY? I'd put quarterly reminders on my calendar (and schedule quarterly deliveries where it makes sense). 
 
^^This is how we create our "tribe"/internal network within a company...giving right from the start, rather than just being 'another seller who wants something'. 
 
 
 
4/ I'd memorize 5-8 customer stories. 
 
Starting with writing a 1 min summary on note cards - with the Champion's name/title, pain felt, problem solved & impact created. 
 
I'd practice telling these stories out loud every morning for 10 minutes...until I don't need the notecards anymore. Then I'd rinse/ repeat, memorizing 5 new stories. 
 
^^This is how we can build confidence & credibility. 
 
 
 
5/ I'd analyze my boss’s personality - LOTS of tools for this - and I'd ask them about their top 2 career goals in our first 1:1 chat. 
 
^^This is how we can start to manage up. 


These are the top 5 things that have paid off the most for me when starting a new role.

What's worked well for you - what would you do if you were starting over?

content:
Challenger says 97% of their clients ask for extra help with this skill.

More than any other they teach.

And it's the least talked about.

What is it? "Constructive Tension"

Challenger says Constructive Tension Is:
 --> A productive force to compel action
 --> Steering the conversation without being aggressive
 --> Used strategically and empathetically to examine conventional ways of thinking, explore assumptions, and probe for answers

"The goal is to highlight an unrecognized, misunderstood, or underappreciated problem or pain point."

While we definitely want to use this approach in Discovery, we're also introducing Constructive Tension in End-of-Year deals when we ask things like:

 --> "Can you walk me through each step of how this project could get a December signature, so we can start set up & training in January?"

 --> "Typically we see customers getting a purchase done fastest when the IT teams meet about integrations at the same InfoSec does security reviews. Any reason this wouldn't work for your teams?"

 --> "Could we schedule a call between our Legal departments instead of waiting for redlines?"

When we do this *empathetically* - in the spirit of teaching Champions how to buy - this can be one of the biggest value adds.

Champions are experts in how to do their jobs, not how to buy our stuff.

Especially at EOY?

content:
11+ years in sales. 6 years as an Enterprise AE. And pipeline management is still hard. But I've learned 2 strategies that I use every day. 
 
Strategies for: 
--> Deciding which deals to focus on 
--> When to give up & move on 
 
 
 
--> Deciding which deals to focus on 
 
Companies have ICPs: Ideal Customer Profiles 
 
I have IOPs: Ideal Opportunity Profiles 
 
When I have to decide how much time, research, and personalization to devote, I give each deal a "grade". 
 
I've narrowed down 8 characteristics of deals that are most likely to close. 
 
I assign points to each characteristic. 
 
My point system looks like this: 
 
 
--> There's a Champion Who Gives the "Inside Scoop": 10 points 
--> They have Specific Goals with Metrics for Each: 10 points 
-->They Invest Heavily in Tech Related to My Product: 10 points 
--> They are Responsive to Calls, Texts, Email: 10 points 
--> There are a Low Number of Obstacles: 10 points 
--> They have Lots of Potential End Users: 15 points 
--> They have a Compelling Event: 20 points 
--> They make Decisions Quickly: 15 points 
 
 
The higher the grade, the more time and energy I spend on it. 
 
 
 
--> When to give up & move on 
 
I use a "3 strikes You're Out" rule. 
 
If there is no response after I reach out 3 times 
 
across 3 different channels (email, text, LinkedIn, phone, Slack, etc.) 
 
I close it out. 
 
 
 
These may sound simple or obvious, but it took me years of agonizing. 
 
 
I wish more companies trained on this kind of practical, day-to-day stuff. 
 
The "basics" of sales are often not simple. 
 
Or obvious.

One of my clients closed the whale this year.
 $2.6M in ARR.

1.) Multi-thread or bust.

Your best deals already exist in your CRM. But if you don’t run this report, you’ll miss them entirely. So here’s the 4-step playbook that led to attainment over 121% for 6 reps. I walk through it with every ramping rep (especially the ones who can’t afford a slow Q1):

This also works for rising reps who need more pipeline....

Step 1: Run a closed-won report for the last 2 years in your CRM. Filter by your vertical, your segment, deal size threshold, employee count range.

Step 2: Group by industry. Look for patterns in what types of companies actually spend money.

Step 3: Find accounts in your book that look like the ones who already bought, AND who have new leadership in the last 3 months. (SalesNav filter.)  These are your lowest-hanging fruit.

Step 4: If possible, prioritize accounts that are already spending something with you. Being an approved vendor can cut months off a deal cycle.

I ran this play with a ramping rep at one of the world's largest tech companies. He inherited 150 accounts across six completely different industries. He didn’t know which accounts to focus on,

60 minutes later he had ~50 records organized by segment, opp size, status, age, new business or add on business, and timespan.

After our call he sent me this email:

"Just this little bit of work is more strategic, organized, and data-driven than others."

Most reps go off gut and anecdote. The ones who run the numbers find the patterns everyone else misses.

content:
⛔️Warning: Don't accept a position with a company “going upmarket” without asking these 5 questions. 
 
When I made the move, I didn’t know about these land mines 💣... 
 
The company I joined was hugely successful. I thought going upmarket would be smooth ⛵️ 
 
I was wrong 🙈 
 
 
Here are 5️⃣ issues I wish I’d asked about: 
 
 
🎥 GOT ENTERPRISE STORIES? 
Most true ENT companies couldn’t care less about success in SMB/ Mid Market. United Airlines will not be impressed with our product's success in a company with 150 employees. 
 
--> Key qq: "What are the best stories about how ENT accounts have created success with this product?" 
 
 
🐏 HOW DO BATTERING RAMS GET PAID? 
Sellers in companies "going upmarket" spend 2-3 years educating the Enterprise about the product's existence. 
 
Since you’ll essentially be a battering ram trying to crack enterprise accounts, how will you get paid? 50/50 split? If so, don't count on making anything more than your base for 2-3 years. 
 
--> Key qq: "Show me the comp plan" 
 
 
📅 DO THE TIMELINES MATCH? 
I had a deal with a 19k person financial services org that took over 24 mos to close. 
 
That wasn't unusual in ENT. Most of the team didn't make quota for 2-3 years. 
 
--> Key qq: "Since you are going upmarket & it takes time to educate the Enterprise market, how will quotas be structured?" 
 
 
🧙🏻‍♂️🔮 WHO ARE THE GURUS? 
Who are their advisors & sales leaders? I wrongly assumed our company was being advised by folks who had experience going upmarket. (ie qualified to give us directions because they had made the journey before.) 
 
Same with Enterprise leaders. Best if they *have made the upmarket journey before*. NOT just leaders who've always been with enterprise orgs. 
 
--> Key qq: "Can you walk me through who our top advisors are? Hiring philosophy for the ENT sales leaders?" 
 
 
👮🏼‍♀️ HOW GOOD ARE WE AT THE BIG 3? 
Security, Reporting & Governance - ENT handles these much differently than SMB. 
 
These 3 issues were why big deals took so long to close-if they closed at all. 
 
I and several of my peers lost 7 figure deals - even though there was pain, motivated Exec buyers & good multi-threading. The deals died because we didn't have one of the Big 3 that ENT orgs required. 
 
--> Key qq: "Can you walk me through how the product meets the Security, Reporting & Governance of ENT orgs? 
 
 
Real talk: Founders get overly confident when there's lots of traction in SMB & MM. 
 
They're convinced that the ENT will “fall in line “. Just deals with extra 0’s. 
 
⚠️NOT true 
 
 
Take it from someone who's been there & got the hoodie. 
 
Asking these questions can save a lot of❤️‍🩹 
 
What did I forget?

content:
Cost of inaction got a rep to President's Club. But if we'd used it two months earlier, it would have killed the deal. Cost of inaction only works after 3 things are true:

1. They've agreed they have a problem worth solving.

If we quantify the cost of inaction before they've bought into the problem, we look irrelevant. They're not ready to hear it.


2. We have a real champion, not just a coach.

A champion has influence, has something to gain personally or professionally, and wants us to win. Not just "someone who takes our calls."

Champions tell us which metrics actually move the needle internally.


3. We've validated pricing with that champion first.

To quantify the cost of doing nothing, we have to know the cost of doing something. If pricing hasn't been discussed, the comparison falls flat.

One more thing:

Never surprise leadership with COI before your champion sees it.

An old boss told me: Kindergartners like surprises. Executives do not.

Build it with your champion. Let them shape it. Then they become the one presenting your math internally, not you.

Cost of inaction is powerful. But timing is everything.

content:
Listen to what happened when a top 1% Enterprise seller used a 1 sentence strategy & won over a Fortune 500 CEO.

Here's how it went down, and how you can do it too.

​
In Q3, one of the Enterprise reps I coach faced a unique dilemma.

​
She had worked hard all year to get a deal going with Lululemon, a $39.2B member of the Fortune 500.

She'd been onsite, worked with ~60 people to multi-thread & come with a Point of View.

She knew her solution was aligned with a C-Level Priority. Problem was, her solution was a small piece of the puzzle and she needed a way to help the CEO understand its importance.

​
A group of champions let the rep know they were presenting to the CEO in a Q3 leadership meeting. 

The AE had to help these champions to show HOW critical her solution was - with a very succinct explanation.
​
​We decided we needed an analogy. 
​

To create the perfect analogy, we went to work researching the CEO. On his public Instagram page, we found our answer.

His Insta was plastered with photos of him & the Lulu team, competing together in triathlons. He'd given multiple interviews on what triathlons meant to his personal and professional life.
​

So we came up with this analogy:

--> "Using the current solution for this initiative would be like using a beach cruiser for the bike portion of a triathlon."

​
If you're unfamiliar with a beach cruiser, it's a bike invented in the 1960's. With the basket in front. Not exactly triathlon material.

Which was exactly why it made the perfect analogy.

​
--> ​"Using the current solution for this initiative would be like using a beach cruiser for the bike portion of a triathlon."
​
​​
The analogy communicated 3 Crucial Realities to the CEO - using language from HIS world:

Their current solution

1/ was OUTDATED
2/ was THE WRONG TOOL for the job
3/ COULD NOT accomplish their objectives 

All without a word about features & functions… which the CEO didn't need to hear about and would have forgotten instantly.
​

​The analogy sealed the deal. The CEO got the picture, and this rep just got a 6-figure Closed Won.

Would that analogy been enough all by itself?

Of course not.

​
This Enterprise rep is a absolute pro, and she'd done all the groundwork.

The on-sites, the multi-threading, the Point of View and Business case.

She had all the right elements. The analogy was the catalyst.

​​
You've got some deals right now where you've laid all the groundwork.

What can you use as your catalyst?

content:
As a new AE, I got ghosted a lot after Pricing meetings. Now I know I was making 3 mistakes. Here's how I fixed that.
 
 
Where I effed up (accidentally):
 
---> Going in blind 
---> Doing all the numbers myself 
---> Yes means nothing without HOW 
 
 
How I fixed it: 
 
---> Going in blind 
 
Presenting pricing to an Executive Sponsor without a Champion looking over the deck first was my 1st problem. 
 
I was going in blind at a crucial point in the deal. (Which also put my Champion at risk.) 
 
I learned to set up a pre-meeting with my Champion. 
 
This sounds like --> 
"Aaron, I'm working on the proposal for Angie. I want to make you look good. And make the best use of Angie's time. Can I send you what I've done so far, and put 15 minutes on your calendar Thursday morning at 9am for us to look at it together?" 
 
 
TL:DR --> No presentation without collaboration 
 
 
 
---> Doing all the numbers myself 
 
Every software company in the world has some sort of ROI tool. 
 
It was easy to plug all the numbers in myself. 
 
Don't repeat my mistake. 
 
 
Our champion - and ideally others from the buying committee- should collaborate on the business case. 
 
If you don’t get their input, they won't believe the numbers. 
 
Buyers need to know where the numbers came from anyway. They're the ones who have to defend them. 
 
And that will happen at an internal meeting you won't be invited to. 
 
 
Asking for an ROI session sounds like --> 
“We have a couple of internal resources to help you put together the business case. Most folks find them helpful because they don’t have to start from scratch. The first pass at this should take 15-20 minutes. How is 9 AM on Thursday?” 
 
 
TL:DR --> No calculation without collaboration 
 
 
 
---> Yes means nothing without HOW 
 
This game changer is from Chris Voss, and fixed my longest running mistake. 
 
What often gets us ghosted after a pricing meeting is telling them how much it will cost in terms of dollars, but giving them no idea how much it will cost in terms of time. 
 
 
Every pricing meeting should include an overview of implementation. 
 
One slide for a small - midsize deal. 
 
For enterprise, the pricing meeting should include folks from implementation and CS. 
 
 
Up to this point, the buying committee has likely only seen people from sales. 
 
Helping Buyers put names and faces with those who will implement & support them is a way to lower risk. 
 
 
The sale may be 'the end' for the rep, but it's just the beginning for the customer. 
 
Clients need to feel secure about what happens in the next chapter of this adventure. 
 
Or they won't go. 
 
 
TL:DR --> No price presentation without implementation 
 
 
Hopefully this saves someone from making my same mistakes. 
 
What did I miss? Let's help some people close their Q4 deals!

"This was all my idea... so I'm on the hook! 😧" That's literally what my Champion texted me while we waited for the contract to get signed.

And it hit me. While it feels risky to be a seller, it’s FAR more risky to be a Buyer.

Buyers use their social capital to start the evaluation. They convince their team to take the meeting. They navigate procurement and legal and security.

And when Buyers are off doing that work, this is “the silent stretch.” They’re not meeting with sellers.

They’re discussing internally. And it’s this space between meetings where deals live or die.

But most sellers disappear in this stretch.

We think our job as sellers is to show up prepared for calls, ask good Discovery questions, present pricing and handle objections. But Buyers make the most important decisions about us in the moments we're not even there.

They're wondering:
"Does this vendor actually get what we're trying to do?"
Does this product really work for companies like ours?"
"Will they be there when things get hard?"

Here are 3 ways I've learned to show Buyers they matter - especially in those silent stretches:

1/ Send signals that you're listening. 
After a call where someone mentioned a concern, send a 30-second video addressing just that concern. 

2/ Make their job easier before they ask.
 Champions are trying to sell internally for us. Help them ‘connect the dots’ by enabling them with specific resources for specific stakeholders.

3/ Stay present without being in the room.
This is where Consensus  is a game-changer. Every stakeholder can interact with a personalized demo on their own time - and sellers can see what questions they're asking, what features they're focused on, what concerns are coming up.

If a deal feels like it might slip at signature, we didn't lose it in the final week. We lost it two months ago when we failed to answer the buyer's unspoken questions:

content:
After 7+ years in Enterprise sales, these are the 5 questions I ask Executives on deals that keep pushing out. 
 
They help me figure out which deals are might be delayed vs. deals that are dying☠️ 
 
There are 5 different areas. And the last one is the most important at EOY.
 
 
Here are the 5 questions: 
 
 
💰1) CONTEXT 
"We were originally working to get this started in Q1. Sounds like this now might be a Q2 thing. 𝗜𝘀 𝘁𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝗱𝘂𝗲 𝘁𝗼 𝗕𝘂𝗱𝗴𝗲𝘁, 𝗕𝗮𝗻𝗱𝘄𝗶𝗱𝘁𝗵 - 𝗼𝗿 𝗯𝗼𝘁𝗵?" 
 
Follow ups: 
 
"Ok got it. What changes in Q2?" 
 
"Has Q2 budget been earmarked already?" 
 
"Curious - what else is being implemented Q2?" 
 
 
 
📊2) PRIORITIES 
"Is there a specific goal or initiative in Q1-Q2 this aligns with?" 
 
 
 
🤔3) TIMING 
"November/December is often when Executives finalize goals for the next year. How are you feeling about your upcoming targets related to [problem I solve]?" 
 
 
 
💥4) IMPACT 
"Based on your current & future targets, when would you need to see an impact from something like [my product]?" 
 
 
 
❓5) PROCESS 
"How long did it take to get through Legal the last time you bought software? How about Security? Based on those experiences, do we think a Q4 timeline is even possible? Or is this more likely a Q1 thing?" 
 
 
 
If they can't (or won't) go into specifics, the deal is probably dying 😭 
 
There is an inverse relationship between vague answers 
 
& deals that close🕵️‍♀️🔍

The difference?

IKEA = 6-month eval + 6-month implementation with his competitors
Wayfair = 24-hour POC deployment, product ready to use immediately


His Discovery calls immediately got better because prospects actually understood what made his product different.

The lesson? Stop living in tech speak.
Find analogies from the real world that everyone can relate to.

content:
The VP ended our interview by saying "We're not hiring anyone in Texas anytime soon." Translation: Thanks, but no thanks. Most people would have just sent a polite thank-you email and moved on.

I did something different.


The Setup:
During the interview, he mentioned a big recruiting meeting coming up in a few weeks. They were scaling at warp speed, BUT he made it clear he didn't see Texas as a priority for hiring.

The VP was focused on the Fortune 500, so he wanted to hire another ENT rep in NYC. (They already had 4.)


My Follow-Up:
As soon as our call ended, I found data showing Dallas ranked #2 behind NYC as the headquarters for Fortune 500 companies. (In a Fortune article, no less.) Yet, the VP had only 1 rep in Texas.

Within 15 minutes of hanging up, I sent him a screenshot with this note:
"Couldn't resist sending this from Fortune, showing Dallas as #2 behind NYC. Seemed like it could be an important data point for your recruiting meeting in a few weeks. More is more on data, no? :)"


The Result:
VP called me back within 5 minutes.
I talked with the recruiter the very next week.
I was the next AE they hired - when they didn't even have an open role in Texas.


Why This Worked:
It didn't just show gratitude - it helped him see a blind spot.
^Just like I'd need to do with prospects who "weren't looking to buy right now."
^^I showed him (in real-time) how I could add value and shift perspective.


The Framework:
--> Listen for upcoming meetings, projects, or priorities during the interview
--> Find ONE relevant insight that challenges their current thinking or adds value
--> Send it fast: screenshot + 2-3 sentence note connecting the dots. Keep it brief and helpful (not salesy)


Bottom Line:
Your interview follow-up isn't just a thank-you note.* It's your first chance to show how you actually work.

Most candidates tell hiring managers what they can do.

Show them instead.


PS-
What's worked for you in interview follow-ups? Share your stories as encouragement (and to spark fresh ideas) for our friends who are looking for new roles!


*PPS-
You should ALWAYS send a thank you note! To everyone you talk to... recruiters, team members, cross functional managers. It is *shocking* how often just that can make you stand out. 🫶

content:
Here's how you can multi-thread without "going around" your Champion
(because ~67% of sellers avoid it ...they're afraid of stepping on their Champion's toes).

Here's the truth: Your Champion actually needs you to multi-thread.

And I learned exactly how to do it without going around them - straight from a VP of Sales who closed $47M in ARR last year.


Here are his 3 insights (and how to use them):

⭕ It's risky to be the champion for a big purchase
Your Champion put their neck on the line to get you in the door. They're using their social capital with every email they send about your solution.
The LAST thing they want? To look like they didn't do their homework.


⭕ 3 Power Levels of personas need to be in an evaluation to de-risk it
Champions are experts at how to do their jobs - not how to buy our thing. They appreciate it when we guide them.

Try this: "Typically when folks evaluate XYZ, leaders from Legal Operations, Finance, and HR all get involved. Would it make sense to include Shonda, your VP of HR, and Christina, your VP of Finance in our next conversation?"

You're not going around them. You're protecting them.


⭕ We should communicate differently to each of the 3 levels Power Levels 
 Each persona cares about different things:

✅ Executives: Does this help us reach goals and/or lower our risk?
✅ Managers: Does this help my team with a metric that matters?
✅ End users: Does this help me do my job easier/faster/better?

EXAMPLE: Here's what a meeting recap email sounds like for a CFO or VP of Finance:

"Anna, I met with your Legal Ops team today about hard savings from workflow automation.

- They quantified $3.6MM in savings / year
 - And they identified these savings will be immediate, as IT involvement isn't needed

You should have the invite for our next meeting on the 28th. Will send you the readout afterward.
Cheers"

Notice what's missing? Any mention of product features. Or even our product's name.

Just quantified impact, timeline, and specific ROI. In a format they can read on their phone without scrolling.

_________________

The bottom line:

When we know how to help our Champions navigate the buying process, everyone wins... literally.

As always - it's about them, not about us/our stuff.

After 15 years and countless 7-figure deals, here are the **3 things nobody tells you to do FIRST** when you start in Enterprise:

I know because I stepped into my first ENT AE role and immediately felt like I'd been dropped in a foreign country without a map.

There I was, week 4, staring at my account list (2 giant insurance companies, 2 "household name" banks) with my heart pounding. I kept hoping there was a guide somewhere on how to land deals with these large accounts.

Yeah, ENT doesn't work like that.


So here are 3 things to do first:

1/ Map the Buying Maze (It's Not a Funnel, It's Spaghetti)
Enterprise buying looks like someone threw pasta at the wall.
Your champion says "I'll check with Legal." Legal loops in Security. Security wants Procurement. Then someone's CEO quits. Start over.

Do this: 
→ Book time with a top performer to map typical buying stages 
→ For each stage, document: Customer options | Your actions | Common roadblocks 
→ Include when to get IT/Legal/Security/Procurement involved

Why it matters: ENT buyers juggle 10-15 stakeholders. When you ask "What's next?" they freeze.

But when you say "At this point, teams typically bring in IT, set meetings with Legal, and polish the business case for the CFO. What makes sense for you?" - now you're guiding, not guessing.


2/ The CSM = Your Secret Weapon
That CSM managing Apple? They've been there 5 yrs. They know everything.

And customers tell them what they'd NEVER tell sales.

Do this ASAP: 
→ Set up weekly syncs with your CSM 
→ Ask in 1st meeting: "What do AEs here typically miss?" "What's one thing I should I ask customers that doesn't usually get asked?" 
→ Share everything - notes, recordings, concerns

CSMs get burned by AEs who overpromise & disappear. Show them you're different.

They'll tell you: "Your champion at Netflix is about to get reorg'd" or "Apple's procurement is backed up 90 days." Intel you can't buy.


3/ Memorize 6 Enterprise Stories (Yes, With Note Cards)
ENT buyers only care about ENT examples. Period.

The system: 
→ Find 6-8 stories from TRUE enterprise accounts 
→ Write each on a note card using STAR: 
• Situation: Sarah, CISO at 5,000-person firm 
• Trouble: Security audits taking 3 weeks, blocking launches 
• Action: Implemented platform with phased rollout 
• Result: Cut audit time to 3 days, saved $2M

→ Practice OUT LOUD for 10 min every morning until automatic
Note cards hit visual + auditory + kinesthetic learning. Triple threat.

When a buyer mentions security concerns, you instantly respond: "That's exactly what Sarah at [similar company] faced..."

Instant credibility.
___

Here's the uncomfy thing about that big ENT promotion: Most AEs waste 6+ mo figuring this out through painful trial & error. (I sure did.)

You can compress the learning curve: 
*Map the chaos. 
*Partner with CSMs. 
*Master your stories.

Everything else is noise.

content:
In May 2021, I had trouble getting out of bed for the 5th week in a row. 
 
Just moving enough to push the covers back, sit up & walk to the kitchen....it was almost too much effort. 
 

Once I was up, all I wanted to do was sit and stare at the wall. 
 
Not an exaggeration. I literally just wanted to sit and stare. 
 

To say this was "not like me" is an understatement. 
 
I've been a driven Type A since birth...."She's got a motor" is how one colleague described my work ethic. 
 
So, even though my brain felt foggy and slow, I realized this was deeply abnormal. 
 

Luckily I reached out to my doctor and started medication for depression the same week. 
 
I was amazed at how much better I felt in the next few weeks, even though it took several months to get the dosage exactly right. 
 

Depression and anxiety run in my family, but I had always been able to manage with coping skills. Journaling, yoga, exercise, etc. 
 
But after a huge loss in our family in 2021, coping skills weren't enough anymore. 

Looking back, I should have started medication months before I did. 
 

That's 1 of the BIGGEST things depression does - clouds your judgment. Including judgment about your own mental health. 
 
HINT: If you are wondering "am I depressed?", you probably are. Worth getting a professional opinion. ASAP. 
 
 
 
What I'm glad I did: 
--> therapy 
--> medication 
--> talking with friends & family (should have done this sooner)
 
 
What I wish I'd done: 
 --> seen a doctor faster
 --> used FMLA to rest & recover, instead of "pushing through"


What you can do:
—> take that one next step you’ve been thinking about
If you've been thinking about getting help, please don't wait. 

_______________________________
 
***ALSO...Sadly there is still a stigma within some families, cultures and religions around mental health. 

When I was growing up, many of my family members didn’t really believe that mental health was “a thing.” 

I was also raised in a fundamentalist Religious denomination where you were just supposed to pray about things. Without taking any other steps. That kind of thinking kept me trapped - for years.

_______________________________

It's been a long journey for me. Hopefully this helps some others get started on their own path.

content:
Kayla closed a $600K ACV deal and secured her President's Club beach chair using this approach. "L-E-A-D".... here's how you can use it.

Premise: If our deals keep slipping, stalling, or ghosting, we're not fighting a closing problem.

We're fighting scattered selling. And scattered selling is a killer.


Here's what helps us overcome scattered selling & move deals forward:

L - Lead the sale
Our buyer is juggling 5 stakeholders, comparing 3 vendors, and terrified of making the wrong decision. If we're waiting for them to tell you what's next, we've already lost.


E - Excavate pain
"What are your pain points?" That's not discovery. Try this instead: "What did you get hired to change?" or "This has probably been a problem for a while. What's making it urgent NOW?"

One question that works almost every time: "Could you walk me through the ripple effects this is having on the business?"


A - Always reduce friction
There are 3 buyer modes: Education (not buying soon), Urgent (needed it yesterday), and Planning (interested but not immediate). Read the room wrong and we're dead. So we ask about *matching* their urgency.

Then teach them HOW to buy: "Typically when companies evaluate this, they involve leaders from Legal, Finance, and HR. Does it make sense to loop them in now?"


D - De-risk to close
Most deals don't die because buyers don't like you. They die because buyers are paralyzed by risk. Your job? Make saying yes feel safer than saying no.

content:
I've watched hundreds of deals die 48 hours before signature. There's one litmus test that predicts which 'done deals' will actually close:

Will our buyer agree to an onboarding introduction meeting?

If they won't, our deal isn't as solid as we think.


Here's why this matters:

The Introduction Meeting = The Real Commitment Test 
Buyers who refuse this meeting aren't ready to sign. Period. 
They're either:
  - Afraid to schedule because they're not confident about internal approval
  - Using your proposal as leverage with another vendor
  - Still shopping around despite telling you otherwise

When they hesitate, ask: "Could you walk me through how this meeting might not be the best next step for your team? And what you have in mind that would work better?"


Why This De-Risks Your Deal:
1. Familiarity Breeds Confidence 
When buyers meet your onboarding team, they start envisioning the partnership. Our brains resist unfamiliar scenarios - this meeting removes that psychological barrier.

2. Process Clarity Eliminates Fear 
Buyers see exactly how implementation works: timelines, training, value realization. No more wondering "what happens after we sign?"

3. Relationship Building Starts Early 
The stronger the relationship between buyer and delivery team, the smoother the onboarding and the better the reference.


How to Set It Up- 

Your email should include 3 elements:
  - Photo of the main onboarding contact (faces create familiarity)
  - Credibility statement about your onboarding team
  - Clear role description of what buyers can expect


The Framework: 
Position it as value for them, not process for you.

"I'd love to introduce you to Sarah, who'll be your implementation lead. She's worked with companies like [similar logo] and has a 95% on-time delivery rate. This 15-minute call will map out your exact go-live timeline."

—

Real buyers embrace next steps.
Tire-kickers avoid them.
Use this test before you celebrate the close.

content:
After working with 1,000+ AEs and watching careers implode, here are the 5 Sales Commandments that separate pros from amateurs:

Thou Shalt Not:

1. Calculate Commission Before Close 
Nothing screams "desperate rookie" like spreadsheets full of fantasy math. I've seen AEs spend houses they haven't earned and cars they can't afford. Count money when it hits your bank account. Not before.

2. Promise Features That Don't Exist 
Your product roadmap isn't a sales tool. It's a lawsuit waiting to happen. Sell what exists today, not what might exist next quarter. Your legal team will thank you.

3. Sell What They Don't Need 
Short-term thinking that kills long-term relationships. Overselling creates churn, bad references, and clawbacks. Build customers, not one-time transactions.

4. Backstab Your Teammates 
Sales floors aren't gladiator arenas. The rep who steals leads, badmouths colleagues, or sabotages team deals always gets exposed. Always. Your reputation travels faster than your quota attainment.

5. "Wing It" in Pricing Conversations 
"Let me get back to you on that" kills momentum and credibility. Know your pricing, discounting authority, and competitive positioning cold. Executives don't respect sellers who can't talk numbers.

—

Break these rules?

Break your career.

What other commandments am I missing?

You're probably working too many deals right now. (I know, I know... hear me out.) Here's the thing nobody wants to admit: Chasing every opportunity is actually killing our close rates.

It's like trying to water 50 plants with one watering can. Most of them end up half-dead anyway.

The truth? Fewer deals = More wins.

Top performers ruthlessly cut the fat from their pipeline.


So how do you know which deals deserve your time?

I use two strategies that changed everything for me:

1) Grade Your Deals (My "IOP" System)
Companies have ICPs. I have IOPs: Ideal Opportunity Profiles.

Think of it like a report card for each deal. I score them based on 8 characteristics:

They have a Clear, Immediate Compelling Event: 20 points
Org is growing rapidly & Makes Decisions Fast: 15 points
Large ARR potential (# of End Users, etc.) : 15 points
Champion Who Gives the "Inside Scoop": 10 points
Responsive (Calls, Texts, Email): 10 points
Invest Heavily in Related Tech: 10 points
Specific Goals with Metrics: 10 points
Low Number of Obstacles: 10 points


The higher the score? That's where I spend my time and energy.
The low scores? They get the bare minimum.



2) The "3 Strikes You're Out" Rule
If I reach out 3 times across 3 different channels (email, text, LinkedIn) and get nothing back?

I close it out. Done.

This might sound obvious, but I spent *years* agonizing over when to let deals go.

Kept them on life support way too long.
Now I just... don't.

________________

Here's what bugs me: Most companies don't train on this practical, day-to-day stuff.

The "basics" of sales are rarely basic. Or obvious.

But once you start giving your pipeline a report card?
Everything changes.

There's one habit that separates struggling AEs from elite sellers: They treat executive meetings like product demos instead of strategy sessions.

While average reps show features and ask basic questions, elite sellers arrive with insights that reshape how executives think about their business.

Here's the exact 5-step intelligence framework that turns executives into champions:

1. Survey Their Current Team First 
Hit LinkedIn Sales Navigator. Filter for team members active in the past 30 days. Send tailored messages focused on outcomes, not features. Ask about pain points and advice for approaching their exec.

Your exec opener: "After talking with 5 of your sales reps in the East, it sounds like AE-created pipeline is a big focus. What are the biggest risks you see to pipe build in the next 3-6 months?"

2. Analyze Their Customer Stories 
Study their case studies and customer logos. What problems do they solve? Who do they serve? What gets mentioned repeatedly - and what's conspicuously absent?

Your exec opener: "You've got impressive logos - Gong, Salesloft, Drift all using your platform. Given that renewals are getting leaner across SaaS, what are the 2 biggest churn risks you're watching next quarter?"

3. Mine RepVue and Glassdoor for Team Intelligence 
71% vs 21% quota attainment tells different stories. Use filters and search functions to find specific insights about team dynamics and performance gaps.

Your exec opener: "Building pipeline has been brutal in 2025. How are you thinking about attainment risks in the next 3 months?"

4. Study Product Reviews for Competitive Gaps 
G2 and Capterra reviews reveal what customers love - and what they're missing. Look for gaps your solution fills.

Your exec opener: "Your customers rave about functionality and ease of use on G2. The only complaint was insufficient CSM time. Is this a top risk you're addressing this quarter?"

5. Consume Their Content Podcasts, speeches, interviews. 
Find their personal stories and philosophies. Reference their own ideas to open conversations.

Your exec opener: "You made a brilliant point about sales-marketing alignment on Kevin Dorsey's podcast. How do lead conversion issues and slower deal velocity rank as risks you're discussing with marketing?"


—

This level of preparation doesn't just impress executives.

It positions you as a strategic advisor, not another vendor.

Your first meetings will be 5x better because you're leading with insight, not interrogation.

content:
Ever walk into a conference and immediately regret every life choice that led you there? Here are 6 things that helped me.

Confession: As an introvert, I used to DREAD conferences. Standing alone, clutching lukewarm coffee, desperately hoping the earth would swallow me whole.

After ~2 years, I realized I was just doing it wrong.

Recently coached a seller heading to her first treasury conference and dreading it. 

Here's the exact 6 things I told her (that transformed how I approach conferences):


1/ Figure out WHO will actually be there
Most conference websites are marketing fluff. Dig deeper:
→ Check speaker titles (reveals attendee seniority)
→ Look for "free tickets to treasury managers" (tells you the audience)
→ Notice if sessions are Strategies vs. How-To's (execs attend the former)

We discovered speakers included retired CFOs and VPs of Treasury. Real decision-makers, not just end users.


2/ Create your "value-first" conversation toolkit
Nothing kills networking faster than forced small talk. Come armed with value:
→ 2 podcast recommendations per persona
→ Names of a few thought leaders + recent news
→ Customer success stories for common challenges

Now instead of awkward silence, she can say: "Just discovered this Treasury podcast by Eleanor Hill on AI implementation. Have you checked it out?"


3/ Stack rank your target accounts
You can't remember 100 accounts while speed-networking. Create a mobile list of:
→ Top 20 "dream" accounts likely to attend
→ Specific folks you want to meet

When you see name badges, you can quickly check priority level.


4/ Focus on executive-level sessions
Skip the technical "how-to" sessions. You're not there to learn the job - you're there to understand the people who do it.

Must-attend sessions:
→ Anything with "CFO" or "VP Treasury" speakers
→ Business problems your software solves
→ AI and future of treasury discussions

These teach you their vocabulary, priorities, and fears.


5/ Master the art of non-salesy follow-up
Instead of collecting LI profiles for follow-up, create reasons for valuable 2nd conversations:

"Based on your challenges, I'd love to introduce you to [customer exec] who recently solved something similar. What's the best way to connect you two?"

They give contact info because they WANT you to follow up.


6/ Set a clear success metric
My client's goal: 10 quality conversations. Not leads. Not demos. Just 10 genuine exchanges where she learned something valuable or provided value.

This removes the desperate "I need to sell something" energy that repels prospects.


Bottom line: Conferences are about showing up with purpose and a plan.

When you know exactly who to meet, what value to provide, and how to follow up meaningfully... suddenly conferences transform from anxiety-inducing nightmares into pipeline accelerators.

 When I was at Outreach, I had 12 large ENT deals sitting in Q4 pipeline.
 And I was drowning.

I realized I was prioritizing the deals with buyers who picked up my calls, scheduled meetings, and were fun to talk to.

 But my VP stopped me cold:

That became my gut-check question.
 Because talking to you ≠ buying from you.


 So I built a simple Deal Grader (A–F, just like back when I was teaching).


 Here are the 8 criteria that actually predict "closeability":

20 pts:  Compelling Event (IPO, board meeting, turnaround plan, new leadership)

20 pts:  Fast-Paced Org (do they move faster than your average customer?)

10 pts:  Real Champion (not a “contact” — someone giving you inside baseball)

10 pts:  Invests Heavily in Related Tech (already shows budget + priorities)

10 pts:  Specific Goals w/ Metrics (6% increase ≠ “we just want to improve”)

10 pts:  Responsiveness (consistent, proactive, not ghosting between steps)

10 pts:  Low Number of Obstacles (no nightmare integrations or 12-step paper process)

10 pts:  Deal Size Drivers (for some: end users, for others: # of sites, etc.)


Add it up. Grade it out of 100.
 If it’s a D? Drop it.
 If it’s an A? Double down.


I used this to quickly sort which of my 12 deals were worth real attention.
It worked then — and I still use it today with Enterprise reps in my Accelerator sessions.


Stop wasting your last 68 working days chasing deals that talk nice but won’t buy.
Deals don’t close because they “feel good.”
Deals close because buyers do what buyers do.

content:
I watched one of my coaching clients clinch a Fortune 500 deal with a single sentence. Here's the 1-sentence strategy that sealed a 6-figure win - and how to build your own:

The Setup: 
My client had spent months building the perfect enterprise deal with a $39B Fortune 500 company. Multi-threaded across 60+ stakeholders. Built consensus. Aligned with C-level priorities. But her solution was a small piece of a massive initiative.
The champions were presenting to the CEO in Q3 leadership review. They needed one compelling way to explain why this "small piece" was actually critical.

The Research: 
We dove deep into the CEO's public presence. His Instagram was filled with triathlon photos - him competing with his team, interviews about how triathlons shaped his leadership philosophy. This wasn't casual interest. This was core identity.

The One-Sentence Close: 
"Using the current solution for this initiative would be like using a beach cruiser for the bike portion of a triathlon."

Why This Worked: 
That single analogy communicated three business realities using his language:
   1/ Current solution = outdated (beach cruiser from the 1960s)
   2/ Wrong tool for the objective (basket bike vs. racing bike)
   3/ Guaranteed failure at scale (you can't win triathlons on beach cruisers)

No features. No functions. No technical details the CEO would forget instantly.


The Catalyst Effect: 
The analogy didn't win the deal alone - she'd done months of enterprise groundwork. But it crystallized everything in terms the CEO immediately understood and couldn't ignore.


Your Framework:
   1/ Research obsessively - social media, podcasts, speeches, interviews
   2/ Find their passion - what do they talk about outside of work?
   3/ Bridge the gap - connect their world to your business case
   4/ Test the analogy - does it explain the core problem/solution clearly?

The Result: Six-figure Closed Won. The CEO got the picture instantly.

—

Your competition is speaking in features and benefits.
You're going to speak in their language.

In 2022, I went into Q4 extremely short on pipeline. Like my pipeline was so small that when I started thinking about it, I got overwhelmed & became paralyzed with fear. Cue spiral into full panic attack mode.

One Saturday morning, I sat down at the computer (after a week of trying to convince myself to prospect but instead just wasted time worrying).

Told myself I would not get up from the computer until I had a solid plan for  creating opps that could close quickly.

These are the 3 things I came up with. They're the same 3 things I coach AEs on today.

-> Previous Exposure
-> New Strategy
-> Industry Shift

After analyzing 100s of closed-won deals, these 3 compelling events show up again and again:

1) PREVIOUS EXPOSURE:
My old boss used to say: "They have to tell us no a couple times before they tell us yes."
→ Pull CRM report of accounts with previous opps 
 → Upload to Sales Nav as an Account List
 → Check if contacts from past opps changed jobs in the last year
 → Find NEW contacts at accounts who previously worked at your current customers

2) NEW STRATEGY:
Look for:
 → New leadership (especially VP/CXO level)
 → Reorganizations
 → New initiatives
Set up Google Alerts for target accounts with terms like "appoints new," "reorganization," "strategic initiative"

3) MASSIVE INDUSTRY SHIFT (external pressure forcing change)
→ Read industry publications for the 2-3 massive shifts in sectors you sell to
 → Look at your Closed-Won deals - what common pressures were those industries facing?
 → Prioritize accounts in those industries that ALSO have previous exposure or new leadership


Outreach That Works - 

Your email should be:
-Less than 75 words
-Lead with an observation about a compelling event at THEIR company
-Your POV on the impact
-How you've helped similar companies (name drop 3-5 customers)

Example: "Saw [Company] announced [compelling event]. Based on what I'm seeing with [Customer A, B, C], the impact is usually [specific outcome]. We've helped those companies [specific result]. Worth a conversation?"

Calling:
-Write the email first (becomes a script)
-Lead with the compelling event
-Send email immediately with subject line: "voicemail"


Reality Check: These won't ALL close in Q4. But they have the HIGHEST PROBABILITY

*Previous Exposure = less education needed, shorter sales cycle
*New Strategy = budget allocated, urgency built in
*Industry Shift = problem is undeniable, status quo isn't an option

When you focus on accounts with these compelling events, you're fishing where the fish are actually biting.

The AEs I coach who do this consistently see 2-3x more meetings booked and 41-57% shorter sales cycles.

content:
"There's one moment in every sales call where buyers either lean in or check out: When we say 'We've helped other companies like yours...' and then fumble the story."

While average reps scramble to remember "that one client who had good results," consistent overachievers have 20+ stories memorized and ready for any situation.

Here's the framework that turns customer stories into deal-closing weapons:


The S.T.A.R. Method for Sales Stories

S - Situation: Set the context fast "Sarah, the VP of Sales at a 500-person SaaS company, was facing their biggest quarter ever..."
T - Trouble: Define the specific problem "Their top 3 reps were spending 40% of their time on manual research instead of selling. Pipeline was suffering."
A - Action: What the customer DID (not what you sold) "Sarah implemented a systematic approach to automate prospect research and prioritize high-value targets."
R - Result: Quantified outcomes "Within 90 days, her team increased qualified meetings by 60% and shortened sales cycles by 3 weeks."


Critical Rules We Can't Miss:

1. Customer = Hero, Your Product = Tool 
Never say "they bought our solution and got results." 
Say "they implemented this strategy using our platform."

2. Specificity = Credibility 
Use first names, titles, company size, and timeframes. 
"Two months ago" hits different than "recently."

3. Match Story to Moment 
Discovery calls need problem-focused stories. 
Pricing calls need ROI-focused stories. 

Prep 3-5 stories per meeting type.


The System: 
Learn one new customer story weekly. 
Practice with flashcards until you can tell each one in under 60 seconds. 
Build a library of 20+ stories across different use cases, company sizes, and outcomes.

—

Stories don't just illustrate your point.
They make buyers believe their success is inevitable.

content:
Can we please talk about the politics around pipeline? 🤫 And if you think there are no politics here ...oh honey... bless your heart

Nobody tells you this when you start, btw.

Your manager won't pull you aside on day one and explain the unwritten rules around pipeline management.

But here's the thing: how you handle pipeline affects your relationship with your manager AND their boss.

Think of pipeline like navigating through unfamiliar territory. There are roads that are safe, shortcuts to take, and routes that will get you pulled over. But nobody gave you the map.

So let me draw you one.

There are 3 main areas where your manager is measured on pipeline:

1) Creating Pipeline
-->Philosophy: When does an opportunity actually count?
Different orgs have wildly different views.
At Salesforce, we had Stage 0 deals - "Aspirational pipe." Meaning they had a problem we could solve & we were actively working it.

For Enterprise reps, this approach makes sense. Helps execs align resources early.

Other teams? "Qualified deals only." Meaning real interest after a demo.

-->Politics: AE-created pipe & CYA
a) AE vs SDR created opps - In some orgs, there's massive pressure to show AE-sourced pipeline. This affects your relationship with the SDR team AND how your manager looks to leadership.

b) CYA piping - Some managers will ask you to add questionable deals just to show coverage. "Put it in so we look good."


2) Moving Deals Through
-->Philosophy: Deal velocity

-->Politics: Also deal velocity (but with more scrutiny)
Your manager is measured on how many deals sit in each stage & how long they stay there.

The bigger the deal, the more eyes on it.


3) Taking Deals Out of Pipeline
-->Philosophy: Forecasting accuracy

-->Politics: CYA (again)
Some managers aren't going to like this one, but I wish someone explained it to me years ago.

With forecasting, sometimes you have to weigh YOUR internal standing against your manager's.

In healthy relationships, you collaborate on this. But sometimes you'll get pressure to leave a dead deal in your pipe because your manager needs the coverage.

**Real talk: Proceed with caution. Understand how much relational capital you have vs your manager vs their boss. And how forecasting accuracy will affect each of you.

______________

How to navigate this:

Ask your manager early: "Different leaders view pipeline differently. I want to make our team look good and make sure we're aligned. How are you thinking about when Opps should be entered? Moved to next stage? Taken out of pipe?"
______________

Important callout ➡️ You may not agree with the politics.
I've fundamentally disagreed with the approach at several places I've worked.
But it's still critical to understand how pipeline works at your org.

Especially these days when PIPs get handed out like after-dinner mints.
Ignore this at your own peril.

Would love to hear from sales leaders: What else should reps understand about pipeline politics?
