content:
Here's what worked to unstick a $1.2M deal that had been in procurement for 2 weeks.

The seller had been sending polite follow-ups to "Brandon" in procurement every few days.

But nothing was moving. So here's what we did instead-


In our 1:1 session with the seller, here was my question: "Who has the most to GAIN if this deal gets signed?"

Not Brandon. Brandon gets paid whether that deal closes or not.


But here's who DOES have skin in the game (which the rep knew because he did great discovery) -->


Sarah (Account Manager): She's responsible for a $20 million spend by Target that the CEO believes should be $50 million. She needs better data to convince Target to carry more products.

Mike (VP of Sales): He reports directly to the CEO and is closely aligned with executives at Target. He knows Sarah needs data to get Target to $50M.

The CEO: He's publicly committed to 2.5x growth at Target and has been talking about it on podcasts.


👉 These people have everything to gain. Brandon in procurement? He just wants clean contracts.


So instead of pestering procurement, here's what we did:

1/ Reached out to Sarah: "Hey, wanted to give you a quick update. We're working with Brandon to get the contract finalized. What's your next Target meeting? Want to make sure we can provide competitive insights beforehand."

2/ Looped in Mike: "Contract is with procurement for final review. Knowing you have that Target strategy session coming up, we can have insights ready within 4 weeks of signature."

3/ Crafted an email to the CEO with subject line: "Closer to $50M at Target"
The message? "Exciting news - we're in final contract review with Brandon. Based on Sarah's upcoming July 25th Target meeting, we should be able to provide competitive insights by July 23rd if things stay on track."


What happened next?

The CEO forwarded that email to Brandon with: "Where are we with this? Need it prioritized."

Deal signed 2 days later. And the rep ended the year above 145%.


The lesson? We gotta stop following up with people who don't care about the timeline.

Instead, we update the people who have everything to gain from our solution working.

Procurement moves when business stakeholders apply pressure. Not when sellers send reminder emails.

It's based on simple human psychology: people will always find reasons to wait. Our job isn't to overcome every objection.

It's to help them understand that waiting has a price tag too.

content:
Here's a simple way to prep for Discovery calls in a world where 73% of B2B customers expect sellers to understand their unique needs. (SFDC report)

We can actually use it in every meeting from Discovery to Deciding on terms. 

And you won't likely get this from Onboarding or Enablement.


-----> Make a list of 10 impacts


We start with 1 problem our product solves. 
 
Then write down 10 impacts of not solving that problem. 
 
Here's an example of the list I made when I started at UserGems 💎 --> 
 
 
10 Impacts of Low Pipeline for a sales leader: 

-> Missing quota 
-> Career damage 
-> Slow revenue growth 
-> Increase Cost of Sale 
-> Decreased Profitability 
-> Not enough New Logos 
-> Infighting with the Marketing team 
-> High Customer Acquisition Cost (CAC) 
-> Increased Pressure on Improving Close Rates 
->Low team morale leads to rep Churn & Recruiting issues 
 
 
 
How can we find these impacts? Here are 3 different ways: 
 
1/ Read our org's customer stories/testimonials. What problems do they mention?

2/  Listen/read like our Buyer: industry podcasts, websites & newsletters. What problems are they always focused on?

3/ Ask a top-performing AE for what problems/impacts they hear ... after we've done our homework (i.e. found at least 4 yourself)
 

Once we find the top 3 problems we solve (directly sourced from our Buyers themselves, not our marketing 1 pagers), use a web search or ChatGPT prompt for the impact of those problems. Compare the results with our customer stories & what our top sellers say.

 
Rinse & repeat til we've got 10 impacts for at least 3 problems our product solves. 
 
 
 
***Now when we hear one of the problems come up on a call, we can ask a question that gives us valuable info on our buyers' business AND gives us credibility.*** 
 

--->Example: 
“Sounds like the economy has taken a toll on your pipeline. How is that affecting revenue growth, and the risks to your business in the next 3-6 months?” 
 
We've just shown we understand their world.

content:
As a new AE, I got ghosted a lot after Pricing meetings. Now I know I was making 3 mistakes. Here's how I fixed them.
 
 
Where I effed up (accidentally):
 
---> Going in blind 
---> Doing all the numbers myself 
---> Yes means nothing without HOW 
 
 
How I fixed it: 
 
---> Going in blind 
 
Presenting pricing to an Executive Sponsor without a Champion looking over the deck first was my 1st problem. 
 
I was going in blind at a crucial point in the deal. (Which also put my Champion at risk.) 
 
I learned to set up a pre-meeting with my Champion. 
 
This sounds like --> 
"Aaron, I'm working on the proposal for Angie. I want to make you look good. And make the best use of Angie's time. Can I send you what I've done so far, and put 15 minutes on your calendar Thursday morning at 9am for us to look at it together?" 
 
 
TL:DR --> No presentation without collaboration 
 
 
 
---> Doing all the numbers myself 
 
Every software company in the world has some sort of ROI tool. 
 
It was easy to plug all the numbers in myself. 
 
Don't repeat my mistake. 
 
 
Our champion - and ideally others from the buying committee- should collaborate on the business case. 
 
If you don’t get their input, they won't believe the numbers. 
 
Buyers need to know where the numbers came from anyway. They're the ones who have to defend them. 
 
And that will happen at an internal meeting you won't be invited to. 
 
 
Asking for an ROI session sounds like --> 
“We have a couple of internal resources to help you put together the business case. Most folks find them helpful because they don’t have to start from scratch. The first pass at this should take 15-20 minutes. How is 9 AM on Thursday?” 
 
 
TL:DR --> No calculation without collaboration 
 
 
 
---> Yes means nothing without HOW 
 
This game changer is from Chris Voss, and fixed my longest running mistake. 
 
What often gets us ghosted after a pricing meeting is telling them how much it will cost in terms of dollars, but giving them no idea how much it will cost in terms of time. 
 
 
Every pricing meeting should include an overview of implementation. 
 
One slide for a small - midsize deal. 
 
For enterprise, the pricing meeting should include folks from implementation and CS. 
 
 
Up to this point, the buying committee has likely only seen people from sales. 
 
Helping Buyers put names and faces with those who will implement & support them is a way to lower risk. 
 
 
The sale may be 'the end' for the rep, but it's just the beginning for the customer. 
 
Clients need to feel secure about what happens in the next chapter of this adventure. 
 
Or they won't go. 
 
 
TL:DR --> No price presentation without implementation 
 

 
Hopefully this saves someone from making my same mistakes.

I was struggling 14 years ago. Very unexpectedly, I became a single parent. 
 
And when I say struggle, I mean things got so tight financially that packs of gum were a frivolous expense. 
 
We did not take vacations or go to amusement parks. Heck, we didn’t even go out to eat. 
 
 
I was determined to neither go into debt, nor ask for money from my parents. 
 
And I was equally adamant that our lives would not stay that way. 
 
I made a plan to pivot to a new industry. 
 
 
And then researched, and networked, and checked out library books, and worked a lot of 18 hour days. 
 
I found a lot of dead ends. 
 
And cried more times than I’d like to remember. 
 
 
And today - after a loooooong series of ups and downs - my life is radically different. 
 
So...“if you’re going through hell, just keep going.” 
 
Rest if you can this weekend, and then keep putting one foot in front of the other. 
 
 
You will get there. 
 
It will all be okay. 
 
And what a story you’ll be able to tell. 🤗

content:
Here's a way to explain how your product is different without using tech jargon. Because people hate jargon (and it's boring as sh*t).

Had a coaching call last week where a seller was struggling to explain why his solution was different.

He kept saying things like "frictionless implementation" and "low-touch deployment."

The prospects weren't getting it.


So we tried something different.


👉 Instead of tech speak, we used an analogy everyone knows*:

"Most [software that solves this problem] like furniture from IKEA. Everything looks the same, and you spend months putting it together yourself."

"We're more like Wayfair. Shows up fully assembled and delivered to the exact spot you want it. You can use it same day."


The difference?

IKEA = 6-month eval + 6-month implementation with his competitors
Wayfair = 24-hour POC deployment, product ready to use immediately


His Discovery calls immediately got better because prospects actually understood what made his product different.

The lesson? Stop living in tech speak.
Find analogies from the real world that everyone can relate to.


ChatGPT is amazing at this btw. Just prompt: "I need an analogy to explain [your solution] vs [competitor approach] using everyday experiences."

What's the best analogy you've used to explain your product?





*and I get that this analogy won't work everywhere. But you get the idea :)

content:
After 5 years in Enterprise sales for billion-dollar companies, I've narrowed it down to 7 things I'm listening for in meetings. 

(Yes, our notetakers might transcribe or flag them. But we're the ones who have to remember them. :)
 
 
 
1/ Despite _________, it's still hard to __________ as measured by _____________.* 
 
2/ This is a ____________ level priority because its impact is __________________* 
 
3/ Why Anything 
 
4/ Why Now 
 
5/ Why Us 
 
6/ Role of Each Person on this call: Talker / Mobilizer / Blocker 
 
7/ Important Context: 
 
 
 
I'm a big fan of templates and systems. 
 
I like to paste these 7 into CRM on the Opportunity page. Before the first  meeting, so we can fill in the blanks as the deal progresses. 
 
We will likely not get all of this^^ in one call. 
 
 
 
Here's what that looked like for one of my past deals at UserGems 💎 
 
1/ Despite customers loving their product, it's hard for the VP Sales to know if they reconnect with past buyers when they change jobs. Their own estimate is 32% of their buyers change jobs within 18 mos. (HR tech / high turnover) But they have no metric for how they track or connect with champions who change jobs. 
 
2/ This is a level #1 priority because CEO & CFO held joint All-Hands to emphasize need for pipeline growth. CXOs want to see 17% YoY growth. VP Sales team is at 6% so far. 
 
3/ Why Anything 
They've tried to do this before but the homegrown system failed. They could rig SalesNave to send an alert of the job change, but couldn't crack the code of automating new role alerts without a bunch of false positives. 
 
4/ Why Now 
VP Sales has pipeline as his #1 priority and doesn't have money for new headcount. Also not enough time for long implementation. Needs fast impact. 
 
5/ Why Us 
He knows we're not the cheapest but heard about us in a sales community and they were talking up our implementation + CS. I'm recommending high touch rollout b/c his RevOps team is already spread thin. 
 
6/ Role of Each Person on this call: Mobilizer & he's brought on new tech before 
 
7/ Important Context: 
VP of Marketing is brand new. They RIF'd almost all SDRs in Q1 so AEs are now prospecting. Marketing also has a Pipeline number, so we'll need VP Marketing on board. VP Sales did intro/ fwd'd my summary email. Working to schedule meeting with both VPs next week. 
 
 
 
How do you think this format would work for you? 
 
Would love to hear how it goes if you give it a try. 

(Or if you use something different that works better!)

content:
After 7+ years in Enterprise tech, I've learned a way to create urgency that doesn’t feel icky.  

We make it Buyer Centric.
Not "Q2 ends June 30th" urgency.
But urgency that matters to THEM.


Easier said than done.

So…let’s talk H2.

7 priorities on executives' minds right now - halfway through 2025:
1/ Checking the Score 
2/ Fixing What's Not Working 
3/ Spotting New Opportunities 
4/ Watching the Competition 
5/ Preparing for Problems 
6/ Tracking Customer Happiness 
7/ Managing Money Flow

Here are 7 ideas on how to tie your solution to these mid-year priorities:

1/ Checking the Score - Executives are like coaches at halftime, reviewing if they're winning or losing against goals.
-> Are they on track or behind on their key metrics? What specific numbers do they need to hit by December to consider 2025 a success? How can your solution help them close gaps?

2/ Fixing What's Not Working - They're making adjustments to underperforming initiatives.
-> What Q1 initiatives have stalled or underdelivered? What did your Champion mention was struggling in your last discovery call? What stories can you share about how similar customers course-corrected using your solution?

3/ Spotting New Opportunities - They're scanning for chances they didn't see in January.
-> What unexpected market shifts have happened since Q1? (This is where I love using Aomni. Saves hours of research on most recent 10-K, company initiatives, etc.) How are your most innovative customers using your solution to capitalize on these changes? Could your buyer get similar results before year-end?

4/ Watching the Competition - They're obsessed with what rivals are doing.
-> Who are they afraid of? Who do they compare themselves to?  Are those competitors already using your solution? If they're not, what advantage could your buyer gain by moving first? If they are, what's the cost of falling further behind?

5/ Preparing for Problems - Smart leaders are building contingency plans.
-> What's your buyer most worried about for H2? How could your solution help them create flexibility or reduce risk? What would it mean if they could navigate those challenges more effectively than peers?

6/ Tracking Customer Happiness - They're analyzing customer feedback at the halfway mark.
-> How satisfied are their customers right now? What feedback trends are they seeing? Have they considered how your solution might directly impact their customer experience metrics before year-end?

7/ Managing Money Flow - Cash is king, especially mid-year.
-> How are they thinking about cash flow? More focused on accelerating revenue or reducing costs? What would it mean if your solution could impact their cash position before the December board meeting?

The key difference between Q4 and mid-year urgency?
In Q4, executives are planning for next year. 
At mid-year, they're trying to save THIS year.

That's your opening.
What mid-year priority are you focusing on with your enterprise buyers right now?

content:
In May 2021, I had trouble getting out of bed for the 4th week in a row. 
 
Just moving enough to push the covers back, sit up & walk to the kitchen....it was almost too much effort.  
 

Once I was up, all I wanted to do was sit and stare at the wall. 
 
Not an exaggeration.  I literally just wanted to sit and stare. 
 

To say this was "not like me" is an understatement. 
 
I've been a driven Type A since birth...."She's got a motor" is how one colleague described my work ethic. 
 

So, even though my brain felt foggy and slow, I realized this was deeply abnormal. 
 
Luckily I reached out to my doctor and started medication for depression the same week. 
 
I was amazed at how much better I felt in the next few weeks, even though it took several months to get the dosage exactly right. 
 

Depression and anxiety run in my family, but I had always been able to manage with coping skills.  Journaling, yoga, exercise, etc. 
 
But after a huge loss in our family, coping skills weren't enough anymore. 

Looking back, I should have started medication months before I did. 
 

That's 1 of the BIGGEST things depression does - clouds your judgment.  Including judgment about your own mental health. 
 
HINT: If you are wondering "am I depressed?", you probably are.  Worth getting a professional opinion.  ASAP. 
 
 
 
What I'm glad I did: 
--> therapy 
--> medication 
--> talking with friends & family (should have done this sooner)
 
 
What I wish I'd done: 
 --> seen a doctor faster
 --> used FMLA to rest & recover, instead of "pushing through"


What you can do:
—> take that one next step you’ve been thinking about

 
May is Mental Health Awareness Month.  If you've been thinking about getting help, please don't wait.   


 
***ALSO...Sadly there is still a stigma within some families, cultures and religions around mental health. 

When I was growing up, many of my family members didn’t really believe that mental health was “a thing.” 

And I was also raised in a fundamentalist Religious denomination where you were just supposed to pray about things. Without taking any other steps. That kind of thinking kept me trapped - for years. 


It has been a long journey for me. Hopefully this helps some others get started on their own path.

Talked with 3 reps currently at 149%, 161% and 198% of quota. Here are 3 things they're ALL doing. (And how you can do them too).


WHAT they're doing:

---> Reducing complexity for buyers
---> Working with all 3 power levels
---> Finding hidden mobilizers 



HOW they're doing it:


---> Reducing complexity for buyers

Time kills deals. And complexity makes everything take longer.

Top ways these 3 reps are making things easer:

1/ "Making sense" selling - Coming with POVs & value adds to help Buyers make good decisions 

2/ Teaching Buyers How to Buy - ending every call with "Typically what comes next is..." to prescribe next steps.
 


---> Working with all 3 power levels

Executives are important to a deal, but they won't make decisions in a vacuum. So if you ONLY focus on execs, your deal is at risk....

Because it is RISKY to be a buyer. If their name is attached to a huge purchase that fails, their job is on the line.

So execs lean on Managers, technical experts/IT and end users in evaluations.

THIS is why multi-threaded deals have a 5X win rate (!!!)

The top reps I talked with know they have to work at all 3 power levels - and communicate WIIFM to each - 

1/ Executive
2/ Managers
3/ End Users



---> Finding hidden mobilizers 

Sellers who target "Mobilizers" are 31% more likely to be high performers.

Top-performers spend their time focused on the 3 who are the best at building consensus & creating change (the Mobilizers): ​
​The Go-Getter
The Skeptic*
The Teacher ​

​*The Skeptic pushes back on the idea because they’re exploring it thoughtfully. 



IMPACT of combining these 3 actions:
---> Closed 26% more deals
---> Brought in 27% more revenue
---> Shortened sales cycles by ~1 month

Reducing complexity, working with all 3 power levels, or finding hidden mobilizers?

content:
Here are 3 of my favorite questions to use in pricing / negotiation calls: 
 
 
#1: What did you have in mind? 
#2: What's closer to what you were expecting? 
#3: What is a number that you could get approved? 
 
 
 
 
How & where I use them: 
 
 
--> What did you have in mind? 
 
Experienced negotiators frequently ask salespeople, "Is this the best you can do?" 
 
It's fair for us to ask what they want. 
 
It's not always price. 
 
 
An alternative way to say this is, "What would make this a good deal for you?"* 
 
Again - I promise it won't always be price. 
 
You might be surprised what they bring up. 
 
 
*This question comes from "Influence is Your Superpower" by Yale professor Zoe Chance. It's the 2.0 version of "Never Split the Difference." Highly recommend. 
 
 
 
--> What’s closer to what you were expecting? 
 
My favorite response to the vague objection "That's too high". 
 
No matter what it is, they almost always think it's too high. :) 
 
Follow up: "Can you tell me more about that number (that you have in mind?)" 
 
This shows the thought/effort they put in. 
 
And their thought process. 
 
 
 
 
--> What is a number you could get approved? 
 
When we hear "My CFO would not approve that". 
 
Before we start throwing out huge discounts... 
 
They likely have seen budget allocations 
 
or heard internal discussions. 
 
Ask them to share. 
 
 
 
 
The theme here is Open-ended negotiation questions- 
rather than defensive reactions 
or explanations of our pricing. 
 
 
They help us uncover 
concerns, 
roadblocks 
and win/wins. 
 
 
Listening > Talking 
Clear > Clever 
 
 
 
What are your favorite questions to ask? 
 
Some of the surprising things folks have asked for?

content:
I sent multi-threading emails to an Executive Buyer for 5 straight months. He never responded - but he did save my deal. 
 
Here's what happened... 
 
I inherited a deal in my 1st year at UserGems. It was multithreaded (kinda) when I got it. 
 
There were 5 people involved from the Buyer side. That was the good news. 
 
Bad news - all 5 people were in the same department. 
 
 
I was concerned and immediately started multi-threading. 
 
Including an introduction between the Executive Buyer and our VP of Marketing. 
 
The Executive Buyer never responded to the intro... but he DID start a separate thread with our VP of marketing. 
 
He never attended a meeting. Never responded to the "keeping you in the loop" emails I sent after those meetings. But he read every one of them. 
 
And 5 months later.... 
 
 
When the buying group threatened to walk away from the deal unless we slashed our pricing by over 60% 
 
We used the thread with our VP of marketing to send the business case to the Executive Buyer. 
 
He understood the value, and ultimately rescued the deal. 
 
 
We don't have to go it alone when we're multi-threading. 
 
Aligning executives can be a powerful way to engage with CXOs and VPs. 
 
The moral of this story is, take heart! "No response" doesn't mean "no impact".

content:
4 of the best & simplest discovery questions for quantifying metrics were ones I learned from Dave Rubinstein.
  
Who's he? He's been a Head of Sales at Meta and also a former VP at Salesforce & Outreach.  
  
His method is so simple. So effective.  
  
  
Here's his post about it:  
"The FASTEST and most efficient way to identify and quantify a problem is using MATH.  
  
Metric  
Actual  
Target  
Holding back  
  
  
Here's the scenario:  
  
AE asks: "What are the key initiatives you are focused on?"  
  
Prospect: 'We are laser-focused on our churn issue."  
  
AE responds: "Got it. Let me walk you through how we can help your churn problem."  
  
NOOOOOOOOOOOOOOOOOOOO  
  
  
  
Try these questions:  
  
1) What is the current churn metric you are focused on? Metric  
  
Prospect response: % of customers that leave the business  
  
  
2) What is your churn today? Actual  
  
Prospect response: We are at 20%  
  
  
3) What is your target? Target  
  
Prospect response: We are at 15% (size of problem)  
  
  
4) What's holding you back? Holding back  
  
Prospect's response will tell you:  
  
THIS is the problem the Prospect is trying to solve  
  
AND how you will assess whether it is big enough to matter."  
  
  
This is brilliant because it speaks an Executive's language  
  
is Buyer focused (on their problems)  
  
and it's a total of 5 questions.

They spray out emails, monitor for events and advise us to react to their signals...some even promise to replace humans (lol AI-SDRs) 🤖 🤡

Sure, some signals are worth reacting to (shout out Champify and Boomerang). But others (🥱 website de-anon) should not be prioritized over chasing one's top prospective accounts. 

Cold outbound is hard. Creating value from nothing is harder than automating an ambulance chase. But many of these tools frankly inspire laziness.  

Stop chasing signals and start building value from scratch!

"Facts tell. Stories sell." We can all nod our heads to this, but how many stories do we tell in our discovery? Demos? Pricing calls?

Do we prep for meetings by pre-planning some stories to share, based on what we've learned about the Buyers in our research?

Do we spend time each week learning at least 1 new customer story, and quizzing ourselves with flashcards until we can tell them by heart?


If we want to get better at this, there's good news.

Lou Adler's S.T.A.R. framework is an easy way to learn and then tell customer stories. 


S= Situation (what was happening /what's the context?)
T= Trouble (what problem were they facing?)
A= Action (what did they do about it?)*
R= Result (what happened next)


*note here that 'buying our thing' is NOT what they did about it. Our thing was a tool they used to take the action, but not the hero of the story. The customer is the hero. 

*note #2- what makes the story feel real here is the person's 1st name, their title, their company or industry, and the timeframe (2 yrs ago / 2 mos ago)

STAR makes it so we can tell relevant customer stories in under 1 minute.


How do you use stories in your sales process?

When I first started in tech sales, I knew nothing.


I had never made a cold call.

Ever.

I had no idea what ACV or ARR meant. (Annual contract value and Annual recurring revenue, btw.)

I had never demo’d anything.


Some people know that I eventually went on to Enterprise Sales roles for 3 multi billion dollar tech companies.

Fewer know how I started from the absolute bottom.

(Oh, and I was at least 7 years older than any of my peers.)


In my first tech sales gig, I typically worked 80 hour weeks.

I went in early to practice cold call scripts.

I stayed up late reading sales books and listening to Gong calls from the top sellers on my team.

I was afraid I was learning too slowly, and that I would “never get it.”


Many days I felt like I would pass out at work - because I got so little sleep.

Even when I had started experiencing some success, I would still panic at work every day.

I constantly worried that any success was some fluke, rather than hard work and persistence.

It took me years to hone and feel confident using the techniques I talk about now.


The point of me sharing is this: I want you to know that you're not alone.


Not only that:

I hope you don’t feel completely overwhelmed, and panic stricken like I did.

I hope you don’t compare your journey to anyone else’s, or beat yourself up for “not getting it”.


Instead:

I hope you learn something that makes you a better salesperson every day, and make a plan to consistently execute it.

I hope you are patient with yourself in this crazy profession where we get so little training.

I hope that you know that it will get better, and you Keep Moving Forward.

After 11 years in sales, I've got good news for anyone who gets "Happy Ears" a lot. 
 
(btw, I spent the early years of my sales career battling that same thing) 
 
Luckily, a mentor shared their secret with me. 
 
 
Here it is: 
 
3 questions + 1 rule for all Opportunities 
 
 
The Three Questions 
--> Why Anything 
--> Why Now 
--> Why Us 
 
 
The One Rule 
--> NONE of the answers can mention any of your product's features as the reason 
 
You can ONLY mention a product feature IF you know the outcome it creates or prevents. 
 
 
 
For a past deal at UserGems 💎 - this sounded like: 
 
--> WHY ANYTHING: Pipeline creation is strategic initiative #1 for Exec Buyer (RVP Sales). They have an aggressive goal: 17% YoY increase 
 
--> WHY NOW: UserGems can be implemented in under 60 days (feature), which means there's still time to impact H2 pipe, and even H2 revenue (impact). 
 
--> WHY US: RVP knows that her biggest competitor started with UserGems last year & they are losing more deals than ever to this competitor. And the RVP's team has seen only 6% increase in ARR and 19% renewal churn. This is the data she's presenting to CFO as proof that 1) the strategy works & 2) there's a high risk of doing nothing. 
 
 
 
If we can't answer the 3 Why's - with metrics 
 
We need to quickly dive deeper with Discovery - or move on 
 
If we show our pipeline some tough love now, we can prevent a lot of pain from Happy Ears in the future.

content:
Last fall I saw a seller use a 1 sentence strategy to win a 6-figure deal with a Fortune 500 CEO.

Here's how it went down, and how you can do it too.

​
In Q3, one of the Enterprise reps I coach faced a unique dilemma.

​
She had worked hard all year to get a deal going with Lululemon, a ~$39.2B member of the Fortune 500.

She'd been onsite, worked with ~60 people to multi-thread & come with a Point of View.

She knew her solution was aligned with a C-Level Priority. Problem was, her solution was a ** small **  piece of the puzzle. And she needed a way to help the CEO understand its importance.

​
A group of champions let the rep know they were presenting to the CEO in a Q3 leadership meeting. 

The AE had to help these champions to show HOW critical her solution was - with a very succinct explanation.
​
​We decided we needed an analogy. 
​

To create the perfect analogy, we went to work researching the CEO. On his public Instagram page, we found our answer.

His Insta was plastered with photos of him & the Lulu team, competing together in triathlons. He'd given multiple interviews on what triathlons meant to his personal and professional life.
​

So we came up with this analogy:

--> "Using the current solution for this initiative would be like using a beach cruiser for the bike portion of a triathlon."

​
If you're unfamiliar with a beach cruiser, it's a bike invented in the 1960's. With the basket in front. Not exactly triathlon material.

Which was exactly why it made the perfect analogy.

​
--> ​"Using the current solution for this initiative would be like using a beach cruiser for the bike portion of a triathlon."
​
​​
The analogy communicated 3 Crucial Realities to the CEO - using language from HIS world:

Their current solution

1/ was OUTDATED
2/ was THE WRONG TOOL for the job
3/ COULD NOT accomplish their objectives 

All without a word about features & functions… which the CEO didn't need to hear about and would have forgotten instantly.
​

​The analogy sealed the deal. The CEO got the picture, and this rep got a 6-figure Closed Won.

Would that analogy been enough all by itself?

Of course not.

​
This Enterprise rep is a absolute pro, and she'd done all the groundwork.

The on-sites, the multi-threading, the Point of View and Business case.

She had all the right elements. The analogy was the catalyst.

​​
You've got some deals right now where you've laid all the groundwork.

What can you use as your catalyst?

 𝘛𝘩𝘦 𝘪𝘯𝘵𝘳𝘰 𝘮𝘦𝘦𝘵𝘪𝘯𝘨 𝘪𝘴 𝘢 𝘭𝘪𝘵𝘮𝘶𝘴 𝘵𝘦𝘴𝘵. 𝘉𝘶𝘺𝘦𝘳𝘴 𝘵𝘩𝘢𝘵 𝘸𝘰𝘯'𝘵 𝘢𝘨𝘳𝘦𝘦 𝘵𝘰 𝘵𝘩𝘪𝘴 𝘮𝘦𝘦𝘵𝘪𝘯𝘨 𝘢𝘳𝘦𝘯'𝘵 𝘳𝘦𝘢𝘥𝘺 𝘵𝘰 𝘴𝘪𝘨𝘯.

 ---> They could be afraid to put a meeting on the books because they're not sure they'll get a signature approved.

𝙒𝙝𝙖𝙩 𝙞𝙩 𝘿𝙤𝙚𝙨:

𝙃𝙤𝙬 𝙒𝙚 𝘾𝙖𝙣 𝙎𝙚𝙩 𝙞𝙩 𝙐𝙥:

No one is clicking the Whitepapers and Case study links we send (check your data).
 
BUT - we can use Herd Theory instead. 

 
 
WHAT it is: 
 
Herd Theory = "people using the actions of others as a guide to sensible behavior." 

aka = Everyone always wants to know what everyone else is doing. 
 
 

HOW it can work for us: 
 
During discovery we listen for 1-2 key pain points. 
 
Then we mention LOTS of others who are using our solution to solve them. 
 
 
 
IRL this sounds like --> 
 
“Earlier in the call you mentioned needing to generate new Pipeline for H1. 
 
Gong & Salesloft & Lattice & PagerDuty & Looker & Pendo & Drift & Procore & OneLogin & Segment & Greenhouse are already using UserGems 💎 to monitor buying signals like new executive hires or promotions. 

It's helped them create new pipeline & increased their deal velocity.

Would it be ok if I shared how they're doing that?” 
 
 
 
Using Herd Theory works better than one case study or whitepaper because, as Thomas Freese writes in "Question Based Selling": 
 
"Surrounding prospects with a credible 'herd' reduces our risk... 
 
 We become the messenger - not the message."


Give it a whirl and see how it works for ya.

Got any stories of how you've used it?

content:
There's an unusual thing Salesforce's top Enterprise AEs do to ace their first meetings with execs.
 
They start discovery before they say a word in a VP+ conversation.
 
Here are 5 ways I've seen it done:

 
 
1️⃣ Survey the Exec's current team 🕵️‍♂️
 
Look for them on LinkedIn Sales Navigator. 
 
Filter to folks active on LinkedIn during the past 30 days.
 
Craft a tailored message focusing on WIIFM (What's In It For Me).
 
NOT what your product does. The outcomes they'll see.
 
Ask about pain points & advice on how to best approach the Exec.
 
 
-> In the Exec meeting, this sounds like:
 
"After talking with 5 of your sales reps in the East, it sounds like AE-created pipeline is a big focus. What are the biggest risks you see to pipe build in the next 3-6 mos?
 
 
 
2️⃣ Look at their Customer Stories 📚
 
What problems do they solve?
 
Who is their customer? SMB? Enterprise?
 
What do people mention... and NOT mention?
 
 
-> Sounds like:
 
"You've got some great logos. Amazing to see Gong, Salesloft & Drift all using your platform. Given that renewals are getting leaner across the SaaS industry, what are the 2 biggest churn risks you're keeping an eye on next quarter?"
 
 
 
3️⃣ Check RepVue & Glassdoor for insights on team dynamics 👀
 
71% vs. 21% of the team hitting...different conversations
 
On Glassdoor, you can filter reviews.
 
You can also use Ctrl F / search for specific words in reviews.
 
 
-> Sounds like:
"Building pipeline has been tougher than ever in 2025. How are you thinking about risks related to attainment in the next 3 months?"
 
 

4️⃣ Explore product reviews on G2, Capterra for valuable feedback. 🌟
 
Look for gaps related to your product (customer service, efficiency, integrations). 
 
 
-> Sounds like: 
"Looks like your customers love your functionality and ease of use on G2. The only negative they mentioned was not having enough time with their CSM each month. Is this one of the top risks you're focused on in the next 3 months?"
 
 
 
5️⃣ Watch Exec's speeches & podcasts for key insights. 🎙️
 
Look for common themes & top takeaways.
 
Especially any personal stories.

Reference their ideas to kick off discussions.
 
-> In Exec Discovery, sounds like: 
"You made a great point about sales & marketing alignment on Kevin Dorsey's podcast. How do fewer lead conversions & slower deal velocity rank as risks you're discussing with your marketing team?"
 
 
 
This type of prep surprises and impresses Executives.
 
Having a POV immediately differentiates us.
 
Our 1st meetings will be 5x better.

content:
5 harsh realities I learned in my 1st Enterprise sales role:

1/ The buying committee was 3x bigger than I expected. 
Just when I thought I had all the stakeholders mapped, another 4 people would appear out of nowhere with veto power. And each one needed their own custom pitch.

2/ My deal timeline estimates were wildly optimistic. 
What I projected as a 3-6 month cycle routinely stretched to 9+ months, with sudden "urgent priorities" derailing momentum for weeks at a time.

3/ Getting ghosted wasn't personal, it was structural. 
My champion wasn't ignoring me - they were drowning in internal politics, navigating procurement processes, and fighting for budget in ways I couldn't see.

4/ ROI conversations were brutal. 
In SMB, I could talk benefits more broadly. In Enterprise, I needed to defend every dollar with specific metrics, case studies, and projections that would hold up to Finance scrutiny. 

5/ Creating a relevant Point of View required 10x the research. 
In Mid-Market, I could get by with learning industry knowledge and finding LinkedIn profiles. In Enterprise, I had to study their earnings calls, SEC filings, and competitive landscape just to hopefully earn 15 minutes of their attention. (BTW - I just started using Aomni for this, and it’s crazy good. Reps at Hubspot, NVIDIA and AMD are also on Aomni. You can check it out here: https://bit.ly/aomni)


If you're experiencing any/all of these - you're not the problem.

Enterprise sales is a completely different game with hidden rules nobody teaches you.

content:
Here are the 8 questions CFOs ask before every software purchase. (And they're brutal.)

Every champion I've ever worked with eventually hits a moment of panic:
"What do I say when Finance starts asking the hard questions?"


👉 Most CFOs won't tell you what they're really thinking. They just kill your deal silently.

But I've spent 13 years watching Enterprise deals die in Finance. And I've learned what CFOs actually need to hear.


Here are the 8 questions every CFO is asking behind closed doors, courtesy of the "Only CFOs" newsletter, as highlighted by Nate Nasralla:

1. Why do we need [X product] now? We were fine before. 
2. What bucket does this fall into, and can you quantify it?
-----Improves efficiencies
-----Increases revenue
-----Mission critical (e.g. cybersecurity)
-----"Candy": nice-to-have tool that doesn't really fit into the above groups 
3. Is the spend in the budget? If not, how will you make up the difference? 
4. How does this tool tie into our company objectives for this year? 
5. What tools do we already have that do something similar? And if similar tools exist, why can't we use those? 
6. Implementation: What are the people / time requirements? 
7. Support costs: Will we need to upgrade soon to enterprise /other tier? 
8. Pricing:
-----If usage-based pricing: I want a detailed analysis on how pricing works and modeling for what our planned usage will look like.
-----If seat-based pricing: I don't want to buy a bunch of extra seats for planned growth. That got a lot of people in trouble when headcount growth halted and layoffs happened.

The deal-killers? Numbers 1, 3, and 5.

At Salesforce, I watched 6-7 figure deals die instantly when the champion couldn't answer those 3 questions clearly.

content:
Multi-threading by asking for intros can work ok. Sometimes. Buuuuuuut... 
 
If we're on a call with a blocker or gate keeper, it can fall flat 🦗 
 
My favorite way is a 3x3x3 method. Maybe it might work for you? 
 
 
Here's the recipe: 
 
--> 3 Buying Personas 
--> 3-Step Sequence 
--> 3 Part Follow up 
 
 
 
--> 3 Buying Personas 
 
Before the 1st call with a Manager, Director or Individual contributor*

Find 3 people with VP+ titles from departments typically involved in buying your offering 
 
 
 
--> 3-Step Sequence 
 
Put them into a 3-step sequence, about 4-7 days before the call 
 
1st touch/1st day = thoughtful comment on a recent LinkedIn post 
 
2nd touch = LinkedIn connection request, mentioning their post 
 
3rd touch = email or LinkedIn message about your meeting 
 
 
IRL at UserGems 💎, this sounds like --> 
"Hi {{first_name}} - Your colleague Callie scheduled a meeting with me, and I thought you might be interested. 
 
Topic is tracking buying signals like Champion's job changes and promotions for repeat business. And how to automatically Multi-thread into deals & accounts. 
 
Executives in (your department) aren't always involved. But some have specific KPIs that are relevant here. 
 
Forwarded you an invite, Either way, will keep you posted." 
 
 
 
--> 3 Part Follow up 
 
#1 Day of the meeting: Short recap of the meeting 
 
#2 Day of the meeting: Put them in a nurture sequence (either thought leadership OR reminding you to recap any additional meetings) 
 
#3 A week later: Ghostwrite an intro email for a Manager/Exec from your team to send. Execs starting their own private channel of communication can be extremely powerful. Start early. 
 
 
 
 
With this 3x3x3, you get both visibility & credibility across their org. 
 
Your meeting attendee can't be a gatekeeper. 
 
Win/win. 
 
 
 
What kind of multi-threading is working well for you?


*I only use this method when our first meeting is NOT with an executive. If a VP/CXO is on our first call, I focus on call prep vs going wider.

content:
Took me 12 years in sales to come up with 3 steps that work for any Discovery call. 
 
 
Now sellers & sales teams train on EMT Discovery - 
 
--> Excavate the Pain 
--> Match the Urgency 
--> Teach them to Buy 
 
 
--> Excavate the Pain 
(aka "The Menu of Pain") 
 
Friction reduction applies to Discovery 
 
Don't ask "essay" questions 
 
Give them multiple choice 
 
 
Here's the formula (thank you, Charles Muhlbauer): 
 
1/ In this role, I talk to [your industry] leaders all day long. 
 
2/ They tell me about their heartburn around problems A, B, and C. 
 
3/ How much of that sounds like your world & what did I miss? 
 
 
IRL at UserGems 💎, this sounds like: 
"Usually, when Sales leaders join these calls they usually want to either Capitalize or Catch up. 

• They had another round layoffs in late 2024, but quotas are not going down. 
• They're facing double-digit growth metrics, even though only 39% of sellers made quota last year. 
• Volume isn't working for outbound anymore. They know spray & pray is over. And so they're looking for a new channel. 
• . . . OR - they're facing none of these challenges, are hitting record high revenue, and want to capitalize to grab market share. 
 
• Curious how much of that sounds like your world? And what did I miss?" 
 
 
 
 
--> Match Their Urgency 
 
There are 3 reasons people show up for Discovery calls. 
 
Figuring this out saves everyone time.** 
 
 
This sounds like: 
 
"Sometimes people join these calls because they are in education mode and just want to understand new tools. 
 
Sometimes people join these calls because they have a big churn, pipeline or revenue problem they needed to solve 6 months ago. 
 
Sometimes people join these calls because they need to do something about big churn, pipeline or revenue in the next 12 months, but it's not urgent. 
 
Curious where would you put yourself on that scale? 
 
Asking because I never want to chase anyone. 
 
If today was purely education, that's ok." 
 
 
**I ask this at the end of the call 
 
After they've gotten the product overview 
 
And BEFORE we talk next steps. Because their answer determines what next steps make sense. 
 
 
 
--> Teach them to Buy 
 
Our Buyers are Experts in how to do their jobs. 
 
Not how to buy our stuff. 
 
We need to be their guide. 
 
 
It's as simple as sharing "what comes next" at the end of every call. 
 
 
This sounds like: 
 
“Typically when folks evaluate XYZ product, leaders from Operations, Finance, and HR all get involved. 
 
Would it make sense to loop in Shonda, your VP of HR, and Christina, your VP of Finance into our conversation? 
 
Your organization may be different.... would someone else be better?" 
 
 
 
Our prospects have pain. 
 
We can act as EMTs. 
 
 
Do you have a simple way you think about Discovery?

Had never cold called before. (In fact it was my greatest fear.)

I knew “coffee was for closers”, and I was terrified of getting fired. Panicked every day. 
 
I typically worked 80 hour weeks. A couple times, I felt like I would pass out at work.

content:
Sales gurus give truly terrible advice sometimes.  Here's one of my least favorites - and it's super popular.  
  
  
Sellers getting advised to ask "What happens if you do nothing?"  
  
  
Real talk: I've never heard anyone phrase it like that in real life.  
  
The concept is good but the phrasing sucks.  
  
Too easy for us to come off as smug or arrogant.  
  
  
  
Here are 3 different ways to use that concept - without sounding like a ... jerk:  
  
  
---> "What might be the ripple effects if the team can't find a better way to accomplish [outcome]?"  
  
---> "What impacts do you see coming if the team doesn't find a different way to get to [this outcome]?"  
  
---> "Our customers who've struggled with this same issue tell us that X, Y & Z [business problems] were getting worse when they couldn't change [problem I solve]. Any of that sound like your world, or what did I miss?"  
  
  
  
Buyers already avoid talking to salespeople until they absolutely have to.  
  
And no one wants to talk to a salesperson who's smug. Let alone open up to them about their problems.  
  
Asking a hard thing in a soft way can be the difference between finding a champion or creating a blocker. 
 
 
Got any favorite ways to ask about the status quo?

content:
After 6+ years in Enterprise sales, I've learned a way to avoid hearing "Just show me the demo." 

"Just show me the demo" is where most sellers lose control of their Discovery calls. 
 
We're not sure what to do next. We freeze.  
 
 
Do we press on & ask more questions to get a little more "pain"? 
 
Is the Buyer always right, so we should just pop open the Demo deck? 
 
 
After working with some of the best sellers in the world at places like Salesforce, Tableau & Outreach, I've noticed a pattern. 
 
The top 1% of sellers approach their Discovery calls like an EMT. 
 
(After all, our Buyers have serious pain. They NEED an EMT.) 
 
 
E  -> Excavate their pain 
M -> Match their urgency 
T -> Teach them to buy 
 
 
We can avoid the trap of "just show me the demo" if we Excavate pain at the very top of the call. 
 
We want to use a multiple choice question. 
 
I call it "The Menu of Pain". 
 
 
Here's the Formula: 
 
  --> "In this role, I talk to [XYZ industry] leaders all day long.  
 
  --> They tell me about their heartburn around problems A, B, and C.  
 
  --> How much of that sounds like your world & what did I miss?" 
 


How it sounds IRL:

 "In this role, I talk to Legal Ops & Chief Legal Officers all day. Usually it’s because they:

  *  Struggle to collaborate within a department/firm OR with clients

   * Aren’t effectively establishing and reinforcing their branding & identity

   * OR - they're under pressure to be more responsive, agile AND reduce costs…

Curious how much of that sounds like your world? And what did I miss?”


 
When we name 3 problems that sound familiar to them, we earn some credibility. (Because we didn't open the call by asking "So what do you guys do?") 
 
And when we invite them to correct us, they'll go even deeper. Those details = gold. 
 
 
So when we actually DO the demo, we can show more of what matters to them. 
 
We can stay in control of our Disco calls, if we show up as an EMT. 



What's the best response you've ever heard when a prospect says "Just show me the demo" ?

content:
⛔️Warning: Don't accept a position with a company “going upmarket” without asking these 5 questions. 
  
When I made the move, I didn’t know about these land mines 💣... 
  
The company I joined was hugely successful. I thought going upmarket would be smooth ⛵️ 
  
I was wrong 🙈 
  
  
Here are 5️⃣ issues I wish I’d asked about: 
  
  
🎥 GOT ENTERPRISE STORIES? 
Most true ENT companies couldn’t care less about success in SMB/ Mid Market. United Airlines will not be impressed with our product's success in a company with 150 employees. 
  
--> Key qq: "What are the best stories about how ENT accounts have created success with this product?" 
  
  
🐏 HOW DO BATTERING RAMS GET PAID?  
Sellers in companies "going upmarket" spend 2-3 years educating the Enterprise about the product's existence. 
  
Since you’ll essentially be a battering ram trying to crack enterprise accounts, how will you get paid? 50/50 split? If so, don't count on making anything more than your base for 2-3 years. 
  
--> Key qq: "Show me the comp plan" 
  
  
📅 DO THE TIMELINES MATCH?  
I had a deal with a 19k person financial services org that took over 24 mos to close. 
  
That wasn't unusual in ENT. Most of the team didn't make quota for 2-3 years. 
  
--> Key qq: "Since you are going upmarket & it takes time to educate the Enterprise market, how will quotas be structured?" 
  
  
🧙🏻‍♂️🔮 WHO ARE THE GURUS? 
Who are their advisors & sales leaders? I wrongly assumed our company was being advised by folks who had experience going upmarket. (ie  qualified to give us directions because they had made the journey before.) 
  
Same with Enterprise leaders. Best if they *have made the upmarket journey before*. NOT just leaders who've always been with enterprise orgs. 
  
--> Key qq: "Can you walk me through who our top advisors are? Hiring philosophy for the ENT sales leaders?" 
  
  
👮🏼‍♀️ HOW GOOD ARE WE AT THE BIG 3?  
Security, Reporting & Governance - ENT handles these much differently than SMB. 
  
These 3 issues were why big deals took so long to close-if they closed at all. 
  
I and several of my peers lost 7 figure deals - even though there was pain, motivated Exec buyers & good multi-threading. The deals died because we didn't have one of the Big 3 that ENT orgs required. 
  
--> Key qq: "Can you walk me through how the product meets the Security, Reporting & Governance of ENT orgs? 
  
  
Real talk: Founders get overly confident when there's lots of traction in SMB & MM. 
  
They're convinced that the ENT will “fall in line “. Just deals with extra 0’s.  
  
⚠️NOT true 
  
  
Take it from someone who's been there & got the hoodie 
  
Asking these questions can save a lot of❤️‍🩹  
  
What did I forget?

content:
3 surprising insights I learned from a VP of Sales changed how I do Multi-Threading.  
  
 Here's what he told me, and how you can use it:  
  
  
--> It's risky to be the champion for a big purchase  
--> 3 levels of personas need to be in an evaluation to de-risk it  
--> We should communicate differently to each of those 3 levels  
  
  
How to turn that into the best Multi-Threaded deals:  
  
1) Knowing who usually buys your product can help de-risk a purchase for your Champion.  
  
Champions are experts in how to do their jobs, not how to buy our stuff.  
  
They appreciate it when we can guide them.  
  
"Typically when folks evaluate XYZ, leaders from Legal Operations, Finance, and HR all get involved. Would it make sense to include Shonda, your VP of HR, and Christina, your VP of Finance in our next conversation?"  
  
  
2) The 3 levels of Personas that get involved in deals all care about different things.  
  
Here's what they each care about:  
  
Executives: does this help us reach goals and/or lower our risk?  
  
Managers: does this help my team?  
  
End users: does this help me?  
  
  
3) We have to speak their "language" when we interact with them - or we'll lose them.  
  
Reps are used to talking about our product, so speaking the language of Executives is the hardest.  
  

Here's what a meeting recap email sounds like for a CFO or VP of Finance:  
  
"Anna,

I met with your Legal Ops team today about hard savings from workflow automation.

     - They quantified $3.6MM in savings / year

     - And they identified these savings will be immediate, as IT involvement isn’t needed

You should have the invite for our next meeting on the 28th. Will send you the readout afterward.

Cheers"


  
We mention Quantifying Impact, how SOON they'll see impact, and SPECIFIC ROI. 

Nothing about our product features or even our product's name.
  
(And they can read it on their cell without scrolling.)  
  
  
 
The reason multi-threading increases win rates by 34% is that it de-risks deals for Champions. (CEB Global)  
  
When we know how to help our Champions, everyone wins.... literally.  
  
And as always - it's about 𝘁𝗵𝗲𝗺, not about us/our stuff.

content:
Here are 3 questions used by top 1% sellers at Salesforce during pricing negotiation calls. 
 
Maybe you can use them to bring in those Q1 deals you're working:  
  
  
#1: What did you have in mind?  
#2: What's closer to what you were expecting?  
#3: What is a number that you could get approved?  
  
  
Here's how & where I've learned to use them:  
  
--> "What did you have in mind?"  
  
  
Experienced negotiators frequently ask salespeople, "Is this the best you can do?" It's a smart question.  
  
It's also fair for us to ask Buyers what they want in the deal.  
  
It's not always price.  
  
  
  
--> "What’s closer to what you were expecting?"  
 
  
This question is my favorite response to the vague objection "That's too high".  
  
No matter what it is, they almost always think it's too high. :)  
  
Follow up: "Can you tell me more about how you got to that number (that you have in mind?)"  
  
This shows the thought/effort they put in.  
  
And what they're using as an anchor.  
  
  
  
--> "What is a number you could get approved?"  
 
  
When we hear "My CFO would not approve that"...  
  
We can ask this question before we start throwing out huge discounts.  
  
Our Champions likely have seen budget allocations,  
  
know the Buying Committee's price sensitivity,  
  
and the dollar amount where procurement gets involved.  
  
Ask them to share.  
  
One of my favorite ways to phrase this: 
  
"Ok, got it. Sounds like your CFO wouldn't approve this number. I'm happy to go back to my team and get creative with this deal. I need to know what target we're aiming for. What is a number you could get approved?"  
  
  
  
Curiosity-based negotiation questions can keep pricing negotiations moving.  
  
Defensive reactions or explanations of our pricing grind talks to a halt.  
  
  
Open ended questions help us uncover  
concerns,  
roadblocks  
and win/wins.  
  
Listening > Talking  
Clear > Clever  
 
What are your favorite negotiation questions?

I struggled with the leap from Mid-Market to Enterprise sales.

Like one day being a top college athlete, and the next,

getting my a$$ handed to me at the pro level.


I had NO idea how different Enterprise would be. 

Luckily, I had great mentors gave me 3 key pieces of advice.



Here's what they said:

---> Build an Internal Network
---> Planning Will Save You
---> Stay in Sync



---> Build an Internal Network
Find out who you'll work with in Legal, Finance, and Deal Desk.

Put a short intro call on their calendar. Find out their story.

Their likes and dislikes. Ask how best to work with them.

Then mark your calendar to reach out to them every few weeks - and ask for nothing.

Establishing relationships before you need something from these teams can be crucial later. (And just a good decent thing to do.)



---> Planning Will Save You

Start creating account plans for your top high-value accounts.

Both to show high-level strategy and drive accountability around execution.

You will use them with all your co-selling teammates, including executive alignment with internal leadership. These shared documents are invaluable.




---> Stay in Sync

Have regular sync/prep meetings on the calendar with your teammates in Pre-sales, Support, and Customer success.

And do not cancel or schedule over these calls. They are sacred.

Regular time together cuts down on miscommunication, saves 100s of Slack messages, and creates alignment.

You'll have fewer fire drills re: deal strategy, saving a renewal, etc.

content:
We make 60% more money when we use a "Buyer Centered" approach. Here are 3 examples of how this can sound for prospecting, demos or late stage presentations.
 
 
🍄  Underlying principle: "Customers don't buy a product. They buy better versions of themselves."**  Like a "power up" in Mario Bros. 

 
 
Here's how it sounds IRL at UserGems 💎

 
1) In a demo--> 
 
🔴 Product Centered: "Excited to show you this new feature that [[blah, blah, blah]]" 
 
🟢Buyer Centered: "Other customers in your industry get excited about [[feature]], because it helps them solve [[problem]] that's caused them [[negative impact]]. Not sure if it makes sense to show that here... maybe [[negative impact]] isn't giving you much heartburn?" 
 
🔑How it's different: The focus is on their problems. AND by ending with a question, you give them control of the demo. Everyone likes being in control. 
 
 
2) Later Stage presentation--> 
 
🔴 Product Centered: "Last time we covered [[Feature 1, 2, 3]]. What you liked about those were XYZ." 
 
🟢Buyer Centered: "The last time we spoke, your priorities were [[list of problems 1, 2, 3 - on a slide!]] Curious how these have changed since last we spoke?" 
 
🔑How it's different: No mention of us or our features. Just their priorities. The slide shows we are paying attention. The question about how things have changed opens the door for them to go deeper. 
 
 
3) Prospecting--> 
 
🔴 Product Centered: "Our software tracks your past Champions. We automate this at scale. And our proprietary tech automates multi-threading in your deals. See our raving G2 reviews & Customer Success stories!" 
 
🟢 Buyer Centered: "Noticed a number of your partners are our clients. Greenhouse stood out. 
 
{{Prospect company}} would probably have ~12,000 past buyers who could buy again. Back of napkin math: 
 
15,000 {{Prospect company}} clients 
x 4 Avg People on a buying committee 
x 20% job change rate (Bureau of Labor stat) 
---------------------------------- 
12,000 potential leads (not counting influencers, power users, admins) 
 
 
p.s. fun fact One of your partners who's 1/4 your size is seeing $4.1m in revenue in under 12mos." 
 
 
🔑 How it's different: Shows the problem we solve for THEM specifically. No mention of features. Just the impact of solving their problem. 
 
 
 
💫 Buyer Centered messaging is magic sauce. 
 
Buyers solve the problem & they become the hero. 
 
We're the "Power Up" they've been looking for. 🍄 
 
 

What's your best advice on how to tweak our language so it's more Buyer Centered?
 
 
 
 
**This genius phrase is from a Medium article by the same name. 
And the 60% more is a Deloitte stat.

content:
"Sales Reps, don't introduce your Sales Engineer as your "technical expert."  
  
It's not good for you, them, or the prospect."  
 
oof... guilty as charged.  When I saw this post by Rew Dickinson, I wished I could re-do all those intros I did in demos. :( 
 
He's got a better way... here's the full post. (And sellers, give him a follow!) 
  
---  
  
This is how I see AEs introduce SEs most often:  
  
AE: "This is Rew, my Solutions Engineer. He can answer all of your technical questions and show you how the software works."  
  
This may be true, but it's not the best intro. It's not the Sales Reps' fault either. SEs should tell their Sales Reps how they would like to be introduced.  
  
---  
  
Here's a better option:  
  
AE: "For this meeting, I was able to get one of our Solutions Engineers, Rew, to join us. He has a great deal of expertise working with our clients and is basically here to offer free advisory and solutions expertise as you are going through this decision-making process. I've given Rew some of the background on your business already, and he may jump in with some more questions to better understand your needs."  
  
---  
  
Notice the difference??  
  
The first introduction paints the SE almost like a human instruction manual on all of the software's features/technicalities. It puts the SE in a position where they have to wait until the prospect has a question before speaking. Then, they become reactive, which is exactly what you don't want them to be.  
  
The second introduction, however, paints the SE as a guide that the client can trust and puts the SE in the position of being a client leader. Which is exactly where you want them to be.  
  
---  
 
Now it's your turn.  
 
How do you introduce your SE? Drop your scripts below.

content:
Knowing these 5 unwritten rules of sales would have gotten me to quota faster - and also lowered my stress level as a new AE... 
 
 
1/ They have to tell us "No" a couple times before they tell us "Yes". 
 
2/ The real Decision Maker will never tell you "I'm the only Decision Maker". 
 
3/ Enterprise deals will "almost die" at least three times before they're actually signed. 
 
4/ Early stage sellers get Happy Ears. Tenured sellers get more & more paranoid. 
 
5/ The more you need the deal, the more likely it is to be a nail-biter, last minute, EOQ signature. 
 

 
Here's the WHY - 
 
1/ The first & second Opps on an account are usually the latter stages of 'brand awareness'. Marketing stats say that you'll need ~20 touches before the org is familiar with you. (Has seen your brand enough to feel it's not as risky to spend $$ with you.) 
 
 
2/ The real DMs know they need to get consensus. It's the sign of a lower level persona - gatekeeper - blocker to say they're the ONLY ones who need to evaluate or sign off. 
 
While there's multiple DMs, there's frequently only 1 signer. And you may never interact with them at all (CFO, etc) 
 
 
3/ Enterprise deals have many more people involved. A huge number of ripple effects across the tech stack, the current process & internal politics. If the deal hasn't been on the brink of death and/or resurrected at least a couple of times, you're not close to the finish line yet. Sad but true. 
 
 
4/ Early career sellers get excited about all the positive things Prospects say. Experienced sellers are always looking for ways the deal can go wrong. Expert sellers proactively bring up typical obstacles so they can smooth out the process for their Buyers. 
 
 
5/ Murphy's Law, sales edition 
 
 
 
What Unwritten Rules of Sales did I miss?

content:
It was one of the lowest points in my career. But it should have been one of the highlights.

Instead, my anxiety exploded to a new high and my mind was constantly racing.


Here's why -

I was coming off 2 years averaging 127% attainment at a small startup.

I had just been hired by a billion dollar, publicly traded technology company.

And after the first few weeks in that role, I went from feeling “on top of the world” to “completely out of my league.”

You know that saying “If you’re the smartest person in the room, you’re in the wrong room”?

Mission accomplished. 😨


EVERYONE on my new team was accomplished and ambitious and whip-smart.
And knew wayyy more than me about all the tech.

If you could see my Google history from that time 🙈 


And it wasn't just the technical stuff.

These sellers had skills that were next level. They were doing things I’d never done.

Account Planning, User Roundtables, creating Centers of Excellence in customer accounts.

Any previous confidence evaporated & I was completely overwhelmed. 

I was afraid I’d fail - big. That I’d inevitably be “found out” and fired.

The exact phrase running through my head was “What if I never sell anything here?”


In desperation, I reached out to a mentor. She was Director of Sales at another public tech company, and she said the most surprising thing I could have imagined.

“I know exactly how you feel.” 

She went on.

“Every time I start a new role or a new company, my initial thought is ‘I can’t hold court with these people.’”

Then she went even further and sent me a YouTube video.

It's a TED talk on Imposter Syndrome​ - by ​Atlassian's CEO.


If you’ve started at a new org, gotten a promotion or changed roles, taking a few minutes to watch it might be the best gift you can give yourself.

Hearing CEO Mike Cannon-Brookes talk about all the times he’s felt like he doesn’t know what he’s doing, and doesn’t deserve to be there - and how he copes with it - forever changed my mindset.

Somehow, it’s even better when you know that his company is worth $54B, and his personal net worth is over $13B.


Once I knew other people - LOTS of people! Successful people! - felt this way, it freed up my mind to take the “next right steps”.

-> Set meetings with the rockstar AEs at my new gig- to learn their secrets.
-> Blocked time each week to read up on the technical stuff.
-> Paid for weekly 1:1 sessions with a sales coach. 


I don’t know what your “next right steps” are.

But if you’re feeling overwhelmed, maybe give that video a look.

Knowing that you’re not alone might be just what you need. (And if you know someone who’s feeling that way - send this along to them as a lil belated Valentine.💝) 


Selling is freaking hard.

Don’t be too rough on yourself.

Whether it’s watching a Ted talk or something else, I hope you show yourself some love today!

content:
2 of the 3 tech unicorns I've worked at train their AEs on 2 core concepts that salespeople don't typically learn: 
 
 
--> Towards v. Away language 
--> Above the Line (ATL) v. Below the Line (BTL) 
 
 
1) Towards v. Away language 
 
-> 80% of people are motivated by moving Away from Pain (more people would run from a German Shepherd than towards a Gold medal*) 
 
-> But sales reps talk about Gain, aka moving Towards: "time back in your day" & ROI 
 
 
Here's how it sounds IRL at UserGems 💎 : 
 
-> Towards sounds like, "Because my product automatically detects buying signals like champion job changes & promotions, your sales reps will save 29% of their time and you'll see a 18x ROI." 
 
-> Away sounds like, "What goes away [by using my product] is sales rep's spending hours on manual research, the low morale from not seeing results, and the frustration of your team missing their number." 
 
 
->>>TL;DR = talk about what problems go away 
 
 
 
 
2) Above the Line (ATL) v. Below the Line (BTL) 
 
-> "The Line" is the 'power line', so Directors, VPs, CXOs = Above the Line 
 
-> BTL thinks about their team v. ATL thinks about market share & risk 
 
 
IRL / UserGems example: 
 
-> BTL value prop sounds like, "What goes away [with my product] is worrying about too little pipeline, missing quota & sales reps quitting." 
 
-> ATL value prop sounds like, "With [my product] you reduce 3 risks: Your top competitor doesn't get in the door first, you don't lose more market share, and you don't have to explain your inaction to investors." 
 
 
->>> TL;DR = choose the right language for your audience 
 
 
 
It takes time and effort to wrap our heads around these. 
 
But there's a reason the unicorns teach them. They win deals. 
 
Wanna try your hand at it? Write your Value Prop "Towards v. Away" language in the comments 
 
 
 

 
*ATL/BTL concepts from Skip Miller’s book Proactive Selling. Credit for "German Shepherds v. Gold Medals" comes from the book Secrets of Question-Based Selling by Thomas Freese

content:
Not saying “I don’t know“ might kill your chances at a great job. 

A Head of Sales once told me they intentionally ask an “impossible” question during the mock demo part in the hiring process. If the candidate pretended to know the answer, they were not offered a job.

Brian LaManna has a great way to handle this - whether it's in a customer call or an interview.

Here's his take:

"𝗕𝘂𝘆𝗲𝗿:
Asks a tough or very specific question

𝗠𝗲:
"That's a great question. I'm actually not sure. Is it okay if I get you the right answer internally and then follow up?"


𝗡𝗼𝘄:
1. Mark it as an action item
2. Find the right answer internally
3. Great excuse to single thread a follow up


Buyers do not expect us to know everything.

It's 10x more of a red flag to pretend that we do 🚩


Experienced sellers can say "I don't know", rookie sellers won't admit it.

We should say it at minimum, once a deal cycle.

The most powerful, boring line to build trust."


How do you handle it when you don't know the answer to a prospect question? 

What's worked well?  And what's bombed?

content:
If I was starting a new sales role today, here are the 5 things I’d do in the first 5 days- 
 
 
1/ Find the accounts in my territory that are most likely to buy (aka the most like past buyers). 
 
I'd do this by creating a CRM report of Closed Won deals for the Past 2 years, with these details: 
 
 
- industry 
- location 
- age of company 
- $ ARR amount 
- # of employees 
- names/personas involved in the purchase 
 
THEN I'd create a report of Prospects with similarities in my territory/account list. 
 
^^This is the low hanging fruit. 
 
 
 
2/ I'd find 3-5 consistent top performers and ask them 3 simple questions: 
 
—-> Who are the best personas for us? 
--> Which are their 2-3 top business problems we solve (+vocabulary they use)? 
--> What's the # 1 thing to do/not do when just starting in this role? 
 
^^This is a shortcut for how to start off with a Bang...without trying to reinvent the wheel. 
 
 
 
3/ I'd set up intro calls with internal folks like Finance/Deal desk, Legal, Product, Support, Solution Consulting, Channel partners, Systems Integrators, etc... anyone who I'll regularly interact with on deals. 
 
Start figuring out the best "Gives" for each person - do they like Starbucks, Slack shout outs, special beverages for EOQ/EOY? I'd put quarterly reminders on my calendar (and schedule quarterly deliveries where it makes sense). 
 
^^This is how we create our "tribe"/internal network within a company...giving right from the start, rather than just being 'another seller who wants something'. 
 
 
 
4/ I'd memorize 5-8 customer stories. 
 
Starting with writing a 1 min summary on note cards - with the Champion's name/title, pain felt, problem solved & impact created. 
 
I'd practice telling these stories out loud every morning for 10 minutes...until I don't need the notecards anymore. Then I'd rinse/ repeat, memorizing 5 new stories. 
 
^^This is how we can build confidence & credibility. 
 
 
 
5/ I'd analyze my boss’s personality - LOTS of tools for this - and I'd ask them about their top 2 career goals in our first 1:1 chat. 
 
^^This is how we can start to manage up. 



These are the top 5 things that have paid off the most for me when starting a new role.

What's worked well for you - what would you do if you were starting over?

content:
Here's the story of how I spent $14.88 to get a $702k deal unstuck.

After 9 months of working closely with my Champion, she said she was ready to sign. But then she went dark. 

What I didn't understand yet: She wasn't ghosting me. She was paralyzed by risk.


I tried calling & emailing with reminders of
--> The problems she was solving for
--> How our solution 'ticked all the boxes'
--> The ROI and business case we collaborated on

Nothing.


In desperation, I went for a walk and put myself in her shoes. What would I be worried about in her position?

I realized we'd done a lot of work around how our solution could solve many of her problems.

We'd done a lot LESS talking about how to ensure her org would adopt our solution.


So here's what I did:

I bought the book "Switch: How to Change When Change is Hard" for $14.88 on Amazon.

Before sending it, I highlighted specific sections about leading organizational change and reducing resistance.

I included a note: "Thought this might help as you roll this out. The highlighted parts reminded me of our conversations."


Two days after it was delivered, she called. Her team formed a "book club" to  apply the lessons book inside their whole department.

Two months later, the deal closed.


Why did this work?

The authors of "The Challenger Sale" explain: The status quo isn't considered one person's fault. But if somebody says, "Hey, we should do this enterprise-wide thing..." now the solution is attached to their name.

It's a lot of risk for our Champions.

Buyers are experts in how to do their jobs. They are NOT experts in:
--> How to buy our stuff
--> Change management
--> Driving organizational adoption


My $14.88 investment showed I understood her real fear: What happens AFTER the purchase.

Now when deals stall near the finish line, I ask myself: Is it about price/features? 

Or is my champion feeling that weight of risk?


What's your best move to help champions with the fear of "What Happens After We Sign"?

content:
Salesforce's top Enterprise AE for a Fortune 50 company shared a giant success secret with me. 
 
Elite team selling, using the "3 G's". Here's how she does it. 
 
And the last one is the most important... 
 
 
She teams up with the SDR, Solutions Consultant (SC/SE), CSM & RVP on 
--> The Grapevine 
--> The Group 
--> The Goal 
 
 
 
The Grapevine - 
She religiously holds a weekly strategy meeting that includes "what I've heard / what you've heard" from each person. 
 
It's brief, keeps everyone on the same page, and saves hundreds of DMs. 
 
 
 
The Group - 
Throughout the week, she often acts as a Project Manager. She keeps clear communication on who is following up with who, aligning roles & titles. 
 
And she keeps track of this in her Account Plan, which the whole group can access. 
 
 
 
The Goal - 
She runs standalone prep calls for upcoming customer-facing meetings. 
 
Her calendar invites always include these 3 notes: 
 
1) The vibe we're going for on this call 
(How do we want them to feel when the call ends? Confident? At ease? Excited?) 
 
2) The 2 things we can't end this meeting without knowing. (Guides discovery questions & gives the group something to listen for.) 
 
3) The next step we're suggesting. (So the team isn't surprised & can offer feedback.) 
 
 
 
Enterprise sales take a huge effort. 
 
The best sellers know it has to be a team sport. 

How are you keeping your internal team on the same page?

content:
Ever notice how the most successful Enterprise AEs act differently than everyone else in Q1 and Q2?

After working with top sellers at Salesforce, Tableau, and Outreach, I've noticed something fascinating: 

The top 1% get there in person. Early. ​

​
I'll never forget my manager asking me in 2019: "How many onsite visits do you have planned for Q1?"

I looked at my calendar. Zero.

Meanwhile, the #1 rep on our team already had 6 customer visits locked in for March alone. She knew going onsite early is a secret weapon.


3 ways onsite visits create an unfair advantage

--> You learn the unspoken truth about culture 
The moment you walk into a company's lobby, you learn more than you would in 10 Zoom calls. Is it modern or traditional? Energetic or subdued? These cultural insights help you position your solution in a way that resonates.

--> You uncover hidden stakeholders 
"Who else should join us for lunch?" This simple question has helped me identify critical influencers who weren't on any org chart. On a videoconference, you only meet who they want you to meet.


--> You build genuine relationships faster IRL
You notice the family photos, sports memorabilia, or diplomas that create real connection points.  A VP of Analytics who usually sat silent with arms crossed on Zoom did a complete turnaround after we met for dinner. She sent me a thank you note that ended with, "Now I feel like I've known you for years." We can't do that with any slide deck.


My best onsite story

In 2019, I had a mid-stage deal with a healthcare analytics company in the Midwest that was starting to stall. I was concerned because we couldn't get the involvement of the CEO. My mobilizer in the deal was the Director of Analytics, but I worried we didn't have an exec Champion.

Once I got onsite and met with their team in the CEO's office, it was clear that the CEO was not involved in most company operations. He was  semi-retired. It was a new VP - a woman named Hope - who was really in charge. Everyone looked at her before they said anything in the meeting.

I'd have never known without being there in person.


How to make it happen

--> Block time NOW - 
Schedule 2-3 days per month exclusively for onsite visits. Look at your calendar - what's the worst day of your week for internal meetings? Block that day for the next 3 mos.

--> Make it easy for them - 
"I'll be in your area on Thursday and would love to buy you coffee" works better than "Can we schedule an onsite meeting?"

--> Come prepared - 
Have a clear agenda, bring the right materials & make every minute count.


With so many sellers hiding behind screens, showing up in person is an unfair advantage. It de-risks deals, builds real relationships & creates the kind of insights that simply can't happen virtually.

When was the last time an in-person meeting completely changed the trajectory of a deal?

"I've had 3 different Account Executives from your company in the last 18 months. No, I don't want to meet."

I will NEVER forget getting that reply when I was excitedly sending out my Q1  I'm-Your-New-AE emails.

It got me thinking about how I could actually add value in those emails - so they'd ASK for a meeting.



Passing along the below list as it's hands down one of the best posts I've seen on "adding value." 
 
It's from Brandon “BMO” Morgan, a Salesforce RVP and their "Coach of the Year" for 2023. 

If you're not following him, you're missing out on some invaluable stuff.
 

 
*****************
 
"Here are the top 10 most valuable things you can do for your customer today: 
 
1/ Help them solve a problem: 
 
- Know your customers. Know the industry you sell to 
- Outline problems you have solved for other customers 
 
 
2/ Repurpose shelfware: 
 
- Don't dodge this. Address this head-on. 
- It will help you build trust and speed up your deal cycles. 
- There is no deal with unrealized value sitting on the shelf. 
 
 
3/ Usage data: 
 
- Help the customer understand how their teams are using your software. 
- Where is their usage strong vs. areas of opportunity for improvement. 
 
 
4/ Help your customer use the product more effectively: 
 
- Have your customer show you how they use your technology 
- Show them how your company uses your technology (if they do) 
 
 
5/ Recap what you have been able to accomplish together: 
 
- What problems have you solved? What ROI have they seen? 
- Customers forget about the impact the solution has had on their org 
 
 
6/ Help your customer learn about your product: 
 
- Customer to customer events 
- Short demo videos 
 
 
7/ Industry trends: 
 
- You have unique insight that your customers don’t always get based on the work you do inside of the industry with your other customers. 
- Share your learnings and industry findings broadly with your customers. 
 
 
8/ Help them understand the value other customers are seeing: 
 
- Is there a use case you can share that you are seeing other customers deploy? 
- What key metrics were impacted? 
 
 
9/ Connect the dots: 
 
- In a lot of cases you are talking to your customer more than they are talking to each other internally. 
- Send recap emails from your conversations with other departments, the problems you identified, and your plan to help solve the problems. 
 
 
10/ Help them sell internally: 
 
- Have your customer pitch you on why they need the solution, what the ROI is, and how they are justifying the cost. 
- Build the deliverable for them (one-sheeter, deck, ROI model, etc). "
