content:
Check out 4 things Rory Evans did to close an outbound deal with a CEO - that started with cold email. 
  
Mohamed Chahin, 𝘾𝙀𝙊 𝙤𝙛 𝙏𝙬𝙖𝙞𝙣 𝙬𝙖𝙨 𝙩𝙝𝙚 𝙗𝙪𝙮𝙚𝙧. 𝗛𝗲 𝙝𝙖𝙨 𝙩𝙝𝙞𝙨 𝙢𝙚𝙨𝙨𝙖𝙜𝙚 𝙛𝙤𝙧 𝙚𝙫𝙚𝙧𝙮𝙤𝙣𝙚 𝙙𝙤𝙞𝙣𝙜 𝙘𝙤𝙡𝙙 𝙤𝙪𝙩𝙗𝙤𝙪𝙣𝙙:  
  
"I BOUGHT. 
  
Here’s what Rory did right to close me... 
  
  
1️⃣ Initial message 
  
- No introduction 
- A short subject line 
- A soft but clear CTA 
- A relevant social proof 
- No surface-level personalization 
- One sentence describing his product 
- Lots of whitespace for mobile-friendly reading 
- A RELEVANT thought-provoking opening question 
  
Rory’s message didn’t get me hooked on talking to him, but it got me hooked to reply. 
  
Which is what you want. You want to qualify as fast as possible. 
  
I will never buy what’s irrelevant, but so often it’s a question of timing. 
  
So he got my reply with an indication on when timing might be better. 
  
  
2️⃣ Follow-up 
  
Rory’s follow-up message had GREAT timing. 
  
And he didn't stop there. He followed up. 
  
I could’ve easily missed that 1st message.  My inbox is full. All the time. 
  
  
3️⃣ Ongoing chat 
  
I replied to the initial message because it was so good. 
  
I replied to the follow-up because the timing was right. 
  
It’s that simple. 
  
Next Rory did something I WISH more sellers would do: 
  
-> He answered my question instead of asking for my time. 
  
-> He answered my question in 8 minutes!!! 8 minutes, people. That’s the bar. 
  
I have yet to meet a successful executive who doesn’t value speed. 
  
  
4️⃣ Closing 
  
This part was the easiest for Rory. 
  
We were in the market, and we didn’t even bother to compare. 
  
You need to be aware of this concept: C-Level time is expensive. [I'm more concerned with time I waste than I am about the cheapest option.] 
  
The less time I have to invest, the more I’m willing to buy the “not cheapest” option. 
  
Again, because it’s so important, I did not compare prices!! 
  
  
This is the beauty of outbound. 
  
Before Rory reached out, I had never heard of his product. 
  
I was happy he showed me a solution I didn’t know existed.  
  
We closed fast because he made it easy for me. 
  
He saved me time. He follow up. He replied fast. 
  
Be like Rory."

The best AEs **incentivize SDRs** to work on their accounts. Here are 2 easy ways to do that.

If you work with an SDR who supports 4 AEs, here's hoping those other 3 don't see this 🤣 


1) KNOW how SDRs are comped -

2) KNOW what the SDRs goals are - 
 - Does SDR want to be an AE?
 - If so, can the SDR run or join Discovery calls?
 - Can AE mentor SDR on developing other AE skills?
 - OR, if the SDR wants a different career path? How can we help?


Sales is always about WIIFM (What’s in it for ME).

This is true for both external Buyers & internal Teammates (ie SDRs).

The savviest & highest performing sellers use WIIFM as their North Star.


Why go to this level of time & effort with SDRs? 

Truly partnering with SDRs can change both your lives.

AEs get more selling time & SDRs book more meetings.

Everyone makes more money. We get to feel good about helping someone else. And sometimes you form a great friendship to boot!

article.description: It’s the end of the year, and we all face the same challenge. Which deals should we focus on - and which ones aren't going anywhere?The tough part is

content:
Here's exactly how I structure my follow-ups to stop deals from slipping or ghosting at the last minute. 
 
Buyers ask themselves 5 crucial questions before they spend money. 
 
So we match our follow ups to each different question of the buying journey. 
 
 
The questions: 
 
 
1/  "Do we Have a Problem or Goal that we Urgently need help with?"  
 
Follow up examples: 
Thought Leadership emphasizing the size / importance of the problem.  
 
Things like articles from Forbes, McKinsey, HBR or an industry specific publication. 
 
Screenshots, summations or info-graphics.  NOT LINKS.  No one reads them. 
 
 
 
2/ "What's out there to Solve the Problem? How do Vendors differ?"  
 
Follow up examples: 
Sample RFP templates with pre-filled criteria.  Easy to read buying guides.  Especially if written by a 3rd party. 
 
 
 
3/ "What Exactly do we need this Solution to do? Who do we feel good about?" 
 
Follow up examples: 
3 bullets of criteria your Buyers commonly use during evaluations (especially differentiators.) 
 
Here's example wording I've used at UserGems 💎:  
 
"Thought you might find it helpful to see how other companies have evaluated tools to track their past champions.  
 
Their criteria are usually:  
  *Data quality & ROI potential 
  *Security (SOC2 type 2 and GDPR) 
  *How easy or hard is it to take action: set up/training, automation, playbooks 
 
Cheers!" 
 
 
 
4/ "Is the Juice worth the Squeeze - both $$$ & Time?" 
 
Follow up examples: 
Screenshots of emails, texts or DMs from customers talking about easy set up. 
 
Love using ones like the Slack pictured here. Feels more organic and authentic than a marketing case study. 
 
 
 
5/ "What's next? How will this get done?"  
 
Follow up examples: 
Visual timelines 
Introductions to the CSM/onboard team 
Custom/short videos from CSM leadership 
 
 
 
When we tailor our follow ups to answer the questions our Buyers are asking themselves - 
 
Even (especially!) the subconscious ones  
 
Our sales cycles can be smoother, faster and easier to forecast. 
 
 
Buyer Experience > Sales Stages 
 
What's your best advice for how to follow up?

On 30 Minutes to President's Club, we talked about a different way. 
 
The 3x3x3 method.  Maybe it might work for you? 
 
 
-->3 Buying Personas

--> 3 Buying Personas 
 
Before the 1st call 
 
Find 3 people with VP+ titles 
 
From departments typically involved in buying your offering 
 
 
 
--> 3-Step Sequence 
 
Put them into a 3-step sequence, about 4-7 days before the call 
 
1st touch/1st day = thoughtful comment on a recent LinkedIn post 
 
2nd touch = LinkedIn connection request, mentioning their post 
 
3rd touch = email or LinkedIn message about your meeting 
 
 
Sounds like --> 
"Hi {{first_name}} - Your colleague Callie scheduled a meeting with me, and I thought you might be interested. 
 
Topic is tracking your past buyers' job changes for repeat business. (Also to lower churn risk.) And how to automatically Multi-thread into deals & accounts. 
 
Executives in (your department) aren't always involved. But some have specific OKRs that are relevant here. 
 
Should I forward an invite? Either way, I'll keep you posted." 
 
 
 
--> 3 Part Follow up 
 
#1 Day of the meeting: Short recap of the meeting 
 
#2 Day of the meeting: Put them in a nurture sequence (either thought leadership OR reminding you to recap any additional meetings) 
 
#3 A week later: Ghostwrite an intro email for a Manager/Exec from your team to send. Execs starting their own private channel of communication can be extremely powerful. Start early. 
  
 
 
With this 3x3x3, you get both visibility & credibility across their org. 
 
Your meeting attendee can't be a gatekeeper. 
 
Win/win. 
 
 
 
What kind of multi-threading is working well for you? 

ps - Multi-threading is essential in Enterprise deals. We're covering ways to get some quick wins in the "Enterprise Deal Quickstart" workshop I'm doing Feb 12-13. See my bio if you'd like to come!

content:
After working at 3 tech unicorns & 11 years in sales, I've finally learned to prep for calls in 5 minutes.  
  
Been tweaking this template for the last 4 years.  
  
It looks like:  
--> XX year old org  
--> # of employees  
--> % growth on LI / sales growing %  
--> Prior Ops? Result of Prior Op?  
--> Tech stack:  
--> Company News?  
--> Who will be On the call: (name/title)  
--> How long in Company/Role:  
  
  
Here's the specific WHY:  
  
--> XX year old org: The older the company, the slower they will make decisions (not always true...but almost always)  
  
--> # of employees: Points to the number of end users, but also probable growth stage  
  
--> % growth on LI & sales growing %: Companies experiencing double or triple-digit growth make faster decisions  
  
--> Prior Ops? Result of Prior Op?: Have they talked to us before? How did it go?  
  
--> Tech stack: Do they invest heavily in tech? Do they use best of breed?  
  
--> Company News: May hold the biggest clues as to why they took the call  
  
--> Who will be On the call: (name/title) If they are Above the Line/ATL, I'll tailor my language to Impact on Risks & Market share. If Below the Line/BTL I'll speak more to Impact for the team / 'what goes away' for team  
  
--> How long in Company/Role: The shorter the time they've been there, the more likely they are to 1) still have budget 2) still be looking to make a big splash  
  
  
  
Here's the overarching WHY:  
--> Research makes 1st calls more impactful 
I know the basics so we can get to deeper things quicker  
  
--> Establishes how I want to run the call  
If growth & sales are down vs way up, those are different calls  
  
--> Sets the tone  
They know I come prepared. So much credibility to be earned by >>not<< asking prospects questions that could be answered by Google  
  
  

Creating repeatable systems in our sales motions not only makes us feel more prepared, it helps us win. 
 
Recent research says we increase win rates 8 to 12% when we use a repeatable process. 
 
And we're 48 to 66% more likely to hit quota.

3 hidden risks to our deals:  focusing too much on execs, missing the real decision-makers & making it hard/complicated to buy.  And the antidotes-


  - Reduce complexity to speed up deals
  - Identify the Mobilizers who drive change
  - Work with all 3 power levels to lower buyer risk

Easy enough to say WHAT to do.

I found out HOW to do these the hard way. Here's what I learned - maybe it will save you some time...



---> Reducing complexity to speed up deals

Time kills deals. And complexity makes everything take longer.

Top ways I've seen reps make things easer:

1/ "Making sense" selling - Coming with POVs & value adds to help Buyers make good decisions 

2/ Using Digital Sales Rooms - Reducing friction by keeping all resources in 1 place vs attached to 40 emails

3/ Teaching Buyers How to Buy - ending every call with "Typically what comes next is..." to prescribe next steps.
 


---> Working with all 3 power levels to lower buyer risk

Executives are important to a deal, but they won't make decisions in a vacuum. So if you ONLY focus on execs, your deal is at risk....

Because it is RISKY to be a buyer. If their name is attached to a huge purchase that fails, their job is on the line.

So execs lean on Managers, technical experts/IT and end users in evaluations.

THIS is why multi-threaded deals have a 5X win rate (!!!)

The top reps I've talked with know they have to work at all 3 power levels - and communicate WIIFM to each - 

1/ Executive
2/ Managers
3/ End Users



---> Identifying the (often hidden) Mobilizers who drive change

Sellers who target "Mobilizers" are 31% more likely to be high performers.
(Challenger data)

Top-performers spend their time focused on the 3 who are the best at building consensus & creating change (the Mobilizers): ​
​The Go-Getter
The Skeptic*
The Teacher ​

​*The Skeptic pushes back on the idea because they’re exploring it thoughtfully. 



IMPACT of these 3 Actions (Challenger data):
---> Closed 26% more deals
---> Brought in 27% more revenue
---> Shortened sales cycles by ~1 mo

content:
3 tech unicorns. 11+ years in sales. 6 years as an Enterprise AE. And pipeline management is still hard.  
  
But I've learned 2 strategies that I use every day.  
  
Strategies for:  
--> Deciding which deals to focus on  
--> When to give up & move on  
  
  
  
--> Deciding which deals to focus on  
  
Companies have ICPs: Ideal Customer Profiles  
  
I have IOPs: Ideal Opportunity Profiles  
  
When I have to decide how much time, research, and personalization to devote, I give each deal a "grade".  
  
I've narrowed down 8 characteristics of deals that are most likely to close.  
  
I assign points to each characteristic.  
  
My point system looks like this:  
  
  
--> There's a Champion Who Gives the "Inside Scoop": 10 points  
--> They have Specific Goals with Metrics for Each: 10 points  
-->They Invest Heavily in Tech Related to My Product: 10 points  
--> They are Responsive to Calls, Texts, Email: 10 points  
--> There are a Low Number of Obstacles: 10 points  
--> They have Lots of Potential End Users: 15 points  
--> They have a Compelling Event: 20 points  
--> They make Decisions Quickly: 15 points  
  
  
The higher the grade, the more time and energy I spend on it.  
  
  
  
--> When to give up & move on  
  
I use a "3 strikes You're Out" rule.  
  
If there is no response after I reach out 3 times  
  
across 3 different channels (email, text, LinkedIn, phone, Slack, etc.)  
  
I close it out. 
  
  
  
These may sound simple or obvious, but it took me years of agonizing.  
  
  
I wish more companies trained on this kind of practical, day-to-day stuff.  
  
The "basics" of sales are often not simple.  
  
Or obvious.

content:
As a new AE, I got ghosted a lot after Pricing meetings.  Now I know I was making 3 mistakes. Here's how I fixed that.
 
 
Where I effed up (accidentally):
 
---> Going in blind 
---> Doing all the numbers myself  
---> Yes means nothing without HOW  
 
 
How I fixed it: 
 
---> Going in blind 
 
Presenting pricing to an Executive Sponsor without a Champion looking over the deck first was my 1st problem. 
 
I was going in blind at a crucial point in the deal. (Which also put my Champion at risk.) 
 
I learned to set up a pre-meeting with my Champion. 
 
This sounds like -->  
"Aaron, I'm working on the proposal for Angie. I want to make you look good. And make the best use of Angie's time. Can I send you what I've done so far, and put 15 minutes on your calendar Thursday morning at 9am for us to look at it together?" 
 
 
TL:DR --> No presentation without collaboration 
 
 
 
---> Doing all the numbers myself 
 
Every software company in the world has some sort of ROI tool.  
 
It was easy to plug all the numbers in myself. 
 
Don't repeat my mistake. 
 
 
Our champion - and ideally others from the buying committee- should collaborate on the business case. 
 
If you don’t get their input, they won't  believe the numbers. 
 
Buyers need to know where the numbers came from anyway. They're the ones who  have to defend them. 
 
And that will happen at an internal meeting you won't be invited to. 
 
 
Asking for an ROI session sounds like -->  
“We have a couple of internal resources to help you put together the business case. Most folks find them helpful because they don’t have to start from scratch. The first pass at this should take 15-20 minutes. How is 9 AM on Thursday?” 
 
 
TL:DR --> No calculation without collaboration 
 
 
 
---> Yes means nothing without HOW  
 
This game changer is from Chris Voss, and fixed my longest running mistake. 
 
What often gets us ghosted after a pricing meeting is telling them how much it will cost in terms of dollars, but giving them no idea how much it will cost in terms of time. 
 
 
Every pricing meeting should include an overview of implementation. 
 
One slide for a small - midsize deal. 
 
For enterprise, the pricing meeting should include folks from implementation and CS. 
 
 
Up to this point, the buying committee has likely only seen people from sales.  
 
Helping Buyers put names and faces with those who will implement & support them is a way to lower risk.  
 
 
The sale may be 'the end' for the rep, but it's just the beginning for the customer. 
 
Clients need to feel secure about what happens in the next chapter of this adventure.  
 
Or they won't go. 
 
 
TL:DR --> No price presentation without implementation 
 
 
Hopefully this saves someone from making my same mistakes. 
 
What did I miss?  Let's help some people close their Q4 deals!

I was struggling 14 years ago. Very unexpectedly, I became a single parent. 
 
And when I say struggle, I mean things got so tight financially that packs of gum were a frivolous expense. 
 
We did not take vacations or go to amusement parks. Heck, we didn’t even go out to eat. 
 
 
I was always worried about money. I had to tell my kids "no" a lot.
 
And I was determined that our lives would not stay that way. 
 
I made a plan to pivot to a new industry. 
 
 
And then researched, and networked, and checked out library books, and worked a lot of 18 hour days. 
 
I found a lot of dead ends. 
 
And cried more times than I’d like to remember. 
 
 
And today - after a loooooong series of ups and downs - my life is radically different. 
 
So...“if you’re going through hell, just keep going.” 
 
Rest if you can this weekend, and then keep putting one foot in front of the other. 
 
 
You will get there. 
 
It will all be okay. 

 
And what a story you’ll be able to tell. 🤗

content:
Last month, a top SaaS leader predicted AI will start replacing 70% of GTM in 2025. That might feel terrifying - or irrelevant. Here’s why it’s neither.

Let’s start with a reassurance, so no one kicks off their morning with a panic attack.

57% of salespeople say they don’t use AI now. So if you haven’t, you’re not alone.

Also, probably a good idea to get started.


Whether you use AI for everything you can - or you’ve never used anything “AI” before…

Here are 2 easy chatGPT prompts you can use in 15 minutes.

And they can help you in every meeting you have today.

Prove me wrong.



PROMPT  1 : Dealing with Objections

—-> [Part One] "I sell [product] to [target audience]. What are some objections buyers might have?"

Most salespeople know common objections. The point of this prompt is to get to:

—-> [Part Two]  “As a salesperson, how can I talk with my prospective buyers with confidence and clarity when they have these concerns? Please suggest 1-3 sentence responses that lead with empathy and at a 5th grade reading level.”

As an example, here’s an answer from chatGPT when I asked about objections related to time-tracking software:

************
Objections related to Privacy and Trust Issues
"That’s a fair concern—no one wants to feel watched. Our software is designed to track processes, not people, and we prioritize transparency. Can I show you how it works?"
************

Empathetic, concise, permission based. (And notice the alliteration??) 



PROMPT 2 - Pricing & Missing Feature Concerns

—-> [Part One]  "You are conducting pricing research. Compare [my company] pricing to [Competitor 1], [Competitor 2], and [Competitor 3]. Include company name, features, pricing tiers, and plan names. Compile data in a table and include a summary of what features my company is missing versus my competitors."

—-> [Part Two] As a salesperson [my company], how can I answer my prospective buyers when they ask about each of these missing features? Please suggest 1-3 sentence responses that lead with empathy and at a 5th grade reading level. 

I won’t spoil it for you. The responses here are jaw-dropping.


If you haven’t jumped on the AI bandwagon yet, you’re not alone.

And also, probably a good idea to get started.

NOT because others are doing it.

Because it’s friggin’ helpful.

content:
$20M is the average net worth of Dr. Julie Garner’s coaching clients, who are entrepreneurs and CEOs. “How to focus” is one of the biggest topics she covers.
​
​Turns out, everyone needs help with this.​
​
​Here’s Dr. Gurner's unusual advice -
​
“There is more to effective focus than simply buckling down, honing in, and doing the work. The under-discussed, yet equally as important, aspect of focus is blocking out.

This can be blocking out simple task distractions such as your cell phone or social media. Or, perhaps more importantly, things that distract you when you could be making moves, building, or creating. These distractions can be deadly to your progress. They derail you. They pull you off course....

Build an environment ripe for focus, building, and moving to your goals. Block out anything that won’t help you get there.”
___
​
​Here are 2 simple ways I’ve implemented that advice as a seller.
1) Calendar blocking
2) Shortcuts & systems to spend less time on Email
​
​
​
1) Calendar blocking
​
​I was afraid to block my calendar for the first half of my sales career.​
​
Afraid I'd miss out on getting 1st calls if XDRs couldn't find a slot,
afraid Buyers would be irritated if I was ever unavailable,
or that my boss would see it & be mad.
​
​And yet, without blocking my calendar, I was constantly reacting to things.​
​I was always busy, but maddeningly unproductive.
Frustrated I never "had time" for important work.​
​
When I finally got fed up & decided to experiment with blocking my calendar out of pure frustration, here are the 3 calendar blocks I started with:

--> Prospecting first thing in the morning
--> Responding to email only a few times per day
--> Internal meetings and admin work on Mondays & Fridays
​
​
Advanced level -
Color coding your calendar for insights on how you spend your time.
​
If you took 5 minutes to set this up and tried it as an experiment for 2 weeks, what could you learn?
​
​

2) Shortcuts & systems to work faster via Email

For me, part of what got in the way of using calendar blocks was how much time I spent on email.​
​
Before creating systems for how I dealt with email, I felt like my inbox was a quicksand swamp.​
​
Here's what I did about it.
​
​
​First step -
Using Outlook “Quickparts” or Gmail Snippets - Even with tools like Outreach, I’ve found these tools are faster and easier for quick emails. Saves so much time for phrases I use frequently.

Worth it to set this up? Consider that saving 15 min/ day every week = 62.5 hours saved per year.​
​
​
Advanced level -
Create custom sequences in Outreach /Salesloft / HubSpot for reminders to send stakeholder updates, multi-threading, etc.
​
FYI - These aren’t automated emails. They’re *automated tasks* to keep me on track in my deals - without depending on memory or cluttering my calendar. The task pops up a template, then I tweak & manually send.
​
​
Any of these intriguing? Or do they just seem scary?

Best ways you block distractions for more selling time?

content:
If you're already a top 5% seller, this will be a refresher. If you're new to a role, it's crucial.

And you won't hear it in an onboarding session.
 
Make a list of 10 impacts. 


Why? We can leverage it in every meeting from Discovery to Deciding on terms. 

 
We start with 1 problem our product solves. 
 
Then write down 10 impacts of not solving that problem. 
 
Here's an example of the list I made when I started at UserGems 💎  --> 
 
 
10 Impacts of Low Pipeline for a sales leader: 
->Missing quota 
->Career damage 
->Slow revenue growth 
->Increase Cost of Sale 
->Decreased Profitability 
->Not enough New Logos 
->Infighting with the Marketing team 
->High Customer Acquisition Cost (CAC) 
->Increased Pressure on Improving Close Rates 
->Low team morale leads to rep Churn & Recruiting issues 
 
 
 
How can we find these impacts? Here are 3 different ways: 
 
-> Read our org's customer stories/testimonials. What problems do they mention?

-> Listen/read like our Buyer: industry podcasts, websites & newsletters.  What problems are they always focused on?

-> Ask a top-performing AE for what problems/impacts they hear ... after we've done our homework (i.e. found at least 4 yourself)
 

Once we find the top 3 problems we solve (directly sourced from our Buyers themselves, not our marketing 1 pagers), use a web search or chatGPT prompt for the impact of those problems.  Compare the results with our customer stories & what our top sellers say.

 
Rinse & repeat til we've got 10 impacts for at least 3 problems our product solves. 
 
 
 
***Now when we hear one of the problems come up on a call, we can ask a question that gives us valuable info on our buyers' business AND gives us credibility.*** 
 
--->Example: 
“Sounds like the economy has taken a toll on your pipeline. How is that affecting revenue growth, and any plans to do a funding round?” 
 
We've just shown we understand their world. 



What's the best way you've found to understand what problems we solve vs what our product does?

content:
The 5 reasons we lose deals:  
  
  
-> We waste or destroy momentum  
  
-> We don't show enough value & get ghosted  
  
-> We chase sh*tty deals, taking time away from quality opportunities  
  
-> We don't define success criteria & their pilot, POC or 1st small rollout fails  
  
-> We don't guide Champions and lose to others who teach them how to buy  
  
  
Let's take the last one first.  
  
Here are 3 ways to guide our Buyers:  
  
  
1) Make a list of all the steps *Buyers* (not us) typically go through when evaluating our solution. Usually:  
 --> Individual demo to Champion  
 --> 2-4 Buying Committee demos  
 --> IT technical overview / Q&A call  
 --> Security / Legal / Procurement  
 --> Quantify Business Case & Pricing Call  
  
2) Make an individual "Typical Next Step" slide for each. At the end of meetings, use these to prompt conversations on the next right thing  
  
3) Block time on our calendars to add the appropriate slide at the end of each of our meeting decks for the week  
  
  
Buyers are experts in how to do their jobs.  
Not how to buy our stuff.  
  
They have a better buying experience  
when we suggest what comes next.  
  
And we build credibility when we show up  
to each meeting as an expert guide.

content:
Challenger says 97% of their clients ask for extra help with this skill.

More than any other they teach.

And it's the least talked about.


What is it?  "Constructive Tension"


Challenger says Constructive Tension Is:
  --> A productive force to compel action
  --> Steering the conversation without being aggressive
  --> Used strategically and empathetically to examine conventional ways of thinking, explore assumptions, and probe for answers

"The goal is to highlight an unrecognized, misunderstood, or underappreciated problem or pain point."


While we definitely want to use this approach in Discovery, we're also introducing Constructive Tension in End-of-Year deals when we ask things like:

  --> "Can you walk me through each step of how this project could get a December signature, so we can start set up & training in January?"

  --> "Typically we see customers getting a purchase done fastest when the IT teams meet about integrations at the same InfoSec does security reviews. Any reason this wouldn't work for your teams?"

  --> "Could we schedule a call between our Legal departments instead of waiting for redlines?"


When we do this *empathetically* - in the spirit of teaching Champions how to buy - this can be one of the biggest value adds.

Champions are experts in how to do their jobs, not how to buy our stuff.

After 7+ years in ENT Sales, I've learned a non-icky way to drive urgency. 

Make the urgency Buyer Centric. 

Easier said than done. So...



Let's take Q4 as an example.

Here are 7 things weighing on executives in December:


1/ Reporting Financial Performance

2/ Next Year's Priorities & Strategies

3/ Innovation and Market Differentiation

4/ Metrics They're Measured/Bonused On

5/  Risks: Gaps, Competitors, Market conditions 

6/ Headcount: How to attract, retain, and develop top talent

7/ Personal life: Balancing End of Year with holiday events & travel 



Here are 11 ideas to tie our solutions to these 7 priorities, to keep Execs engaged in our Q4 and Q1 deals: 


1/ Reporting Financial Performance - 
Are they excited to announce their results or dreading it? How will you help them repeat good results or improve on bad outcomes?

2/ Next Year's Priorities & Strategies - 
What have you heard from your Champion about these? What success stories will you tell about how others achieved those same things, so Buyers are excited to move forward?

3/ Innovation and Market Differentiation -
How does your solution help them stand out? Can they get 1st movers advantage & grab market share? Does it help them provide a better customer experience?

4/ Metrics They're Measured/Bonused On - If they're a public company, check out their Schedule 14A (annual proxy statement) on their investor relations page. How will you help your Champion make money?

5/  Risks: Gaps, Competitors, Market conditions - 
Are all their competitors working with you? Can you help them do more with less? Do you help them thrive, even in tough times? (Key is business impact, not features)

6/ Headcount: How to attract, retain, and develop top talent -
Will you help them give employees reasons to come & stay - something the org only gets by being your customer?

7/ Personal life: Balancing End of Year with holiday events & travel -
Can you help them see around corners re: possible roadblocks to your deal because of Security, Legal or Procurement? Can you use a Visual Timeline or MAP to show them exactly how the deal gets done before they go on holiday vacay?


These 11 ideas are the WHAT.

content:
After 11 years in sales, I've got good news for anyone who gets "Happy Ears" a lot.  
  
(btw, I spent the early years of my sales career battling that same thing)  
  
Luckily, a mentor shared their secret with me.  
  
  
Here it is:  
  
3 Questions + 1 Rule for all Opportunities  
  
  
The Three Questions  
--> Why Anything  
--> Why Now  
--> Why Us  
  
  
The One Rule  
--> NONE of the answers can mention any of your product's features as the reason  
  
You can ONLY mention a product feature IF you know the outcome it creates or prevents.  
  
  
 *********** 
For a past deal at UserGems 💎 - this sounded like:  
  
--> WHY ANYTHING: Pipeline creation is strategic initiative #1 for Exec Buyer (RVP Sales) in 2025. They have an aggressive goal: 17% YoY increase  
  
--> WHY NOW: UserGems can be implemented in under 60 days (feature), which means there's still time to impact Q1 pipe, and even Q1 revenue (impact).  
  
--> WHY US: RVP knows that her biggest competitor started with UserGems last year & they are losing more deals than ever to this competitor. And the RVP's team has seen only 6% increase in ARR and 19% renewal churn. This is the data she's presenting to CFO as proof that 1) the strategy works & 2) there's a high risk of doing nothing.  

***********  
  
  
If we can't answer the 3 Why's - with metrics  
  
We need to quickly dive deeper with Discovery - or move on  
  
If we show our pipeline some tough love now, we can prevent a lot of pain from Happy Ears in the future.


How do you think about testing the deals in your pipe?

After 7+ years in Enterprise sales, these are the 5 questions I ask Executives on deals that keep pushing out. 
  
They help me figure out which deals are might be delayed  vs. deals that are dying☠️  
  
There are 5 different areas. And the last one is the most important at EOY.
  
  
Here are the 5 questions:  
  
  
💰1) CONTEXT 
"We were originally working to get this started in Q1.  Sounds like this now might be a Q2 thing. 𝗜𝘀 𝘁𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝗱𝘂𝗲 𝘁𝗼 𝗕𝘂𝗱𝗴𝗲𝘁, 𝗕𝗮𝗻𝗱𝘄𝗶𝗱𝘁𝗵 - 𝗼𝗿 𝗯𝗼𝘁𝗵?"  
  
Follow ups:  
 
"Ok got it. What changes in Q2?"  
  
"Has Q2 budget been earmarked already?"  
  
"Curious - what else is being implemented Q2?"  
  
 
 
📊2) PRIORITIES 
"Is there a specific goal or initiative in Q1-Q2 this aligns with?"  
  
  
  
🤔3) TIMING  
"November/December is often when Executives finalize goals for the next year. How are you feeling about your upcoming targets related to [problem I solve]?"  
  
  
  
💥4) IMPACT 
"Based on your current & future targets, when would you need to see an impact from something like [my product]?"  
  
  
  
❓5) PROCESS 
"How long did it take to get through Legal the last time you bought software? How about Security?  Based on those experiences, do we think a Q4 timeline is even possible? Or is this more likely a Q1 thing?"  
  
  
 
If they can't (or won't) go into specifics,  the deal is probably dying 😭

& deals that close🕵️‍♀️🔍

content:
No one is clicking the links we send to our Whitepapers and Case studies.

It's a waste of our energy.  Sorry not sorry. (check your data)
 
BUT - we can use Herd Theory instead. 
 
 
WHAT it is: 
 
Herd Theory = "people using the actions of others as a guide to sensible behavior." 

aka = Everyone always wants to know what everyone else is doing. 
 
 

HOW it can work for us: 
 
During discovery we listen for 1-2 key pain points. 
 
Then we mention LOTS of others who are using our solution to solve them. 
 
 
 
IRL this sounds like --> 
 
“Earlier in the call you mentioned needing to generate new Pipeline for Q1. 
 
Gong & Salesloft & Lattice & PagerDuty & Looker & Pendo & Drift & Procore & OneLogin & Segment & Greenhouse are already using UserGems 💎 to monitor buying signals like new executive hires or promotions. 

It's helped them create new pipeline & increased their deal velocity.

Would it be ok if I shared how they're doing that?” 
 
 
 
Using Herd Theory works better than one case study or whitepaper because, as Thomas Freese writes in "Question Based Selling": 
 
"Surrounding prospects with a credible 'herd' reduces our risk... 
 
 We become the messenger - not the message."


Give it a whirl and see how it works for ya.

Got any stories of how you've used it?

content:
They had terrible Glassdoor ratings. "Run from this place like a 🏡on 🔥"  was the actual title of one review. 

I interviewed with them anyway.

Here's why.
 

They passed my 3 Question Test.
  
When the company gets bad reviews, here's how I decide whether to interview. 
 
Maybe they’ll be helpful to you: 
 
=> What are the dates? 
=> What are the patterns? 
=> Has something changed? 
 
 
1/ What are the dates? 
If we see a bunch of negative reviews that happened 3 years ago, but not so much now... 
 
They probably addressed those issues or brought in a different leader. 
 
 
2/ What are the patterns? 
If the bad reviews are all recent, one of the first things I always look for is patterns. 
 
Are all the reviews talking about things like Micromanagement? 
Crazy quotas? 
Chaos? 
 
If there are no patterns, is it possible that disgruntled folks are the only ones leaving reviews? 
 
 
3/ Has something changed? 
 
Do the recent reviews mention 
-A Process overhaul 
-New owners or Investors 
-Hiring different Leadership 
 
Seeing that a company took action to address a bad situation is a GREAT sign. 
 
 
*****If you take the interview, definitely DO ask them about the Glassdoor issue.***** 
 
 
How they answer will tell you a lot about them ... and the company. 
 
Are they defensive? 
Do they dodge the question? 
Or are they super transparent?  

 
Gently asking about this can sound like--> 
 
"Kelly, I was doing my due diligence for our call today & noticed some negative Glassdoor reviews around [issue 1] and [issue 2]. 
 
I know that not everything online is 'gospel.' I take it with a grain of salt for sure. 
 
Could you help me understand a little more here?" 
 
 
We ask a hard thing in a soft way. 
 
(Which shows the kind of salesperson we are.) 
 
They can envision us taking the same approach to crucial conversations with clients and prospects. 


In my case, the 2 VPs I talked with were so gracious and humble. And straightforward - they didn't dance around any issues. 
 
Which made me feel really good about those leaders. And open to working with them. 
 
They were in my top 2 companies by the end of the interview process.  

  
Don't hesitate. 
 
Investigate.

content:
There's an unusual thing Salesforce's top Enterprise AEs do to ace their first meetings with execs.
 
They start discovery before they say a word in a VP+ conversation.
 
Here are 5 ways I've seen it done:

 
 
1️⃣ Survey the Exec's current team 🕵️‍♂️
 
Look for them on LinkedIn Sales Navigator. 
 
Filter to folks active on LinkedIn during the past 30 days.
 
Craft a tailored message focusing on WIIFM (What's In It For Me).
 
NOT what your product does. The outcomes they'll see.
 
Ask about pain points & advice on how to best approach the Exec.
 
 
-> In the Exec meeting, this sounds like:
 
"After talking with 5 of your sales reps in the East, it sounds like AE-created pipeline is a big focus. What are the biggest risks you see to pipe build in the next 3-6 mos?
 
 
 
2️⃣ Look at their Customer Stories 📚
 
What problems do they solve?
 
Who is their customer? SMB? Enterprise?
 
What do people mention... and NOT mention?
 
 
-> Sounds like:
 
"You've got some great logos. Amazing to see Gong, Salesloft & Drift all using your platform. Given that renewals are getting leaner across the SaaS industry, what are the 2 biggest churn risks you're keeping an eye on next quarter?"
 
 
 
3️⃣ Check RepVue & Glassdoor for insights on team dynamics 👀
 
71% vs. 21% of the team hitting...different conversations
 
On Glassdoor, you can filter reviews.
 
You can also use Ctrl F / search for specific words in reviews.
 
 
-> Sounds like:
"Looks like building pipeline has been tough. Found these quotes from reps on Glassdoor (put screenshots on slides). Also understand these aren't the full story. How are you thinking about risks related to attainment & retention in the next 3 months? 
 
 

4️⃣ Explore product reviews on G2, Capterra for valuable feedback. 🌟
 
Look for gaps related to your product (customer service, efficiency, integrations). 
 
 
-> Sounds like: 
"Looks like your customers love your functionality on G2. The only thing they mentioned was not having enough time with their CSM each month. Is this one of the top 3 risks you're focused on in the next 3 months?"
 
 
 
5️⃣ Watch Exec's speeches & podcasts for key insights. 🎙️
 
Look for common themes & top takeaways.
 
Especially any personal stories.

Reference their ideas to kick off discussions.
 
-> In Exec Discovery, sounds like: 
"You made a great point about sales & marketing alignment on Kevin Dorsey's podcast. How do fewer lead conversions & slower deal velocity rank as risks you're discussing with your marketing team?"
 
 
 
This type of prep surprises and impresses Executives.
 
Having a POV immediately differentiates us.
 
Our 1st meetings will be 5x better.

content:
Took me 12 years in sales to come up with 3 steps that work for any Discovery call. 
 
 
E.M.T. 🚑 
 
-->  Excavate the Pain 
-->  Match the Urgency 
-->  Teach them to Buy 
 
 
-->  Excavate the Pain  
(aka "The Menu of Pain") 
  
Friction reduction applies to Discovery  
  
Don't ask "essay" questions  
  
Give them multiple choice  
  
  
Here's the formula (thank you, Charles Muhlbauer):  
  
1/ In this role, I talk to [your industry] leaders all day long.  
 
2/ They tell me about their heartburn around problems A, B, and C.  
 
3/ How much of that sounds like your world & what did I miss?  
  
  
IRL at UserGems 💎  this sounds like:  
"Usually, when Sales leaders join these calls they usually want to either Capitalize or Catch up.  
• They had layoffs in the last 18 mos, but quotas are not going down.  
• They're facing double-digit growth metrics. And not sure how they're going to hit them.  
• They've seen Pipeline dry up in these market conditions. And so they're looking for a new channel.  
• . . . OR - they're facing none of these challenges, are hitting record high revenue, and want to capitalize to grab market share.  
  
• Curious how much of that sounds like your world? And what did I miss?"  
  
  
  
  
--> Match Their Urgency  
  
There are 3 reasons people show up for Discovery calls.  
  
Figuring this out saves everyone time.**  
  
  
This sounds like:  
  
"Sometimes people join these calls because they are in education mode and just want to understand new tools.  
  
Sometimes people join these calls because they have a big churn, pipeline or revenue problem they needed to solve 6 months ago.  
  
Sometimes people join these calls because they need to do something about big churn, pipeline or revenue in the next 12 months, but it's not urgent.  
  
Curious where would you put yourself on that scale?  
  
Asking because I never want to chase anyone.  
  
If today was purely education, that's ok."  
  
  
**I ask this at the end of the call  
  
After they've gotten the product overview  
  
And BEFORE we talk next steps. Because their answer determines what next steps make sense.  
 
 
 
-->  Teach them to Buy 
 
Our Buyers are Experts in how to do their jobs. 
 
Not how to buy our stuff. 
 
We need to be their guide. 
 
 
It's as simple as sharing "what comes next" at the end of every call. 
 
 
This sounds like:  
 
“Typically when folks evaluate XYZ product, leaders from Operations, Finance, and HR all get involved.  
 
Would it make sense to loop in Shonda, your VP of HR, and Christina, your VP of Finance into our conversation?  
 
Your organization may be different.... would someone else be better?"  
 
 
 
Our prospects have pain. 
 
We can act as EMTs. 
 
 
Do you have a simple way you think about Discovery?

content:
Before you send that DocuSign -

and I speak from personal experience here -

There's 1 question we should ask ourselves so we don't celebrate too soon: 


--> 𝗛𝗮𝘃𝗲 𝗼𝘂𝗿 𝗕𝘂𝘆𝗲𝗿𝘀 𝗮𝗴𝗿𝗲𝗲𝗱 𝘁𝗼 𝗮𝗻 𝗜𝗻𝘁𝗿𝗼𝗱𝘂𝗰𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 𝗠𝗲𝗲𝘁𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝘄𝗶𝘁𝗵 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗼𝗻𝗯𝗼𝗮𝗿𝗱𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝘁𝗲𝗮𝗺?


​𝙒𝙝𝙮 𝙞𝙩'𝙨 𝙄𝙢𝙥𝙤𝙧𝙩𝙖𝙣𝙩:

We're so close...and yet so far. Opportunities still stall, ghost & fall apart at this stage.

 𝘛𝘩𝘦 𝘪𝘯𝘵𝘳𝘰 𝘮𝘦𝘦𝘵𝘪𝘯𝘨 𝘪𝘴 𝘢 𝘭𝘪𝘵𝘮𝘶𝘴 𝘵𝘦𝘴𝘵. 𝘉𝘶𝘺𝘦𝘳𝘴 𝘵𝘩𝘢𝘵 𝘸𝘰𝘯'𝘵 𝘢𝘨𝘳𝘦𝘦 𝘵𝘰 𝘵𝘩𝘪𝘴 𝘮𝘦𝘦𝘵𝘪𝘯𝘨 𝘢𝘳𝘦𝘯'𝘵 𝘳𝘦𝘢𝘥𝘺 𝘵𝘰 𝘴𝘪𝘨𝘯.

Why are they not ready?

 ---> They could be afraid to put a meeting on the books because they're not sure they'll get a signature approved. 

In this case, we need to do some work to uncover what risk they see in the deal.

 ---> They may just want to use our quote as leverage to negotiate a lower price with another vendor. :((

 ---> Could be something else entirely.


Either way, if they won't set a date for this introduction meeting we can ask:

"Could you walk me through how this meeting might not be the best next step for your team? And what you have in mind that would work better?"


𝙒𝙝𝙖𝙩 𝙞𝙩 𝘿𝙤𝙚𝙨:

𝘐𝘵 𝘥𝘦-𝘳𝘪𝘴𝘬𝘴 𝘵𝘩𝘦 𝘥𝘦𝘢𝘭.

 ---> When our Buyers meet & talk with the onboarding person/team, they get more familiar with each other. They can envision working together. 

Our brains can resist things that are unfamiliar. This meeting lowers that risk.


 --->  Our Buyers see all the steps for getting their teams set up, trained, and seeing value from the purchase. They get those meetings scheduled. 

So they're no longer wondering what comes next after signing. 


𝙃𝙤𝙬 𝙒𝙚 𝘾𝙖𝙣 𝙎𝙚𝙩 𝙞𝙩 𝙐𝙥:

Below is a sample email I've used for years to set up these meetings.
​
​𝘛𝘩𝘦𝘳𝘦 𝘢𝘳𝘦 3 𝘤𝘳𝘶𝘤𝘪𝘢𝘭 𝘦𝘭𝘦𝘮𝘦𝘯𝘵𝘴:

 --->  A picture of the main point-of-contact for Onboarding. This is crucial. Seeing their face makes the new person automatically feel more familiar to Buyers.

 --->  A compliment for the Onboarding person/ team. Do they work with our top clients? Do they have years of expertise? Do customers rave about them? Put those details in there.

 --->  A short sentence about their role. What can Buyers expect from them? How will they work with the Buyers?



If you have deals that are getting close to closing - or deals that seem to be stalling at late stages - 

I encourage you to consider trying a version of this Onboarding Introduction strategy.
​
You might be surprised how your Buyers respond. And how it can speed up some deals.

content:
Sales gurus give truly terrible advice sometimes.  Here's one of my least favorites - and it's super popular.  
  
  
Sellers getting advised to ask "What happens if you do nothing?"  
  
  
Real talk: I've never heard anyone phrase it like that in real life.  
  
The concept is good but the phrasing sucks.  
  
Too easy for us to come off as smug or arrogant.  
  
  
  
Here are 3 different ways to use that concept - without sounding like a ... jerk:  
  
  
---> "What might be the ripple effects if the team can't find a better way to accomplish [outcome]?"  
  
---> "What impacts do you see coming if the team doesn't find a different way to get to [this outcome]?"  
  
---> "Our customers who've struggled with this same issue tell us that X, Y & Z [business problems] were getting worse when they couldn't change [problem I solve]. Any of that sound like your world, or what did I miss?"  
  
  
  
Buyers already avoid talking to salespeople until they absolutely have to.  
  
And no one wants to talk to a salesperson who's smug. Let alone open up to them about their problems.  
  
Asking a hard thing in a soft way can be the difference between finding a champion or creating a blocker. 
 
 
Got any favorite ways to ask about the status quo?

content:
Sometimes we don’t need more tactics. 
 
Sometimes we need hope.  
 
 
October 11 years ago was one of those times for me. 
 
The small company I worked for was  acquired by a huge corporation, and the culture was drastically changing. (Not for the better.) 
 
I was in the middle of a divorce. 
 
With 3 very small kiddos. 
 
 
Many days I was so overwhelmed that I sat at my computer, feeling unable to move. 
 
Paralyzed by everything I needed to do. 
 
Not even knowing where to start. 
 
 
My sister saw how I was struggling. She started emailing me encouraging quotes every day, and I saved them. 
 
Now I’m going to share some of my favorites with you. 
 
I got a little misty as I wrote these out again, remembering how much they meant to me at the time. 
 
I hope they encourage you: 
 
𝘌𝘹𝘱𝘦𝘤𝘵 𝘵𝘰 𝘩𝘢𝘷𝘦 𝘩𝘰𝘱𝘦 𝘳𝘦𝘬𝘪𝘯𝘥𝘭𝘦𝘥. 𝘌𝘹𝘱𝘦𝘤𝘵 𝘺𝘰𝘶𝘳 𝘱𝘳𝘢𝘺𝘦𝘳𝘴 𝘵𝘰 𝘣𝘦 𝘢𝘯𝘴𝘸𝘦𝘳𝘦𝘥 𝘪𝘯 𝘸𝘰𝘯𝘥𝘳𝘰𝘶𝘴 𝘸𝘢𝘺𝘴. 𝘛𝘩𝘦 𝘥𝘳𝘺 𝘴𝘦𝘢𝘴𝘰𝘯𝘴 𝘪𝘯 𝘭𝘪𝘧𝘦 𝘥𝘰 𝘯𝘰𝘵 𝘭𝘢𝘴𝘵. 𝘛𝘩𝘦 𝘴𝘱𝘳𝘪𝘯𝘨 𝘳𝘢𝘪𝘯𝘴 𝘸𝘪𝘭𝘭 𝘤𝘰𝘮𝘦 𝘢𝘨𝘢𝘪𝘯.  
- Sarah Ban Breathnach 
​ 
​𝘉𝘦 𝘤𝘰𝘮𝘧𝘰𝘳𝘵𝘦𝘥, 𝘥𝘦𝘢𝘳 𝘴𝘰𝘶𝘭! 𝘛𝘩𝘦𝘳𝘦 𝘪𝘴 𝘢𝘭𝘸𝘢𝘺𝘴 𝘭𝘪𝘨𝘩𝘵 𝘣𝘦𝘩𝘪𝘯𝘥 𝘵𝘩𝘦 𝘤𝘭𝘰𝘶𝘥𝘴.  
- Louisa May Alcott 
​ 
​𝘕𝘰 𝘸𝘪𝘯𝘵𝘦𝘳 𝘭𝘢𝘴𝘵𝘴 𝘧𝘰𝘳𝘦𝘷𝘦𝘳; 𝘯𝘰 𝘴𝘱𝘳𝘪𝘯𝘨 𝘴𝘬𝘪𝘱𝘴 𝘪𝘵𝘴 𝘵𝘶𝘳𝘯. - Hal Borland 
​ 
​𝘉𝘦 𝘤𝘰𝘶𝘳𝘢𝘨𝘦𝘰𝘶𝘴! 𝘏𝘢𝘷𝘦 𝘧𝘢𝘪𝘵𝘩! 𝘎𝘰 𝘧𝘰𝘳𝘸𝘢𝘳𝘥.  
- Thomas A. Edison 
​ 
​𝘛𝘩𝘦 𝘧𝘢𝘤𝘵 𝘪𝘴, 𝘵𝘩𝘢𝘵 𝘵𝘰 𝘥𝘰 𝘢𝘯𝘺𝘵𝘩𝘪𝘯𝘨 𝘪𝘯 𝘵𝘩𝘦 𝘸𝘰𝘳𝘭𝘥 𝘸𝘰𝘳𝘵𝘩 𝘥𝘰𝘪𝘯𝘨, 𝘸𝘦 𝘮𝘶𝘴𝘵 𝘯𝘰𝘵 𝘴𝘵𝘢𝘯𝘥 𝘣𝘢𝘤𝘬 𝘴𝘩𝘪𝘷𝘦𝘳𝘪𝘯𝘨 𝘢𝘯𝘥 𝘵𝘩𝘪𝘯𝘬𝘪𝘯𝘨 𝘰𝘧 𝘵𝘩𝘦 𝘤𝘰𝘭𝘥 𝘢𝘯𝘥 𝘥𝘢𝘯𝘨𝘦𝘳, 𝘣𝘶𝘵 𝘫𝘶𝘮𝘱 𝘪𝘯 𝘢𝘯𝘥 𝘴𝘤𝘳𝘢𝘮𝘣𝘭𝘦 𝘵𝘩𝘳𝘰𝘶𝘨𝘩 𝘢𝘴 𝘸𝘦𝘭𝘭 𝘢𝘴 𝘸𝘦 𝘤𝘢𝘯. 
- Robert Cushing 
​ 
​𝘞𝘦 𝘤𝘢𝘯 𝘥𝘰 𝘢𝘯𝘺𝘵𝘩𝘪𝘯𝘨 𝘸𝘦 𝘸𝘢𝘯𝘵 𝘵𝘰 𝘥𝘰 𝘪𝘧 𝘸𝘦 𝘴𝘵𝘪𝘤𝘬 𝘵𝘰 𝘪𝘵 𝘭𝘰𝘯𝘨 𝘦𝘯𝘰𝘶𝘨𝘩.  
- Helen Keller 
 
 
___

So, feel the feelings. And then figure out how you’ll keep moving forward.

Job seekers: 3 specific things you can do to stand out, get initial interviews, and impress hiring managers: 
 
You'll beat out 1000's of other applicants. 
 
I've rarely talked publicly about these, but they're what I did to get my foot in the door. Then hired by 3 multi-billion $ companies.  
  
==> Build a Groundswell  
Multi-thread the team you want to join. So the hiring manager hears "the buzz" about you before you even reach out. 
  
Ask for their advice in a SHORT note: 
  
“Would value your advice on XYZ company. I’m thinking of applying & would love to hear about your experience there. Have 2 specific questions for you.” 
  
If they agree, you can ask: 
  
“It looks like skills A,B & C are important in this role. In the past, I've done things like (relevant success metrics 1&2). It also seems like ____ (skill/experience I have) would add value. To what extent have you found it to be impactful?" 
  
“What's the 1 thing you'd fix about XYZ company if you had a magic wand?” 
  
> send a Thank You note.  
  
 
==> Be Instantly Memorable  
Pattern Interrupts are what people remember. 
  
Our brains are conditioned to gloss over things that are always the same. (It's how we got home from the store, but don't remember the drive.) 
  
One way to stand out is to use a "secret weapon" I learned from a mentor who's now SVP Sales at a Fortune500. 
  
It won't all fit in a LinkedIn post, but you can see it & get a template with the details in the c*mments. 
  
  
==> Come with a Point of View  
95% of candidates won't put in the work on this. 
  
Bad for them - great for you. 
  
Using a POV is one of the best pattern interrupts when reaching out to a hiring manager to get an interview. Or in the interview itself. Or both. 
  
It sounds like:  
  
"Taylor, I'm excited about this role. It looks like your org announced earlier this year they're focused on (company news 1) and (news 2).  
  
I think that probably means you're looking for folks with ______ experience. People who are comfortable with __________ conversations, and who know their way around ________.  
  
That's what many companies seem to be prioritizing, but what did I miss that you're focused on? 
  
Would love to connect to go deeper into this." 
  
These days, we have to stand out to even get an interview. 
  
Applying online has an 80% failure rate (Forbes).

content:
I was surprised when a CMO recently told me that he'd never been asked this question on a Discovery call. But he definitely wants to answer it.  
  
Here it is:  
  
"How can I best match your urgency?"  
  
  
Here's how the full version sounds at the end of a Discovery call:  
  
  
"Mary, it was great to talk with you today.  
  
Would it be ok to ask 1 more question?  
  
There are typically 3 reasons folks join these first calls.  
  
--> Sometimes people join these calls because they are in education mode and just want to understand new tools.  
  
--> Sometimes people join these calls because they have a big problem they needed to solve 6 months ago.  
  
--> And, sometimes people join these calls because they probably need to do something about this problem in the next 12 months, but it's not urgent.  
  
  
 Curious where would you put yourself on that scale? Asking because I never want to chase anyone.  
  
If today was purely education, that's ok."  
  
  
 
Asking about urgency at the end of the call helps us know what Next Steps to suggest. 
 
It's a win/win question, as it helps us align with executive priorities and makes our Buyers feel heard.  
 
Curious what others are doing...What do you think works the best to close out your Discovery / first calls? 
  
  
  
p.s.  The full CMO interview also covered his least favorite questions.  
  
And his comments on what sellers do to make him feel disrespected as a Buyer(!) 
  
We rarely get to hear directly from execs at this level. It was eye opening. Details in the comments.

content:
I sent multi-threading emails to an Executive Buyer for 5 straight months.  He never responded - but he did save my deal. 
 
Here's what happened... 
 

I inherited a deal in my 1st year at UserGems.  It was multithreaded (kinda) when I got it.   
 
There were 5 people involved from the Buyer side.  That was the good news. 
 
Bad news - all 5 people were in the same department.   
 
 
I was concerned and immediately started multi-threading. 
 
Including an introduction between the Executive Buyer and our VP of Marketing. 
 
The Executive Buyer never responded to the intro... but he DID start a separate thread with our VP of marketing. 
 
He never attended a meeting.  Never responded to the "keeping you in the loop" emails I sent after those meetings. But he read every one of them. 
 
And 5 months later....  
 
 
When the buying group threatened to walk away from the deal unless we slashed our pricing by over 60% 
 
We used the thread with our VP of marketing to send the business case to the Executive Buyer. 
 
He understood the value, and ultimately rescued the deal. 
 
 
We don't have to go it alone when we're multi-threading. 
 
Aligning executives can be a powerful way to engage with CXOs and VPs. 
 
The moral of this story is, take heart!  "No response" doesn't mean "no impact".

content:
Salesforce's top Enterprise AE for a Fortune 50 company shared a giant success secret with me.  
  
Elite team selling, using the "3 G's".  Here's how she does it.  
  
And the last one is the most important... 
  
 
She teams up with the SDR, Solutions Consultant (SC/SE), CSM & RVP on  
--> The Grapevine  
--> The Group  
--> The Goal  
  
  
  
The Grapevine -  
She religiously holds a weekly strategy meeting that includes "what I've heard / what you've heard" from each person.  
  
It's brief, keeps everyone on the same page, and saves hundreds of DMs.  
  
  
  
The Group -  
Throughout the week, she often acts as a Project Manager. She keeps clear communication on who is following up with who, aligning roles & titles.  
  
And she keeps track of this in her Account Plan, which the whole group can access.  
  
  
  
The Goal -  
She runs standalone prep calls for upcoming customer-facing meetings.  
  
Her calendar invites always include these 3 notes:  
 
1) The vibe we're going for on this call  
(How do we want them to feel when the call ends? Confident? At ease? Excited?)  
  
2) The 2 things we can't end this meeting without knowing. (Guides discovery questions & gives the group something to listen for.)  
  
3) The next step we're suggesting. (So the team isn't surprised & can offer feedback.)  
  
  
  
Enterprise sales take a huge effort. 
 
The best sellers know it has to be a team sport.  
  
We can use The 3 G's as a framework to keep the whole team pulling together.

content:
Listen to what just happened when a top 1% Enterprise seller used a 1 sentence strategy & won over a Fortune 500 CEO.

Here's how it went down, and how you can do it too.

​
In Q3, one of the Enterprise reps I coach faced a unique dilemma.

​
She had worked hard all year to get a deal going with Lululemon, a $39.2B member of the Fortune 500.

She'd been onsite, worked with ~60 people to multi-thread & come with a Point of View.*

She knew her solution was aligned with a C-Level Priority. Problem was, her solution was a small piece of the puzzle and she needed a way to help the CEO understand its importance.

​
A group of champions let the rep know they were presenting to the CEO in a Q3 leadership meeting. 

The AE had to help these champions to show HOW critical her solution was - with a very succinct explanation.
​
​We decided we needed an analogy. 
​

To create the perfect analogy, we went to work researching the CEO. On his public Instagram page, we found our answer.

His Insta was plastered with photos of him & the Lulu team, competing together in triathlons. He'd given multiple interviews on what triathlons meant to his personal and professional life.
​

So we came up with this analogy:

--> "Using the current solution for this initiative would be like using a beach cruiser for the bike portion of a triathlon."

​
If you're unfamiliar with a beach cruiser, it's a bike invented in the 1960's. With the basket in front. Not exactly triathlon material.

Which was exactly why it made the perfect analogy.

​
--> ​"Using the current solution for this initiative would be like using a beach cruiser for the bike portion of a triathlon."
​
​​
The analogy communicated 3 Crucial Realities to the CEO - using language from HIS world:

Their current solution

1/ was OUTDATED
2/ was THE WRONG TOOL for the job
3/ COULD NOT accomplish their objectives 

All without a word about features & functions… which the CEO didn't need to hear about and would have forgotten instantly.
​

​The analogy sealed the deal. The CEO got the picture, and this rep just got a 6-figure Closed Won.

Would that analogy been enough all by itself?

Of course not.

​
This Enterprise rep is a absolute pro, and she'd done all the groundwork.*

The on-sites, the multi-threading, the Point of View and Business case.*

She had all the right elements. The analogy was the catalyst.

​​
You've got some deals right now where you've laid all the groundwork.

What can you use as your catalyst?
​


​*ps - Keeping multiple champions organized and equipped with the POV, the Business Case, ROI and all the resources you've worked on together throughout the entire deal cycle is  > incredibly hard work <

The Enterprise and MM sellers I coach are seeing HUGE success using Aligned Deal Rooms for this groundwork. So the catalyst can do its work.

content:
5 career lessons I learned the hard way: 


1/ Keep a list of logos you've worked with. 

2/ Ask for recommendations before you need them. 

3/ When you get a compliment from a boss, client or co-worker, save it somewhere. 

4/ Using a personal CRM is something almost no one does - and can be worth millions.

5/ Set a calendar time block to Update all these regularly. Make this a habit. Not a goal.



Here's why - 

1/ You think you'll always remember that prospecting win or that big deal you closed. But 5 years from now, will you remember them all?  Keep a list. Even if it's a simple Google doc.

2/ Most people only ask for recommendations when they need them. When they get laid off, when they're interviewing for a promotion, etc. LinkedIn recommendations are referral letters that live FOREVER. Ask for them early.

3/ Screenshots of compliments are great social proof when interviewing. Keep those in an email folder or personal drive somewhere, so you can pull them out when you need them in the future.

4/ The personal CRM is highly underrated. Your network is your net worth. Hugely successful Venture Capitalists have written about using these to keep in touch with their network. If it's good enough for them....

5/ "We do not rise to the level of our goals. We FALL to the level  of our SYSTEMS." -James Clear, Atomic Habits.

content:
My career looks amazing on paper 
 
 
-went from teaching to tech sales 
-worked my way to being a top rep 
-got hired + promoted at billion $ companies 
 
 
What many folks don't know is that I: 
 
- had to Google tech sales terms for months in my 1st role (ARR, ASP, MRR...wtf?)
- bombed a final interview for an AE job  
- only hit 30% of my quota one year  
 
 
Why do I tell you this? 
 
Because LinkedIn makes my career look incredible.   
 
And it definitely has been. 
 
BUT... 
 
 
What you can't see is all the sh*t that will never make the "highlight" reel. 
 
 
All the times that I: 
 
-->  Struggled with the learning curve in a new role 
 
--> Became convinced that I forgot how to sell or just 'got lucky' in my past jobs 
 
--> Saw others who onboarded with me get better territories - which meant they did a lot less work & got much better results 
 
 
So if that's where you are, you're not alone. 
 
There is no such thing as an "easy" career in sales.  
 
I can't think of a single successful seller I know who had a simple path. 
 
 

If you're going through hell right now, take a deep breath. Keep moving forward. 
 
And don't compare your path to anyone else's.

content:
Friends, I have to say that the Sales Success Summit was the best event I've been to this year.  Here are my 5 big takeaways:

1/ Getting to hear Brandon Fluharty 🐝speak live on how to be a Purposeful Performer was a huge highlight.

Even thought I follow his content every day, I still walked away with 2 action items (see my notes / 2nd pic).

content:
Here's a simple tweak to make Discovery more of a conversation, and less of an interrogation.  
  
We switch "Why" questions to "How" or "What" questions.  
  
Here are 5 examples of what this can sound like:  
  
  
"Why is XYZ your top priority?" --> "What prompted that need?"  
  
  
"Why is this a priority now?" --> "How are you thinking about this differently than last year?"  
  
  
"Why do you ask?" --> "Sounds like you have a specific reason for asking. Mind unpacking what's driving that?  
  
  
"Why do you think your team missed their targets?" -->  
"You said the team missed their targets. What do you think caused that?"  
  
  
"Why would you push this decision to next quarter?" --> "Sounds like this is a Q3/Q4 priority. How much of that is budget vs bandwidth... or something else?"  
  
  
  
Asking "why would you / why did you" can quickly put people on the defensive.  
  
Asking "what / how" questions invites them to share their perspective.  
  
Consultation > interrogation

content:
Just had an eye-opening chat with a VP of Sales hiring for 3 AE roles 👀 
 
In under 1 minute, he named 3 things that separate exceptional candidates from the average. 
 
🎉The good news is, you can do them all in under 15 minutes. 
 
 
 
🥱4 things average candidates miss: 
 
 
--> "They don't call or email me or my team." 
 
--> "They don't connect or message me on LinkedIn." 
 
--> "They don't ask any questions (aka no Discovery)." 
 
--> "They don't follow up on phone screenings, mentioning specific takeaways." 
 
 
 
🏆 Winning formula from standout candidates: 
 
 
--> "She asked about my priorities. I gave her all the answers! I'm an open book." 
 
--> "She sent me a note after our screening call. We only talked for 15 min, but she remembered 2 key points." 
 
--> "He called me to follow up. He called my team to see what it was like working with me. He had a POV on why he'd be a fit."** 
 
 
**important note: This call earned him a 2nd interview. Despite scoring a 'maybe' on the sales skills assessment.  
 
 
 
This sales leader received 347 resumes for 3 open roles. 
 
They did screening calls with 36 candidates. 
 
Only 3 AEs stood out. 
 
 
Sometimes we overthink. And when we're under stress from needing to find a new job, we can let our best practices slip. 
 
The stand-out sellers treat the interview process like a sales cycle. 
 
 
Sales leaders chime in...what are candidates doing these days that impress you?  
 
Sellers - what's working the best for you in the interview process? 
 
 
 
ps. If you'd like more specific ideas on how to stand out, you might like the $0 "Stand Out" resource I've created. And I'm hosting a free workshop on 10/23.

🌟 An SVP of Sales showed me 1 simple way to personalize a prospecting email. 

Do the math for them. 

 
Here’s an example I used IRL at UserGems 💎  
 
 
"Hey [Prospect name],

I noticed Greenhouse among your partners, and guess what? They're acing the 'second sale' game when job changes happen.

Imagine if your ~12,000 past buyers could buy again. Check out this quick math:

15,000 [Prospect company] clients
x 4 Avg People on buying committee
x 20% job change rate
----------------------------------
= 12,000 potential leads


 
p.s. BTW - a partner 1/4 your size raked in $4.1m in revenue in just 12 months. 
 
Cheers!" 
 
 
 
Key ingredients:
- Using their public info
- Industry benchmark data
- Predicting outcomes based on data


Why it works:
- Demonstrates deep understanding of their business
- Personalizes the message to the max
- Connects those dots --> insights


Can’t get much more personal & relevant than that. 



Seasonal tip:

October is budget season for LOTS of our Buyers. 

Do the math & help them justify why you belong in their budget.

Because as much as we need to close Q3 - Q4 deals, we'll also need pipeline in Q1.

Some of my old posts make me cringe a little now.  
 
Like, they’re not the worst advice.  
 
But I’ve since learned better.  
 
 
And there have definitely been times where I’ve tried to model a post  
 
based on what went viral for someone else, but it felt "off" for me 
 
because I wasn't using my own voice.  
 
 
Funny thing is, I noticed the same thing in sales.  
 
 
As a new seller, sometimes I tried to just  copy top performers. 
 
Used certain disco questions or ways of demoing...  
 
And some of it just didn't ring True for me.   
 
 
The sooner I re-worked the talk tracks I felt icky about, the more comfortable I got.  
 
And the more comfortable I was, the better my results got.  
 
 
So if you've got some cold emails, or discovery questions or demo scripts that aren't working for you 
 
Maybe they make you cringe a little (or a lot) 
 
Consider a little experiment: 
 
 
Re-write the stuff in your own words. 
 
Use your version for 1-2 weeks. 
 
Compare your results. 
 
 
You'll learn something either way. 
 
 
And also, don't be so hard on yourself. Everyone struggles. 
 
No one gets it exactly right all the time.  
 
It just takes a while to find your voice.

content:
3 surprising insights I learned from a VP of Sales changed how I do Multi-Threading.  
  
 Here's what he told me, and how you can use it:  
  
  
--> It's risky to be the champion for a big purchase  
--> 3 levels of personas need to be in an evaluation to de-risk it  
--> We should communicate differently to each of those 3 levels  
  
  
How to turn that into the best Multi-Threaded deals:  
  
1) Knowing who usually buys your product can help de-risk a purchase for your Champion.  
  
Champions are experts in how to do their jobs, not how to buy our stuff.  
  
They appreciate it when we can guide them.  
  
"Typically when folks evaluate XYZ, leaders from Operations, Finance, and HR all get involved. Would it make sense to include Shonda, your VP of HR, and Christina, your VP of Finance in our next conversation?"  
  
  
2) The 3 levels of Personas that get involved in deals all care about different things.  
  
Here's what they each care about:  
  
Executives: does this help us reach goals and/or lower our risk?  
  
Managers: does this help my team?  
  
End users: does this help me?  
  
  
3) We have to speak their "language" when we interact with them - or we'll lose them.  
  
Reps are used to talking about our product, so speaking the language of Executives is the hardest.  
  
Here's what a meeting recap email sounds like for a CFO or VP of Finance:  
  
"Christina,  
  
I met with your Ops team today about the 𝗿𝗶𝘀𝗸 in your data.  
 - We will 𝗾𝘂𝗮𝗻𝘁𝗶𝗳𝘆 the 𝗶𝗺𝗽𝗮𝗰𝘁 to Revenue Growth when we meet 2/28.  
 - Your specific ROI (based on the calculations done by your Ops teams) will be covered on the 28th as well.  
  
You should have the 2/28 meeting invite. Will send you the readout afterward.  
  
Cheers"  
  
  
We mention RISK, Quantifying Impact, and SPECIFIC ROI.  
  
(And they can read it on their cell without scrolling.)  
  
  
 
The reason multi-threading increases win rates by 34% is that it de-risks deals for Champions. (CEB Global)  
  
When we know how to help our Champions, everyone wins.... literally.  
  
And as always - it's about 𝘁𝗵𝗲𝗺, not about us/our stuff.  
  
 
  
What working well for you with multi-threading 
 
?

content:
Even after 5 years as an enterprise AE at multiple unicorn companies, I still keep a list of 9 discovery questions up on my monitor. 
 
The ones I know I must remember to ask. 
 
Even after I hear "pain I can solve". 
 
 
There are 2 reasons these questions are important: 
--> Qualification 
--> Momentum 
 
 
Qualification 
The answers help you know if a deal is real or if you are just educating them about a "nice to have". 
 
 
Momentum 
If the deal is real - THESE are the answers you come BACK to if [when] the deal slows down. 
 
--> When they have to spend time building a business case. 
 
--> When they dread asking their legal to review. 
 
--> When they have to go ask for a signature. 
 
 
Coming back to these answers to keep momentum sounds like: 
 
--> "I know it's hard to commit to 3 more meetings to build/finalize the business case. But imagine how you'll feel when you led the initiative that helped stop this 3-year issue of [pain I can solve]." 
 
--> "Getting through legal is never anyone's favorite part. But since your team needs to change [pain I can solve] by Q3, we need to start now so we can get you set up, trained & ready by end of Q2." 
 
--> "Your CRO said this [pain I can solve] is a top initiative for Q3. Should we get the proposal review meeting set up by June 6, so that she has enough time to review it before the June 30 board meeting?" 
 
 
And that is why people say deals are won or lost in discovery.

content:
Multi-threading matters most when the deal is in procurement. Here's why.  
  
The reason the deal even got to Procurement to begin with is that it’s tied to a problem.  
  
Something the business cares deeply about.  
  
Procurement does not care about that.  
  
(Or at least not in the same way).  
  
  
So Procurement has no urgency & worse,  
  
they'll use our EOM urgency against us.  
  
  
The way to put pressure on Procurement is through the champion/executive buyer.  
  
They're the ones with the problem. They are the ones that need the solution.  
  
So we have to keep them multi-threaded all the way through to the end of the deal.  
  
  
Once the deal goes to Procurement, we need to provide status updates.  
  
To everyone in the business who cares about getting this done.  
  
And we need to do that individually.  
  
No mass texts/emails.  
  
  
When deals go into procurement, many times it feels like the dark side of the moon.  
  
Even for our buyers.  
  
When we provide updates, it’s valuable.  
  
  
And when we can show how getting it through Procurement gets their problem solved faster  
  
The internals stakeholders will put the pressure on procurement.  
  
Way more effective than us sending Procurement another email "just checking in“.  
  
  
If we have a deal in Procurement right now, we need to get our Buyers an update.  
  
It's a better use of our time than refreshing DocuSign.

content:
⛔️Warning: Don't accept a position with a company “going upmarket” without asking these 5 questions. 
  
When I made the move, I didn’t know about these land mines 💣... 
  
The company I joined was hugely successful. I thought going upmarket would be smooth ⛵️ 
  
I was wrong 🙈 
  
  
Here are 5️⃣ issues I wish I’d asked about: 
  
  
🎥 GOT ENTERPRISE STORIES? 
Most true ENT companies couldn’t care less about success in SMB/ Mid Market. United Airlines will not be impressed with our product's success in a company with 150 employees. 
  
--> Key qq: "What are the best stories about how ENT accounts have created success with this product?" 
  
  
🐏 HOW DO BATTERING RAMS GET PAID?  
Sellers in companies "going upmarket" spend 2-3 years educating the Enterprise about the product's existence. 
  
Since you’ll essentially be a battering ram trying to crack enterprise accounts, how will you get paid? 50/50 split? If so, don't count on making anything more than your base for 2-3 years. 
  
--> Key qq: "Show me the comp plan" 
  
  
📅 DO THE TIMELINES MATCH?  
I had a deal with a 19k person financial services org that took over 24 mos to close. 
  
That wasn't unusual in ENT. Most of the team didn't make quota for 2-3 years. 
  
--> Key qq: "Since you are going upmarket & it takes time to educate the Enterprise market, how will quotas be structured?" 
  
  
🧙🏻‍♂️🔮 WHO ARE THE GURUS? 
Who are their advisors & sales leaders? I wrongly assumed our company was being advised by folks who had experience going upmarket. (ie  qualified to give us directions because they had made the journey before.) 
  
Same with Enterprise leaders. Best if they *have made the upmarket journey before*. NOT just leaders who've always been with enterprise orgs. 
  
--> Key qq: "Can you walk me through who our top advisors are? Hiring philosophy for the ENT sales leaders?" 
  
  
👮🏼‍♀️ HOW GOOD ARE WE AT THE BIG 3?  
Security, Reporting & Governance - ENT handles these much differently than SMB. 
  
These 3 issues were why big deals took so long to close-if they closed at all. 
  
I and several of my peers lost 7 figure deals - even though there was pain, motivated Exec buyers & good multi-threading. The deals died because we didn't have one of the Big 3 that ENT orgs required. 
  
--> Key qq: "Can you walk me through how the product meets the Security, Reporting & Governance of ENT orgs? 
  
  
Real talk: Founders get overly confident when there's lots of traction in SMB & MM. 
  
They're convinced that the ENT will “fall in line “. Just deals with extra 0’s.  
  
⚠️NOT true 
  
  
Take it from someone who's been there & got the hoodie 
  
Asking these questions can save a lot of❤️‍🩹

content:
"Just show me the demo" is where most sellers lose control of their Discovery calls. 
 
We freeze.  
 
We're not sure what to do next. 
 
 
Do we press on & ask more questions to get a little more "pain"? 
 
Is the Buyer always right, so we should just pop open the Demo deck? 
 
 
After working with some of the best sellers in the world at places like Salesforce, Tableau & Outreach, I've noticed a pattern. 
 
The top 1% of sellers approach their Discovery calls like an EMT. 
 
(After all, our Buyers have serious pain. They NEED an EMT.) 
 
 
E  -> Excavate their pain 
M -> Match their urgency 
T -> Teach them to buy 
 
 
We can avoid the trap of "just show me the demo" if we Excavate pain at the very top of the call. 
 
We want to use a multiple choice question. 
 
I call it "The Menu of Pain". 
 
 
It sounds like: 
 
  --> "In this role, I talk to [XYZ industry] leaders all day long.  
 
  --> They tell me about their heartburn around problems A, B, and C.  
 
  --> How much of that sounds like your world & what did I miss?" 
 
 
When we name 3 problems that sound familiar to them, we earn some credibility. 
 
(Because we didn't open the call by asking "So what do you guys do?") 
 
And when we invite them to correct us, they'll go even deeper. Those details = gold. 
 
 
So when we actually DO the demo, we can show them more of what matters to them. 
 
Stay in control of your Disco calls. 
 
Show up as an EMT.

content:
Here are 3 questions used by top 1% sellers at Salesforce during pricing negotiation calls. 
 
Maybe you can use them to bring in those Q3 deals you're working:  
  
  
#1: What did you have in mind?  
#2: What's closer to what you were expecting?  
#3: What is a number that you could get approved?  
  
  
Here's how & where I've learned to use them:  
  
--> "What did you have in mind?"  
  
  
Experienced negotiators frequently ask salespeople, "Is this the best you can do?" It's a smart question.  
  
It's also fair for us to ask Buyers what they want in the deal.  
  
It's not always price.  
  
  
  
--> "What’s closer to what you were expecting?"  
 
  
This question is my favorite response to the vague objection "That's too high".  
  
No matter what it is, they almost always think it's too high. :)  
  
Follow up: "Can you tell me more about how you got to that number (that you have in mind?)"  
  
This shows the thought/effort they put in.  
  
And what they're using as an anchor.  
  
  
  
--> "What is a number you could get approved?"  
 
  
When we hear "My CFO would not approve that"...  
  
We can ask this question before we start throwing out huge discounts.  
  
Our Champions likely have seen budget allocations,  
  
know the Buying Committee's price sensitivity,  
  
and the dollar amount where procurement gets involved.  
  
Ask them to share.  
  
One of my favorite ways to phrase this: 
  
"Ok, got it. Sounds like your CFO wouldn't approve this number. I'm happy to go back to my team and get creative with this deal. I need to know what target we're aiming for. What is a number you could get approved?"  
  
  
  
Curiosity-based negotiation questions can keep pricing negotiations moving.  
  
Defensive reactions or explanations of our pricing grind talks to a halt.  
  
  
Open ended questions help us uncover  
concerns,  
roadblocks  
and win/wins.  
  
Listening > Talking  
Clear > Clever  
 
What are your favorite negotiation questions? 
  
  
PS -  
There are 3 Silent deal killers that can keep us from ever getting to the negotiation phase.  
 
Learning how to avoid them can make the difference between hitting quota & missing quota.

content:
"Sales Reps, don't introduce your Sales Engineer as your "technical expert."  
  
It's not good for you, them, or the prospect."  
 
oof... guilty as charged.  When I saw this post last week by Rew Dickinson, I wished I could re-do all the intros I did in demos. :( 
 
He's got a better way... here's the full post. (And sellers, give him a follow!) 
  
---  
  
This is how I see AEs introduce SEs most often:  
  
AE: "This is Rew, my Solutions Engineer. He can answer all of your technical questions and show you how the software works."  
  
This may be true, but it's not the best intro. It's not the Sales Reps' fault either. SEs should tell their Sales Reps how they would like to be introduced.  
  
---  
  
Here's a better option:  
  
AE: "For this meeting, I was able to get one of our Solutions Engineers, Rew, to join us. He has a great deal of expertise working with our clients and is basically here to offer free advisory and solutions expertise as you are going through this decision-making process. I've given Rew some of the background on your business already, and he may jump in with some more questions to better understand your needs."  
  
---  
  
Notice the difference??  
  
The first introduction paints the SE almost like a human instruction manual on all of the software's features/technicalities. It puts the SE in a position where they have to wait until the prospect has a question before speaking. Then, they become reactive, which is exactly what you don't want them to be.  
  
The second introduction, however, paints the SE as a guide that the client can trust and puts the SE in the position of being a client leader. Which is exactly where you want them to be.  
  
---  
 
Now it's your turn.  
 
How do you introduce your SE? Drop your scripts below.

content:
3 tech unicorns. 11+ years in sales. 6 years as an Enterprise AE. And pipeline management is still hard.  
  
But I've learned 2 strategies that I use every day.  
  
Strategies for:  
--> Deciding which deals to focus on  
--> When to give up & move on  
  
  
  
--> Deciding which deals to focus on  
  
Companies have ICPs: Ideal Customer Profiles  
  
I have IOPs: Ideal Opportunity Profiles  
  
When I have to decide how much time, research, and personalization to devote, I give each deal a "grade".  
  
I've narrowed down 8 characteristics of deals that are most likely to close.  
  
I assign points to each characteristic.  
  
My point system looks like this:  
  
  
--> There's a Champion Who Gives the "Inside Scoop": 10 points  
--> They have Specific Goals with Metrics for Each: 10 points  
-->They Invest Heavily in Tech Related to My Product: 10 points  
--> They are Responsive to Calls, Texts, Email: 10 points  
--> There are a Low Number of Obstacles: 10 points  
--> They have Lots of Potential End Users: 15 points  
--> They have a Compelling Event: 20 points  
--> They make Decisions Quickly: 15 points  
  
  
The higher the grade, the more time and energy I spend on it.  
  
  
  
--> When to give up & move on  
  
I use a "3 strikes You're Out" rule.  
  
If there is no response after I reach out 3 times  
  
across 3 different channels (email, text, LinkedIn, phone, Slack, etc.)  
  
I close it out. 
  
  
  
These may sound simple or obvious, but it took me years of agonizing.  
  
  
I wish more companies trained on this kind of practical, day-to-day stuff.  
  
The "basics" of sales are often not simple.  
  
Or obvious.
