content:
After working at 3 tech unicorns & 11 years in sales, I've finally learned to prep for calls in 5 minutes.  
  
Been tweaking this template for the last 4 years.  
  
It looks like:  
--> XX year old org  
--> # of employees  
--> % growth on LI / sales growing %  
--> RepVue: % attainment & Avg ARR  
--> Prior Ops? Result of Prior Op?  
--> Tech stack:  
--> Company News?  
--> Who will be On the call: (name/title)  
--> How long in Company/Role:  
  
  
Here's the specific WHY:  
  
--> XX year old org: The older the company, the slower they will make decisions (not always true...but almost always)  
  
--> # of employees: Points to the number of end users, but also probable growth stage  
  
--> % growth on LI & sales growing %: Companies experiencing double or triple-digit growth make faster decisions  
  
--> RepVue: % attainment & Avg ARR: If reps are doing poorly, this will impact morale, retention, hiring (ie the pain & motivation of DMs)  
  
--> Prior Ops? Result of Prior Op?: Have they talked to us before? How did it go?  
  
--> Tech stack: Do they invest heavily in tech? Do they use best of breed?  
  
--> Company News: May hold the biggest clues as to why they took the call  
  
--> Who will be On the call: (name/title) If they are Above the Line/ATL, I'll tailor my language to Impact on Risks & Market share. If Below the Line/BTL I'll speak more to Impact for the team / 'what goes away' for team  
  
--> How long in Company/Role: The shorter the time they've been there, the more likely they are to 1) still have budget 2) still be looking to make a big splash  
  
  
  
Here's the overarching WHY:  
--> Research makes 1st calls more impactful 
I know the basics so we can get to deeper things quicker  
  
--> Establishes how I want to run the call  
If growth & sales are down vs way up, those are different calls  
  
--> Sets the tone  
They know I come prepared. So much credibility to be earned by >>not<< asking prospects questions that could be answered by Google  
  
  
Creating repeatable systems in our sales motions not only makes us feel more prepared, it helps us win. 
 
Recent research says we increase win rates 8 to 12% when we use a repeatable process. 
 
And we're 48 to 66% more likely to hit quota.

-> Clarity for all - Gets everyone on the same page 
 
 
 
---> Why 
-> "Buyers Buy Backwards"* 
-> 65% of people are visual learners 
-> Brains process images 60,000 faster > text (3M corp) 
 
 
 
---> When 
-> After prospect asks for quotes 
-> Any meeting re: quotes/pricing 
-> Every time a milestone date shifts

-> Use a free template like the one below

content:
August is the time to reach out to opps where we lost to "No Budget."   
 
Here's why -  
 
October is budget planning season. 
 
A rough timeline (esp in tech)- 
   --> Oct / Plan next fiscal budget requests 
   --> Nov / Present requests to ELT 
   --> Dec / Budget is finalized 
   --> Jan / Spending begins  
 
 
Most orgs will need  *at least* 4-6 weeks to evaluate whether they want to ask for budget for new/replacement tech. 
 
(Reaching out in August goes even better if we got to a mid/late stage evaluation last time, as most of the work is already done.) 
 
 
 
Here's how this can sound: 
 
"Hey Alex, 
 
In April your team was dealing with  [problem I solve], and that was creating [negative impact]. When you looked at ways to fix that, it seemed like [1 of our differentiators] might be a good solution. Sounded like the budget was the biggest hurdle. 
 
Many of our customers have shared that they start budget planning in October.  
 
If your team wanted to take another look at a partnership, you might need some time leading up to budget planning time.  
 
Would another chat make sense this week ?" 
 
 
 
How do you like to re-engage past opportunities? 
 
How does timing play a role on when you re-engage?

content:
2 of the 3 tech unicorns I've worked at train their AEs on 2 core concepts that salespeople don't typically learn:  
  
  
--> Towards v. Away language  
--> Above the Line (ATL) v. Below the Line (BTL)  
  
  
1) Towards v. Away language  
  
-> 80% of people are motivated by moving Away from Pain (more people would run from a German Shepherd than towards a Gold medal*)  
  
-> But sales reps talk about Gain, aka moving Towards: "time back in your day" & ROI  
  
  
Here's how it sounds IRL at UserGems 💎  :  
  
-> Towards sounds like, "Because my product automatically finds champion job changes & promotions, your sales reps will save 29% of their time and you'll see a 12x ROI."  
  
-> Away sounds like, "What goes away [by using my product] is sales rep's spending hours on manual research, the low morale from not seeing results, and the frustration of your team missing their number. Again."  
  
  
->>>TL;DR = talk about what problems go away  
  
  
  
  
2) Above the Line (ATL) v. Below the Line (BTL)  
  
-> "The Line" is the 'power line', so Directors, VPs, CXOs = Above the Line  
  
-> BTL thinks about their team v. ATL thinks about market share & risk  
  
  
IRL / UserGems example:  
  
-> BTL value prop sounds like, "What goes away [with my product] is worrying about too little pipeline, missing quota & sales reps quitting."  
  
-> ATL value prop sounds like, "With [my product] you reduce 3 risks: Your top competitor doesn't get in the door first, you don't lose more market share, and you don't have to explain your inaction to investors."  
  
  
->>> TL;DR = choose the right language for your audience  
  
  
  
It takes time and effort to wrap our heads around these.  
  
But there's a reason the unicorns teach them. They win deals.  
  
Wanna try your hand at it? Write your Value Prop "Towards v. Away" language in the comments  
  
  
  
  
  
*ATL/BTL concepts from Skip Miller’s book Proactive Selling. Credit for "German Shepherds v. Gold Medals" comes from the book Secrets of Question-Based Selling by Thomas Freese

content:
If you're using the same questions for every Discovery call, here are 3 things that can make for a much better call.  
  
Here's a 3 step approach, and the last step is the most important:  
  
  
--> Know Before You Go  
--> Remember the Power Line  
--> Choose Your Own Adventure  
  
  
  
--> Know Before You Go  
  
In your pre-call prep, look for context / clues.  
  
How long have attendees been in their role?  
  
How long at the Company?  
  
--> New-to-Company folks: Want to make a splash  
  
--> In same role awhile: May be working on a promotion  
  
--> Long time in role/company: Job security concerns? New initiatives?  
  
  
  
--> Remember the Power Line  
  
ATL = Above the Line (Director + Above)  
  
BTL = Below the Line (Manager + Below)  
  
  
BTL cares about the impact on themselves + their team  
  
ATL cares about Risks, C-Level initiatives, market share, profitability/stock price  
  
  
  
--> Choose Your Own Adventure  
  
BTL questions sound like  
  
*"How does this compare to how your team works now?"  
  
*"How would you see your team using something like this?" 
  
*"To what extent would this impact Metrics your team is trying to hit?" 
  
  
  
ATL questions sound like  
  
*"How did this problem rank on your SKO Top Priorities slide?" 
  
*"What ripple effects is this problem creating across the business?" 
  
*"To what extent would solving the problem help with risks you see in the next 3-6 months?' 
  
  
  
Better questions = better meetings  
  
Better meetings = better opps  
  
Better opps = more wins

content:
Old-school VPs of Sales taught us to use phrases that are kinda gross🤮  
  
For everything from Discovery to Demos to Negotiating.  
  
Here's how to transform 2 cringe-y questions (so our prospects don't make this face):  
  
  
1) "What was your favorite feature during the demo?"  
  
*Why the phrasing is gross: it's manipulative  
  
It's either fishing for a compliment (weird). Or a cheap attempt at getting someone to "sell themselves"  
  
*What we mean: I only want to talk about stuff that matters to you.  
  
  
--> Better: "Where did we miss the mark for you on the demo?"  
  
*Why it's better: It's humble. It allows for the fact that we may have missed something important to them. It shows transparency = first step to trust.  
  
It's phrased as a negative - removing human's tendency to push back automatically when we're afraid we might get 'sold'.  
  
And on areas where we DID miss the mark - it's so much better to know early! Helps us pivot, prioritize, or part as friends.  
  
  
  
2) Any reason you wouldn't want to sign now- especially with an EOQ discount?  
  
*Why it's gross: it's disingenuous  
  
It's a close-ended question designed to get a quick confirmation.  
  
*What we really mean: Should I put this in commit?  
  
  
--> Better: "We talked about getting this started in Q3 so you could see results by Q4.  
  
In my experience, it'll be really hectic for you trying to get a signature from your execs at EOQ.  
  
Is EOQ really the best time?"  
  
  
*Why it's better: It's Buyer-centric. If a Q3 timeline is important, it helps them think through all the steps. And obstacles.  
  
Which helps us accurately forecast.  
  
Everyone wins.  
  
  
  
Gain clarity.  
  
Lose the ick.  
  
What other gross phrases should we re-frame?

content:
My career looks amazing... on paper  
  
  
-went from teaching to tech sales  
-worked my way to being a top rep  
-got hired + promoted at billion $ companies  
  
  
What many folks don't know is that I:  
  
- had to Google basic tech sales terms (ARR, ASP, MRR) for months in my first role  
- bombed a final interview for an AE job  
- only hit 30% of my quota one year  
  
  
Why do I tell you this?  
  
Because LinkedIn makes my career look amazing.  
  
And it definitely has been.  
  
BUT...  
  
  
What you can't see is all the sh*t that will never make the "highlight" reel.  
  
  
All the times that I :  
  
--> Struggled with the learning curve in a new role  
  
--> Became convinced that I forgot how to sell or just 'got lucky' in my past jobs  
  
--> Saw others who onboarded with me get better territories - which meant they did a lot less work & got much better results  
  
  
So if that's where you are, you're not alone.  
  
There is no such thing as an "easy" career in sales.  
  
I can't think of a single successful seller I know who had a simple path.  
  
  
If you're going through hell right now, just keep going. Don't panic.  
  
And don't compare your path to anyone else's.  
  
Take a deep breath. Keep moving forward.  
  
  
🤗🤗🤗

content:
Ever wonder why our deals take so effing long? After you hear this VP describe his last buying experience, you'll know. 
 
Here's what he said: 
 
 
"After I was 'sold' on a solution, it took over 9 months to earn approval for use within my organization. 
 
First, I had to get approval to access a tool we use internally to... request vendor approval. 
 
Then, I had to collect supporting documents and fill out extensive questionnaires to compile: 
 
- Risks 
- Benefits 
- Roll-out plan 
 
 
Getting through that allowed us to kick off internal reviews for security and legal. 
 
Those processes were… not fast. 
 
 
Months later, I had enough approvals to earn a project manager to help onboard the solution. 
 
That kicked off another few months of conversations. 
 
 
Throughout this process, there were many “exit points” where I could have just dropped the project and resumed focus on my core job. 
 
I didn’t abandon it for two reasons: 
 
- I’m confident the solution will make my org better 
 
- I’m highly motivated to make an impact for my team 
 
Selling is hard. Buying is even harder." 
*** 
 
This was a highly motivated, savvy buyer. And the deal still took 9 months. 
 
When the org has 30,000 employees  
 
or we don't have a strong champion 
 
or our buyers are less motivated  
 
...it can take MUCH longer. 
 
 
How are we thinking about maintaining the momentum in those deals?  
 
What kind of touches are we sending in between meetings?  
 
What else should we be doing? 
 
That's what we're covering in "3 Secrets of Deals that Don't Stall."

content:
Executives do not hate cold prospecting emails. 
 
They hate BAD cold prospecting emails. 
 
Check out 4 things Rory Evans did to close an outbound deal with a CEO - that started with cold email. 
  
𝙈𝙤𝙝𝙖𝙢𝙚𝙙 𝘾𝙝𝙖𝙝𝙞𝙣,𝘾𝙀𝙊 𝙤𝙛 𝙏𝙬𝙖𝙞𝙣 𝙬𝙖𝙨 𝙩𝙝𝙚 𝙗𝙪𝙮𝙚𝙧. 𝗛𝗲 𝙝𝙖𝙨 𝙩𝙝𝙞𝙨 𝙢𝙚𝙨𝙨𝙖𝙜𝙚 𝙛𝙤𝙧 𝙚𝙫𝙚𝙧𝙮𝙤𝙣𝙚 𝙙𝙤𝙞𝙣𝙜 𝙘𝙤𝙡𝙙 𝙤𝙪𝙩𝙗𝙤𝙪𝙣𝙙:  
  
"I BOUGHT. 
  
Here’s what Rory did right to close me... 
  
  
1️⃣ Initial message 
  
- No introduction 
- A short subject line 
- A soft but clear CTA 
- A relevant social proof 
- No surface-level personalization 
- One sentence describing his product 
- Lots of whitespace for mobile-friendly reading 
- A RELEVANT thought-provoking opening question 
  
Rory’s message didn’t get me hooked on talking to him, but it got me hooked to reply. 
  
Which is what you want. You want to qualify as fast as possible. 
  
I will never buy what’s irrelevant, but so often it’s a question of timing. 
  
So he got my reply with an indication on when timing might be better. 
  
  
2️⃣ Follow-up 
  
Rory’s follow-up message had GREAT timing. 
  
And he didn't stop there. He followed up. 
  
I could’ve easily missed that 1st message.   
My inbox is full. All the time. 
  
  
3️⃣ Ongoing chat 
  
I replied to the initial message because it was so good. 
  
I replied to the follow-up because the timing was right. 
  
It’s that simple. 
  
Next Rory did something I WISH more sellers would do: 
  
-> He answered my question instead of asking for my time. 
  
-> He answered my question in 8 minutes!!! 8 minutes, people. That’s the bar. 
  
I have yet to meet a successful executive who doesn’t value speed. 
  
  
4️⃣ Closing 
  
This part was the easiest for Rory. 
  
We were in the market, and we didn’t even bother to compare. 
  
You need to be aware of this concept: C-Level time is expensive. [I'm more concerned with time I waste than I am about the cheapest option.] 
  
The less time I have to invest, the more I’m willing to buy the “not cheapest” option. 
  
Again, because it’s so important, I did not compare prices!! 
  
  
This is the beauty of outbound. 
  
Before Rory reached out, I had never heard of his product. 
  
I was happy he showed me a solution I didn’t know existed.  
  
We closed fast because he made it easy for me. 
  
He saved me time. He follow up. He replied fast. 
  
Be like Rory."

My #1 cold calling tactic is "Insight They Would Pay to Hear" Opener.  
 
You want them to *forget* that it's a cold call. 
 
How? You lead with insights (value). 
 
Here's a talk track. 
 
-- 
 
[after permission based opener] 
 
"The reason I'm calling is that most of the VP Sales we work with tell us that Outbound gets harder every day. 5 years ago, it took 300 activities to book one outbound meeting. Today, it’s quadrupled to 1200 activities, according to Insight Partners. 
 
We help some of your competitors like  
________ and _____ use signals like champion job changes and warm customer referrals to be more strategic, intentional and efficient in creating new pipeline.  
 
And I'm wondering if you might be open to learning more when I'm not completely calling you out of the blue?" 
 
*** 
 
How do we know if we've got the right  valuable insight? 
 
We hear responses like: 
 
--> "I never thought about it like that."

content:
I just talked with a VP of Sales hiring for 3 open AE roles.  My jaw fell open when he told me what most candidates don't do.  
 
In under 1 minute, he told me 4 things that average sellers aren't doing when they apply. 
 
--> The good news is, you can do them all in under 15 minutes. 
 
 
Here's what he said about typical AE candidates: 
 
 
--> "They don't call or email me or my team." 
 
--> "They don't connect or message me on LinkedIn." 
 
--> "They don't ask any questions (aka no Discovery)." 
 
--> "They don't follow up on phone screenings, mentioning specific takeaways." 
 
 
 
But the candidates that stood out...Here's what they did instead: 
 
 
--> "She asked about my priorities.  I gave her all the answers!  I'm an open book." 
 
--> "She sent me a note after our screening call.  We only talked for 15 min, but she remembered 2 key points." 
 
--> "He called me to follow up.  He called my team to see what it was like working with me.  He had a POV on why he'd be a fit."** 
 
 
**important note here:  This candidate scored a 'maybe' on the sales skills assessment.  But this call earned him a 2nd interview. 
 
 
 
This sales leader received 347 resumes for 3 open roles. 
 
They did screening calls with 36 candidates. 
 
Only 3 AEs stood out. 
 
 
Sometimes we overthink.  And when we're under stress from needing to find a new job, we can let our best practices slip. 
 
The stand-out sellers treat the interview process like a sales cycle. 
 
When we remember that, and it's not hard to stand out.

4 of the best & simplest discovery questions for quantifying metrics were posted by David Rubinstein. 
 
Who's he? Just a leader who's been a Head of Sales at Meta. And a former Salesforce & Outreach VP. 
 
His method is so simple. So effective. 
 
 
Here it is: 
 
"This is the FASTEST and most efficient way to identify and quantify a problem using MATH.  
 
Metric 
Actual 
Target 
Holding back 
 
Here's the scenario: 
 
AE asks: "What are the key initiatives you are focussed on?" 
 
Prospect: 'We are laser-focused on our churn issue." 
 
AE responds: "Got it. Let me walk you through how we can help your churn problem." 
 
NOOOOOOOOOOOOOOOOOOOO 
 
 
 
Try these questions: 
 
1) What is the current churn metric you are focused on? Metric 
 
Prospect response: % of customers that leave the business 
 
 
2) What is your churn today? Actual 
 
Prospect response: We are at 20% 
 
 
3) What is your target? Target 
 
Prospect response: We are at 15% (size of problem) 
 
 
4) What's holding you back? Holding back 
 
Prospect's response will tell you: 
 
THIS is the problem the Prospect is trying to solve  
 
AND how you will assess whether it is big enough to matter."

content:
I’ve been onboarded at 3 billion-dollar tech giants.  And doing this 1 thing helped me more than anything I learned in onboarding sessions.  
 
Listing 10 impacts. 
 
 
Start with 1 problem your product solves. 
 
Then make a list of 10 impacts of not solving that problem. 
 
Here's an example of the list I made when I started at UserGems 💎  --> 
 
 
10 Impacts of Low Pipeline for a sales leader: 
->Missing quota 
->Career damage 
->Slow revenue growth 
->Increase Cost of Sale 
->Decreased Profitability 
->Not enough New Logos 
->Infighting with the Marketing team 
->High Customer Acquisition Cost (CAC) 
->Increased Pressure on Improving Close Rates 
->Low team morale leads to rep Churn & Recruiting issues 
 
 
 
How can you find these impacts? Here are 3 different ways: 
 
->Read your org's website & marketing materials 
 
->Read/listen like your Buyer: industry podcasts, websites & newsletters 
 
->Ask a top-performing AE ... after you've done your homework (i.e. found at least 4 yourself) 
 
 
Rinse & repeat til you've got 10 impacts for at least 3 problems your product solves. 
 
 
 
***Now when you hear one of the problems come up on a call, you can ask a question that gives you valuable info on your buyers' business AND gives you credibility.*** 
 
--->Example: 
“Sounds like the economy has taken a toll on your pipeline. How is that affecting your reps’ morale? How much concern is there about rep churn?” 
 
You've just shown you understand their world.

content:
Last Friday night a 7-year-old I’ve never met closed me on 2 deals in under 5 minutes. It was a consultative sale that started with a pattern interrupt.  
 
Then a compelling story and a valuable insight. 
 
Pretty much a sales MasterClass.  
 
 
Here’s what happened:  
 
Hadley and her 9 year old brother Harrison created a pattern interrupt when they didn’t just stand behind the table they’d set up to sell popcorn outside of Lowe’s.  
 
They came up to me and told me a story.  
 
 
Hadley & Harrison raved about how they just got back from Boy Scout camp.  
 
They had such a great time they were already out selling popcorn to raise money so they could go to camp again next year. 
 
Hadley was especially excited because now girls can go to camp, too.  (!!) 
 
 
They sucked me in with the story, so I told them I’d buy one bag. I asked which one they thought was the best.  
 
This is when Hadley piped up. “The white cheddar is the most popular... and it’s a good deal!“  
 
 
Note that she said this with complete confidence, even though the bags of popcorn were $15 each.  
 
Let’s give massive props to her for that right there. 
 
 
So not only did I buy one bag. I bought two.  
 
Because they: 
→ Created a pattern interrupt by walking up to me 
→ Told me a quick story with an emotional element 
→ Gave me an insight-> White Cheddar is the most popular! 
 
 
There’s so much power in those 3 things, no matter how old we are or how long we have been in sales.  
 
 
ps This was a super fast sale :)  B2B sales can feel like they drag on foreverrrrr.  Especially if they lose momentum. content:
After 4 years in Enterprise sales for 3 big SaaS companies, I've learned 5 ways to do Discovery BEFORE a first meeting with Executives: 
 
Here they are: 
 
 
 
--> Talk to their current team 
 
Look for them on LinkedIn Sales Nav.  
 
Filter to folks active on LinkedIn during the past 30 days.  
 
Send a short message about how your product helps them.  
 
Ask for their advice on how to approach the Exec. 50 words max. 
 
 
 -> Working this into Discovery sounds like: 
 
"After talking with 5 of your sales reps in the East, it sounds like AE-created pipeline is a big focus. What are the biggest risks you see to pipe build in the next 3-6 mos? 
 
 
 
 
--> Look at the Customer Stories on their Website 
 
What problems do they solve?  
 
Who is their customer? SMB? Enterprise? 
 
What do people mention... and NOT mention? 
 
 
 -> Working this into Discovery sounds like: 
 
"You've got some great logos. Amazing to see Gong, Salesloft & Drift all using your platform. What are the 2 biggest churn risks you're keeping an eye on next quarter? " 
 
 
 
 
--> RepVue / Glassdoor Reviews 
 
If you're in tech, check RepVue to see if folks are hitting quota. 
 
71% vs. 21% of the team hitting...different conversations  
 
On Glassdoor, you can filter reviews. 
 
Hit the drop-down to select the department you sell into. 
 
You can also use Ctrl F to search for specific words in reviews. 
 
 
 -> Working this into Discovery sounds like: 
"Some of my customers say that building pipeline has been tough these past few months. And that they're worried about reps leaving because of it.  Maybe your experience has been similar? How are you thinking about risks related to creating pipeline in the next 3 months? 
 
 
 
 
--> Look at sites where their Product is reviewed 
 
In tech, this could be G2, Capterra, Featured Customers, etc. 
 
Look for gaps related to your product (customer service, efficiency, integrations). 
 
 
 -> Working this into Discovery sounds like: 
"Looks like your customers love your functionality on G2. The only thing they disliked was not having enough time with their CSM each month. Is this one of the top 3 risks to customer retention you're focused on in the next 3 months?" 
 
 
 
 
--> Search on YouTube for any speeches, webinars, or Podcasts featuring the Exec. 
 
 -> Working this into Discovery sounds like: 
"You made a great point about sales & marketing alignment on Kevin Dorsey's podcast. How do lower lead conversion & deal velocity rank as risks you're talking about with your marketing team?" 
 
 
 
 
This type of prep surprises & impresses Execs. 
 
It immediately differentiates you. 
 
Preparation > product features.

content:
If I was starting a new sales role today, here are the 5 things I’d do in the first 5 days- 
 
 
1/ Find the accounts in my territory that are most likely to buy (aka the most like past buyers). 
 
I'd do this by creating a CRM report of 
Closed Won deals for the Past 2 years, with these details: 
 
 
- industry 
- location 
- age of company 
- $ ARR amount 
- # of employees 
- names/personas involved in the purchase 
 
THEN I'd create a report of Prospects with similarities in my territory/account list. 
 
^^This is the low hanging fruit. 
 
 
 
2/ I'd find 3-5 consistent top performers and ask them 3 simple questions: 
 
—-> Who are the best personas for us? 
--> Which are their 2-3 top business problems we solve (+vocabulary they use)? 
--> What's the # 1 thing to do/not do when just starting in this role? 
 
^^This is a shortcut for how to start off with a Bang...without trying to reinvent the wheel. 
 
 
 
3/ I'd immediately set up intro calls with internal folks like Finance/Deal desk, Legal, Product, Support, Solution Consulting, Channel partners, Systems Integrators, etc... anyone who I'll regularly interact with on deals. 
 
Start figuring out the best "Gives" for each person - do they like Starbucks, Slack shout outs, special beverages for EOQ/EOY? I'd put quarterly reminders on my calendar (and schedule quarterly deliveries where it makes sense). 
 
^^This is how we create our "tribe"/internal network within a company...rather than just being 'another seller who wants something'. 
 
 
 
4/ I'd memorize 5-8 customer stories. 
 
Starting with writing a 1 min summary on note cards - with the Champion's name/title, pain felt, problem solved & impact created. 
 
I'd practice telling these stories out loud every morning for 10 minutes...until I don't need the notecards anymore. Then I'd rinse/ repeat, memorizing 5 new stories. 
 
^^This is how we build confidence & credibility. 
 
 
 
5/ I'd analyze my boss’s personality - using tools like Humantic AI  - and I'd ask them about their top 2 career goals in our first 1:1 chat. 
 
^^This is how we manage up. 
 
 
 
Success in any sales rarely happens by accident. 
 
“The Separation is the Preparation.” 
 
What are the first things you do when starting a new sales role?
